rows.label: sec-appendix-a.3
rows.text: For any requested error $0<\eta<1/2$, the experiment of Section 5 applies to every $k$. Each of the $k$ blocks supplies its signs in one query, and after the final Walsh matrix the first position is measured with probability $p=\Phi^2$. On the promise, either $p\ge c=\delta^2$ or $p\le c/4$. Start each trial in fresh registers and repeat independently $$ \rho=\lceil16c^{-1}\ln(1/\eta)\rceil $$ times. Let $Z$ count how often the measured position is the first one, and return one if $Z\ge\rho c/2$ and zero otherwise. Standard Chernoff bounds give the following. | Promised case | Wrong decision | Tail bound used | | --- | --- | --- | | $p\ge c$ | $Z<\rho c/2$ | At most $\exp(-\rho c/8)$, hence at most $\exp(-\rho c/16)$. | | $p\le c/4$ | $Z\ge\rho c/2$ | At most $\exp(-\rho c/16)$, by the upper tail at $p=c/4$ and monotonicity. | Each error is at most $\eta$, and the cap is $k\rho=O_k(\log(1/\eta))$ on every input, where the subscript absorbs $c^{-1}=2^{10k}$. In a coherent comparison the trials run in separate registers on the same fixed input, and the resulting product state has the same joint outcome probabilities as independent measurements.

rows.label: sec-appendix-a.4
rows.text: The factors $1/\sqrt m$ from the initial and final copies of $u$ and the $k-1$ factors $1/\sqrt m$ from the Walsh matrices give $\Phi=N/2^{t(k+1)}$ for an integer $N$. Since $m=4^t$ and $\sqrt m=2^t$, the test $\Phi\ge2^{-5k}$ is equivalent to $2^{5k}N\ge2^{t(k+1)}$, and the small-value test is $2^{5k+1}|N|\le2^{t(k+1)}$. This is why the construction uses powers of four: the denominators become powers of two and both thresholds become integer comparisons. Words of $O(k\log m)$ bits suffice, including the threshold shifts. The [circuit construction](https://github.com/wcook04/quartic-query-lean/blob/v1.0.2/docs/reasoning_record.md#forr_circuit) gives the arithmetic and the gate count. **The small circuit.** The [explicit circuit for the four-column board](/library/quartic/reconstruction/#AC-example-tests) has $S=180$ non-input gates, so each candidate has $K=4+3+2(180+2)=371$ tests. (The reconstruction's board uses different address inputs, with $\Phi=\pm1/2$ instead of $\pm1$; the circuit computes the same promise and value on all eight-bit strings, so its counts apply to both examples.) In the circuit's zero-based numbering, write $x,y$ for input bits $6$ and $7$, the last two. Gates $1$ and $2$ compute $u=\neg x$, then $v=u\lor y$. On $a^+$ these two input bits are zero. To test gate $2$, read the recorded outputs $u$ and $v$ from the transcript and read $y$ from the address input itself. If $(u,y,v)=(1,0,0)$, the recorded $v$ is wrong, since $1\lor0=1$. Gate $178$ reports promise membership and gate $179$ the address digit. Every cell holds $6$ pointer bits and $360$ transcript bits, so with four cells in each of four columns the board has $4[4+16+4(6+360)]=5936$ input bits. **Why the choice of $L$ in Section 7.3 works.** For fixed $k$, Bansal and Sinha's lower bound for this one-sided promise is at least a positive constant depending on $k$ times $m^{1-1/k}/(\log_2(km))^{1-1/k}$ ([2021](#cite-BansalSinha2021), Theorem 1.3 and Corollary 1.4). Dividing by $m^{1-1/k}/(\log_2m)^2$ gives a factor of order $(\log m)^{1+1/k}$, which tends to infinity and absorbs the constant. **Input length.** A column contains $m$ string bits, $rkm$ address-input bits, and $2^r$ cells, each with $(m-1)\ell$ pointer bits and $rS$ transcript bits. The function therefore has $n=m\bigl[m+rkm+2^r((m-1)\ell+rS)\bigr]$ input bits, which is $O_k(m^{22}(\log m)^3)$ since $2^r=m^{20}$. Both query bounds concern this same $n$-bit function, with $m$ counting its columns.

rows.label: sec-appendix-b
sec-appendix-b.1
rows.text: Suppose one input $U$ is drawn from a distribution $\mu$, and $\beta$ bounds the probability of computing $P(U)$ with at most $L$ bit queries. Draw $r$ independent inputs $U_1,\ldots,U_r$ from $\mu$. A single algorithm may interleave its reads in any order, but must respect the limit $L$ on each input on every run. We prove that its chance of producing the whole word $(P(U_1),\ldots,P(U_r))$ is at most $\beta^r$. The algorithm may also use random coins and other data drawn jointly independently of the inputs. The separately capped model is due to Shaltiel, and we follow Drucker's conditional-probability argument ([Shaltiel 2003](#cite-Shaltiel2003); [Drucker 2012](#cite-Drucker2012), sec. 1.3 and Lemmas 3.1–3.2). Start with $P(x,y)=x\mathbin{\rm AND}y$, which equals one only on $11$. Give the four bit pairs equal probability and allow one query. If the first bit is zero, the answer is certainly zero; if it is one, the unread second bit is fair, so either guess succeeds with probability $1/2$. The best success is $(1+1/2)/2=3/4$. With two independent pairs and one read allowed from each, consider the first query, to the first pair. The best success still available for the second pair is $3/4$ in either case. After a zero reply the product of the two best probabilities is $1\cdot(3/4)$, and after a one reply it is $(1/2)(3/4)$. Their average is $9/16=(3/4)^2$. For general $P$, fix all the coins and other independent data, leaving a deterministic tree. Fix a history $\tau$ of queries and replies with positive probability, and for each input $U_h$ let $E_h(\tau)$ be the set of values consistent with its recorded bits. A tuple in $E_1(\tau)\times\cdots\times E_r(\tau)$ reproduces the first reply, hence the same second query and reply, and so on to the end of $\tau$; conversely every tuple producing that history lies in this product. So conditioning on the history leaves independent inputs with laws $\mu(\cdot\mid E_h(\tau))$. Write $V_h(\tau)$ for the best success on $U_h$ under this conditional law with its remaining queries, the original $L$ less the number already used on $U_h$. Suppose the next query reads $U_h$. Reading that bit and continuing optimally for each reply $b$ is one permissible strategy before the query, so $$ \sum_b\Pr(b\mid\tau) V_h(\tau b)\le V_h(\tau). $$ For every other input, the conditional law and the remaining allowance are the same before and after this query. Multiplying the inequality by the other $V$'s shows that the conditional expected product after one query is at most its current value. The initial product is at most $\beta^r$. At a leaf the tree outputs a fixed word $s$. By the independence just proved, the conditional probability that $s$ is correct is $\prod_h\Pr(P(U_h)=s_h\mid\tau)$, and each factor is at most $V_h(\tau)$ because guessing $s_h$ is an available strategy. Averaging over leaves (there are at most $rL$ reads per run) and then over the coins and other data proves the bound. Return to [the end of Section 7.3](#light-column-sum).

rows.label: sec-appendix-b.2
rows.text:
This example shows the bookkeeping of the predictor in Section 7.3: the decision tree's query count and the predictor's count of reads in the target strings advance separately. It says nothing about the hardness of Forrelation. To see both branches with only four input bits, replace Forrelation by parity, $a\oplus b$, which equals one when the two bits differ. The target column is column $2$, whose two address strings are the independent pairs $(a,b)$ and $(c,d)$ of fair bits, so its address is $(a\oplus b,c\oplus d)$. Allow the predictor one read in total from these four bits. It generates all other address strings and row bits itself and fills every cell with zeros. Write $B_{2,s}$ for the cell of column $2$ at label $s$, and $q$ for the predictor's count of target reads. | Query number | Tree names | Predictor action | | --- | --- | --- | | $1$ | Row $1$, column $1$ | Supply the generated bit, $q=0$. | | $2$ | $a$ | Read it, so $q=1$. | | $3$, if $a=1$ | Row $2$, column $3$ | Supply the generated bit, $q=1$. | | $3$, if $a=0$ | $c$ | Stop and output $00$ before reading $c$. | | $4$, if $a=1$ | First domain bit in $B_{2,10}$ | Output $10$ before this read. | On the $a=1$ branch, $10$ is correct exactly when $b=0$ and $c=d$, so this branch together with a correct label has probability $(1/2)(1/2)(1/2)=1/8$. On the $a=0$ branch the default $00$ is also correct when $b=0$ and $c=d$, contributing another $1/8$. The predictor therefore succeeds with probability $1/4$, whereas the probability that the tree stays within one target read and queries the true cell at time four is only $1/8$. The difference comes entirely from correct default guesses. For one fair pair, reading either bit leaves its parity uniformly random, so the product bound of Appendix B.1 is $(1/2)^2=1/4$. The [same four-query tree in the reconstruction](/library/quartic/reconstruction/#CL-simulator-example) numbers rows and columns from zero.
**Question 4 (two query counts).** In this example, change the $a=0$ branch so that query three names the first domain bit in $B_{2,00}$, and suppose the tree stops after that read. What is the probability that $a=0$ and this is the true cell? Including the $a=1$ branch, what is the probability that the tree queries the true cell at time three or four and uses at most one target read in the whole run? Repeat the latter calculation if the $a=0$ branch reads $c$ *after* the cell query. ([Answer](#answer-4).)

rows.label: sec-appendix-c
rows.text:
**Why balanced cheat sheets stop at a cube.** In the cheat-sheet construction ([Aaronson et al. 2016](#cite-ABK2016), sec. 3.1), each of the $n$ input bits of a partial function $g$ is replaced by the answer to its own AND–OR instance on $n^2$ bits, giving $n^3$ bits before certificates are added. In one instance, arrange the bits in $n$ rows of $n$ bits; its answer is $1$ exactly when every row contains a $1$. A $1$ is certified by the position of one $1$ in every row, and a $0$ by one row of zeros, so $n$ bit values suffice to verify each answer once their positions are given. Up to logarithmic factors, the composition and cheat-sheet argument then gives randomized lower bound $R(g)n^2$ and quantum upper bound $n$ when $Q(g)$ is polylogarithmic. Since $R(g)\le n$, this reaches at most a cubic separation. In OpenAI's construction an address input has about $m$ bits while the quantum search costs about $\sqrt m$, so the hardness of the partial function can contribute almost two powers of the quantum cost; the comparisons of Section 4 are what make the square-root search possible.

**Related search problems.** The search of Section 4 differs from quantum minimum finding, which uses an order ([Dürr and Høyer 1996](#cite-DH1996)), and from search with bounded-error tests for fixed Boolean answers ([Høyer et al. 2003](#cite-HMW2003)). Three comparisons can form a directed cycle, and the comparison model allows each of two columns to be returned with probability $1/2$, so declaring one outcome the correct one need not give success above $1/2$.

**Certificate complexity.** For a fixed input, its certificate size is the least number of bit positions one can specify so that every input agreeing there has the same value, and the certificate complexity is the largest such size. One might hope that a function with large certificate complexity automatically has large randomized query complexity. Ben-David and Kothari construct total functions whose randomized query complexity is smaller than their certificate complexity ([Ben-David and Kothari 2026](#cite-BDK2026), secs. 2–3), so the randomized lower bound here needs its own argument.

rows.label: sec-appendix-d
rows.text: **Projection check.** The Walsh sums for the second sign block are $(2,-2,-2,-2)$, and their dot product with the first sign block $(-1,-1,-1,-1)$ is $4$. So $\Phi=4/8=1/2$ and the probability is $\Phi^2=1/4$. **[Question 1](#question-1).** All four bits in column $2$ are ones, its three pointers lead to zeros, and its transcripts contain the correct gate outputs. The domain bits are $(0,1)$, so the first membership test fails at all four labels. The recorded value bits are $00$, so each digit $1$ in the label gives one more failure. The failure counts at $00,01,10,11$ are $1,2,2,3$. **[Question 2](#question-2).** On the fixed-arrow board the weights after pivot $2$ are $(1,0,0,1)$, and the probabilities of keeping each column against $4$ are $(1,0,1,0)$, leaving $(1,0,0,0)$. A single unamplified preparation succeeds with probability $q=1/4$, and every success returns column $1$, so $\theta=\pi/6$. One iteration gives $\sin^2(3\pi/6)=1$ and two give $\sin^2(5\pi/6)=1/4$. In the unequal-weight example the new weights are $(1,0,1/4,0)$. Dividing by four gives the probabilities of drawing and keeping each column, $(1/4,0,1/16,0)$, which add to $5/16$, so the conditional probabilities are $(4/5,0,1/5,0)$. **[Question 3](#question-3).** Each zero lies in a read position with probability $2/4$. With independent selection, the selected zero was read with probability $\mathbb EZ/4=1/2$. Under the second rule, reading at least one zero suffices, which has probability $1-(1/2)^4=15/16$ because the rows are fixed and the zeros independent. For adaptive queries the identity $\mathbb EZ/4$ still holds for independent $I$: once the run on the first board is fixed, exactly $Z$ of the four choices of $I$ select a discovered zero. **[Question 4](#question-4).** The label $00$ in the third query is the true address when $a=0,b=0,c=d$, with probability $(1/2)(1/2)(1/2)=1/8$, and if the tree stops then, it used one target read. The other branch gives a true-cell query at time four within the same allowance when $a=1,b=0,c=d$, also with probability $1/8$. The events are disjoint, so their union has probability $1/4$. If $c$ is read afterwards, the $a=0$ branch makes two target reads; the cell query still happened, but the run exceeds the allowance. Only the $a=1$ event counts, with probability $1/8$. **[Question 5](#question-5).** At $k=4$ the exponent $4-2/k$ is $3.5$, so the ratio (8.1) diverges for every $\alpha<3.5$. At $\alpha=3.5$ the power $2-1/k-\alpha/2$ of $m$ is zero, leaving a reciprocal power of $\log m$. Choosing $k=5$ gives $2-1/5-3.5/2=1/20>0$, which excludes the power $3.5$. **[Question 6](#question-6).** With the winner's correct cell, its pointer names a zero in the other column. Every pointer in the other direction, from any cell of the other column, names a row of the winner's column string, which is all ones. So exactly one of the two bits read is zero, and the comparison returns the winner. The other column's estimated address only decides which of its cells is read, and every choice reads a one. **Combined explanation.** When the winner's own address is estimated correctly, its pointer names a zero in the other column, and every pointer in the reverse direction names a one, so the comparison returns the winner. After $T$ pivots other than the winner, its weight is still at least $(1-\varepsilon)^T\ge1-T\varepsilon>1/2$, while the expected total weight of the ideal procedure is at most $m/2^T$; this bounds the probability of missing it. Before it is listed, the sampler's acceptance probability is at least $1/(2m)$ and it fails to find a pivot with probability at most $\varepsilon$ per stage. Once listed, a column cannot be removed. In the classical simulation, stop at the cell query and output its label, or stop earlier with a default if another target read would exceed $L$; a query to the true cell of a light column is then a correct prediction. For $G\le c\,mL$ the three terms of (7.1) are at most $4cL/m$, $c$ and $c\,mL\,m^{-10}$, and since $L\le m$ they sum to at most $4c+c+c/m^8$. The constructed functions exclude every exponent below four, and the universal deterministic bound of Aaronson, Ben-David, Kothari, Rao and Tal gives the inequality at exponent four.

rows.label: sec-appendix-e
rows.text: The Boolean query bound uses one property of the quantum sampler: conditional on success, the measured column number has the law (4.1), and the listed candidates are then verified. Lean proves this measured-label law and uses it in the formal proof of the headline theorem. The [full amplification proof](/library/quartic/reconstruction/#upper-returned-register) in the reconstruction proves a stronger statement in ordinary mathematics: it identifies the normalized successful state in a designated output register, including the preparation's original workspace, with records of earlier trials in additional registers. Equality of measured-label laws alone does not identify this state. Lean proves a retained-factor identity when success is specified by a set of basis labels; the full statement for an arbitrary fixed success projector, including identification of the output subsystem after compilation and uncomputation, is not yet fully formalized. The [theorem index](https://github.com/wcook04/quartic-query-lean/blob/v1.0.2/docs/proof_index.md#src-amplification) gives the scope of these results. The [theorem index](https://github.com/wcook04/quartic-query-lean/blob/v1.0.2/docs/proof_index.md) connects the other statements of this paper to their Lean definitions and proofs. For example, the [winning condition](https://github.com/wcook04/quartic-query-lean/blob/v1.0.2/docs/proof_index.md#def-wins) requires every address input of a winning column to lie in the promise, which is condition 2 of Section 2.2 and excludes column $2$ in the [example of Section 6](#domain-bit-board). The [family theorem](https://github.com/wcook04/quartic-query-lean/blob/v1.0.2/docs/proof_index.md#thm-headline) uses one circuit for both query bounds. The [optimal-exponent theorem](https://github.com/wcook04/quartic-query-lean/blob/v1.0.2/docs/proof_index.md#thm-alpha) combines the constructed family with a formal proof of the universal quartic bound. For the classical bound, Lean proves that the difference between the probabilities that the algorithm outputs $1$ on the two boards is at most the right side of (7.1). This difference is at most the probability in (7.1) that the two runs differ, and the contradiction in Section 7.4 needs only the difference.

rows.text:
# Reconstructing OpenAI’s nearly quartic query separation

*Comparing candidates and predicting a hidden address*

Written by AI systems under the direction of Will Cook · November 2026

**Abstract.** OpenAI recently showed that for every fixed integer $k\ge2$ there are total Boolean functions $F_{k,m}$ with $Q(F_{k,m})=\widetilde O_k(\sqrt m)$ and $R(F_{k,m})=\widetilde\Omega_k(m^{2-1/k})$, so that for every $\alpha<4$ some total function has $R(f)\ge Q(f)^\alpha$ ([OpenAI 2026](#cite-OpenAI2026)). Together with the bound $R(f)=O(Q(f)^4)$ of Aaronson, Ben-David, Kothari, Rao and Tal, this shows that the critical exponent of randomized relative to quantum query complexity is four, and it refutes their conjecture that $R(f)=O(Q(f)^3)$ for all total functions. The construction places pointer certificates in cells addressed by answers to $k$-fold Forrelation instances. In this companion we derive the sampling rule of OpenAI's quantum tournament, whose comparisons may have arbitrary outcome probabilities, by requiring every pairwise bias to cancel; and we base the randomized lower bound on the observation that a query to a hidden cell names the cell's address before any answer is returned.



**About this paper.** The separation theorem, its construction and its proof are OpenAI's ([OpenAI 2026](#cite-OpenAI2026)). AI systems wrote this paper, its two companion texts and a Lean development of the theorem, under the direction of Will Cook. No human expert has reviewed them, and the correspondence between the Lean statements and OpenAI's paper has been compared by AI agents only. Section 7 lists the results of the reconstruction that go beyond OpenAI's paper, and Section 8 says what the Lean development checks.

rows.label: sec-1
rows.text: In the query model an algorithm computes a function $f\colon\{0,1\}^N\to\{0,1\}$ by reading input bits, and we charge one unit for each bit it reads. We write $R(f)$ and $Q(f)$ for the bounded-error randomized and quantum query complexities of $f$. For total functions these measures are polynomially related, and the natural question is how large the largest polynomial gap can be. Following Aaronson, Ben-David and Kothari ([Aaronson et al. 2016](#cite-ABK2016), sec. 2.3), the *critical exponent* of $R$ relative to $Q$ is the infimum of the exponents $r$ such that $R(f)=O(Q(f)^r)$ holds for all total $f$. Grover's algorithm ([Grover 1996](#cite-Grover1996)) gives a quadratic gap for the OR function, and for many years this was believed to be the largest gap for total functions. Aaronson, Ben-David and Kothari ([Aaronson et al. 2016](#cite-ABK2016)) refuted this with the cheat-sheet technique and a power $2.5$ separation, up to logarithmic factors. Improvements in the underlying partial-function separations then gave power $8/3-o(1)$ by Tal ([Tal 2020](#cite-Tal2020)), and power $3-o(1)$ by Bansal and Sinha ([Bansal and Sinha 2021](#cite-BansalSinha2021)) and, independently, Sherstov, Storozhenko and Wu ([Sherstov et al. 2023](#cite-SSW2023)). On the other side, Aaronson, Ben-David, Kothari, Rao and Tal ([Aaronson et al. 2021](#cite-ABKRT2021)) used Huang's sensitivity theorem ([Huang 2019](#cite-Huang2019)) to prove $D(f)=O(Q(f)^4)$, and conjectured that $R(f)=O(Q(f)^3)$ ([Aaronson et al. 2021](#cite-ABKRT2021), Conjecture 2). OpenAI's theorem closes the gap between these exponents. \Needspace{12\baselineskip} **Theorem 1** (OpenAI ([OpenAI 2026](#cite-OpenAI2026), Theorem 1.1)). *For every total Boolean function $f$, $R(f)=O((1+Q(f))^4)$. For each fixed integer $k\ge2$ there are positive constants $c_k$, $C_k$ and $b_k$ and total Boolean functions $F_{k,m}$, defined for powers of four $m$, such that for all sufficiently large $m$, with $\ell=\log_2m$,* $$ Q(F_{k,m})\le C_k\sqrt m\,\ell^{b_k}, \qquad R(F_{k,m})\ge c_k\,\frac{m^{2-1/k}}{\ell^2}. \tag{1} $$ *Consequently the critical exponent of $R$ relative to $Q$ is four.* The first statement is the theorem of Aaronson, Ben-David, Kothari, Rao and Tal, which OpenAI reproves for completeness; the new content is the family $F_{k,m}$, which satisfies both bounds in (1) for the same function. The proof gives $b_k=6$ and the finite form $R(F_{k,m})>\lfloor mL/100\rfloor$ of OpenAI's Proposition 4.2, with $L=\lfloor m^{1-1/k}/\ell^2\rfloor$, from which Section 6 derives $c_k=1/400$. The Lean theorem for Theorem 1 states this finite form, with both bounds beyond a threshold; Section 8 lists which formal statement carries which form. In powers of $Q$ the family gives $R=\widetilde\Omega(Q^{4-2/k})$, so already $k=3$ gives power $10/3$ and refutes the cubic conjecture, and larger fixed $k$ approach four. ### 1.1 Overview of techniques The input consists of $m$ *columns*. Column $i$ holds an $m$-bit string $X_i$, a few address inputs, and an array of cells. The function asks whether some column *wins*: its string is all ones, and its cell at the address computed from its address inputs contains a correct certificate pointing to a zero in every other string. At most one column can win. Pointers from a column to zeros in other columns go back to the pointer functions of Göös, Pitassi and Watson ([Göös et al. 2018](#cite-GPW2018)) and of Ambainis et al. ([Ambainis et al. 2017](#cite-ABBLSS2017)), and cells addressed by answers to partial-function instances to the cheat sheets of ([Aaronson et al. 2016](#cite-ABK2016)). *The cost of plain search.* Checking that a given column wins costs about $\sqrt m$ quantum queries, by Grover search over its roughly $m$ local tests. One way to find a winner would be to search over the $m$ columns with this check inside the search. But then the costs multiply to $\sqrt m\cdot\sqrt m=m$, the cost of balanced AND–OR cheat sheets built from the same partial function, whose bounds $\widetilde O(m)$ and $\widetilde\Omega(m^{3-1/k})$ give power $3-1/k$ ([Aaronson et al. 2016](#cite-ABK2016), sec. 3). The new construction instead lists a few candidates with cheap comparisons and verifies only those, so the two costs add to $\widetilde O_k(\sqrt m)$. The classical bound drops to $m^{2-1/k}$, and in powers of $\sqrt m$ the exponent rises from $3-1/k$ to $4-2/k$. *Why the pointers point outward.* The winner's certificate stores, for every other column, the row of a zero in that column's string. A comparison between two columns reads one pointer in each direction. If the winner's address is decoded correctly, its pointer finds a zero in the rival, while no rival pointer can find a zero in the winner's all-one string. So the winner is selected with high probability even when the rival's address inputs violate their promise. *Comparisons with arbitrary outcome probabilities.* A loser's address may be undefined, and its decoder can then return any distribution over addresses. So the probability that one loser beats another can lie anywhere in $[0,1]$, with no gap from $1/2$, and majority voting cannot turn these comparisons into the fixed tournament that quantum minimum finding ([Dürr and Høyer 1996](#cite-DH1996)) or king finding ([Mande et al. 2023](#cite-MPS2023)) would need. OpenAI's tournament instead samples pivots with weights equal to the probability of beating all earlier pivots; Section 4 derives this rule from the requirement that every pairwise bias cancel. *The classical bound.* The hard distributions differ only in one hidden zero and one cell of a uniformly random column. A decision tree notices the difference only if it finds that zero, invests many queries in that column's address inputs, or queries the correct cell while investing few. The last event is a correct prediction of $r$ independent hard values, because the index of a cell query already names its address; a direct-product theorem with per-input caps bounds it, and a capped simulation avoids conditioning on which columns the tree investigates. Ben-David and Kothari ([Ben-David and Kothari 2026](#cite-BDK2026)) and Ambainis, Iraids and Kokainis ([Ambainis et al. 2026](#cite-AIK2026)) also compare candidate witnesses, in separations of certificate complexity from randomized and quantum query complexity. *Organization.* Section 2 fixes conventions and the address function, Section 3 defines $F_{k,m}$, Sections 4 to 6 prove the two bounds and the exponent, Section 7 describes further results of the reconstruction and Section 8 the Lean development. The [worked exposition](/library/quartic/exposition/) develops the argument through small examples, and the [full proof reconstruction](/library/quartic/reconstruction/) gives every supporting derivation.

rows.label: sec-2
rows.text:
All query bounds are worst-case: an algorithm with query cap $q$ makes at most $q$ queries on every input and every branch of its randomness or measurements, and computation between queries is free. For a partial function the cap applies on every input, and the error bound only on the promise. We write $R_\varepsilon$ and $Q_\varepsilon$ for error at most $\varepsilon$ and $R=R_{1/3}$, $Q=Q_{1/3}$. The quantum algorithm has a standard bit oracle: an access into the arrays below computes the global bit index reversibly from the column, cell and wire labels, and reads a pointer of $\ell$ bits one bit at a time. We write $[m]=\{1,\ldots,m\}$, use logarithms to base two, and let constants depend on the fixed integer $k$, as in $O_k(\cdot)$.

We require a partial function $P$ with a low-query quantum algorithm on its promise, a nearly linear exact circuit for checking its domain and value, and high randomized query complexity. Each property has one job in the construction.

| Property of $P$ | What it buys |
|---|---|
| Cheap quantum decoding on the promise | cheap address decoding, hence cheap comparisons |
| An exact circuit of size $\widetilde O_k(m)$ for the domain bit and the value | cheap checking of a proposed address, including promise membership |
| $R(P)>L$ with $L$ close to $m^{1-1/k}$ | an address that is hard to compute classically |

The Walsh–Hadamard form of $k$-fold Forrelation, introduced by Aaronson and Ambainis ([Aaronson and Ambainis 2018](#cite-AA2018)), supplies all three. An input is $k$ blocks of $m$ bits; if $x_j(a)$ is the bit at coordinate $a$ of block $j$, we read it as the sign $z_j(a)=(-1)^{x_j(a)}$, so a sign query is a bit query. Let $H$ be the normalized Walsh–Hadamard matrix of order $m$, $u=m^{-1/2}(1,\ldots,1)^{\mathsf T}$ and $D_z$ the diagonal matrix of a sign vector, and put
$$
 \Phi=u^{\mathsf T}D_{z_1}H D_{z_2}H\cdots H D_{z_k}u,\qquad \delta=2^{-5k}.
$$
Set $P=1$ when $\Phi\ge\delta$, $P=0$ when $|\Phi|\le\delta/2$, and leave $P$ undefined elsewhere. Applying the unitary product to $u$ and projecting onto $u$ succeeds with probability $\Phi^2$; for fixed $k$ the two promised cases have a constant gap, and repetition with all trial registers retained gives the decoder. The projection probability depends only on $|\Phi|$, whereas an input with $\Phi\le-\delta$ lies outside the promise, so the decoder alone cannot certify an answer. For the exact circuit we compute the signed numerator of $\Phi$ by $k-1$ unnormalized fast Walsh–Hadamard transforms on integers of $O_k(\ell)$ bits and test the two defining inequalities after clearing denominators. The denominator is $m(\sqrt m)^{k-1}$, which is an integer when $m$ is a power of four; this is why $m$ ranges over powers of four.

**Lemma 2** (OpenAI ([OpenAI 2026](#cite-OpenAI2026), Lemma 2.1)). *Fix $k\ge2$. For all sufficiently large powers of four $m$,*
$$
 L:=\left\lfloor m^{1-1/k}/\ell^2\right\rfloor < R(P).
\tag{3}
$$
*For every $0<\eta<1/2$ a reversible quantum algorithm with $O_k(1+\log(1/\eta))$ queries on every input computes $P$ with error at most $\eta$ on its domain. There is an exact fan-in-two circuit with $S=O_k(m\ell^2)$ gates whose two outputs are the domain bit of $P$ and, on the domain, its value.*

OpenAI imports (3) from the lower bound of Bansal and Sinha ([Bansal and Sinha 2021](#cite-BansalSinha2021), Corollary 1.4). The Lean development and the full reconstruction prove (3) directly, by a different route described in Section 7.

rows.label: sec-3
rows.text:
Fix $k\ge2$ and a power of four $m$, and put $r=20\ell$. The input of $F_{k,m}$ consists of the following bits for each column $i\in[m]$; every bit is part of the input, so a cell is an arbitrary bit string and no part of the input is trusted.

- The *string* $X_i\in\{0,1\}^m$. An all-one string protects a genuine winner: no pointer can find a zero in it.
- The *address inputs* $A_{i,1},\ldots,A_{i,r}$, each an input to $P$. When their values are all defined they form the *true address* $s_i=(P(A_{i,1}),\ldots,P(A_{i,r}))$. Computing it is cheap quantumly and hard classically.
- The *cells* $B_{i,s}$, one for each $s\in\{0,1\}^r$, so $2^r=m^{20}$ cells. A cell contains one $\ell$-bit row pointer $p_{i,s,j}$ for each column $j\ne i$, and for each $h\le r$ a proposed *transcript*: one bit per non-input gate of the circuit of Lemma 2 evaluated on $A_{i,h}$. Since $m=2^\ell$, every pointer word names a row.

The input length is $m\bigl(m+rkm+2^r((m-1)\ell+rS)\bigr)=O_k(m^{22}\ell^3)$, so logarithms of the input length are $O_k(\ell)$.

Column $i$ **wins** if $X_i=1^m$, all its address inputs belong to the domain of $P$, and its cell at the true address is correct. Precisely, column $i$ wins if the following four conditions hold.

1. $X_i=1^m$ (the string is all ones).
2. Each $A_{i,h}$ lies in the domain of $P$ (the true address $s_i$ is defined).
3. Each transcript in $B_{i,s_i}$ equals the true evaluation of the circuit on $A_{i,h}$ (the cell certifies the address).
4. $X_j[p_{i,s_i,j}]=0$ for every $j\ne i$ (the cell points to a zero in every other string).

We set $F_{k,m}=1$ if some column wins and $F_{k,m}=0$ otherwise; this defines $F_{k,m}$ on every input, including inputs whose address inputs violate the promise. Two distinct columns cannot both win, since the pointer from one would have to name a zero in the other's all-one string.

To verify column $i$ at a proposed address $s$, we use exact local tests. We check that $X_i[a]=1$ for every row $a$, that $X_j[p_{i,s,j}]=0$ for every $j\ne i$, and, in the transcript for each $A_{i,h}$, that each gate bit agrees with the gate applied to its inputs and that the two output bits equal $(1,s_h)$. By induction in circuit order, a transcript consistent at every gate equals the true evaluation. So a false transcript disagrees at some gate, and a true transcript for an off-promise input or a wrong address bit disagrees at an output. Consequently, for a column that does not win, some test fails at *every* address. There are
$$
 K=m+(m-1)+r(S+2)
\tag{2}
$$
tests, so $K=O_k(m\ell^3)$. Checking a gate costs at most three queries, and following a pointer costs $\ell+1$.

The construction thus supplies two interfaces, and the rest of the proof uses only these.

| Operation | Guarantee used |
|---|---|
| Comparison of two columns | a winner beats every rival with high probability; comparisons between losers may behave arbitrarily |
| Verification at a measured address | every column that does not win fails some exact test at every address |

\Needspace{16\baselineskip}

![A comparison between the winner $i^\star$ and a rival $j$. Decoding the address inputs of $i^\star$ selects its cell $B_{i^\star,s_{i^\star}}$, whose pointer into $X_j$ stores row 6, and $X_j[6]=0$. The rival's cell $B_{j,t}$, at any decoded address $t$, can only point to a one in $X_{i^\star}=1^m$. The comparison therefore selects $i^\star$.](figures/expert_column.svg)

rows.label: sec-4
rows.text: ### 4.1 Comparing two columns For $i\ne j$, decode addresses $s$ for $i$ and $t$ for $j$, each in its own workspace. Read $X_j[p_{i,s,j}]$ and $X_i[p_{j,t,i}]$. If exactly one of these bits is zero, select the column whose pointer found that zero; otherwise select the smaller index. A self-comparison selects neither column and reads no pointer. Suppose $i=i^\star$ is the winning column. If the algorithm decodes its address correctly, it reads a zero in $X_j$ and a one in $X_{i^\star}=1^m$, so it selects $i^\star$ whatever address it decodes for $j$, and even when no address of $j$ is defined. Write $\varepsilon$ for the allowed error in decoding a whole address on promised inputs, and use error $\varepsilon/r$ for each of its $r$ bits. We order each unordered pair canonically and run a single comparison experiment, with both decoded addresses retained; asking whether $i$ beat $j$ or $j$ beat $i$ reads the same measured outcome. Writing $a_{ij}$ for the probability that this experiment selects $i$, and $a_{ii}=0$ for the self-comparison, we have $$ a_{ij}+a_{ji}=1\quad(i\ne j),\qquad a_{ii}=0. \tag{4} $$ The winner is *dominant*: $a_{i^\star j}\ge1-\varepsilon$ for every $j\ne i^\star$. One comparison, or its inverse, uses $c=O_k(r\log(r/\varepsilon)+\ell)$ queries. ### 4.2 A tournament for probabilistic comparisons **Proposition 3** (OpenAI ([OpenAI 2026](#cite-OpenAI2026), Proposition 3.2)). *Let $T=\lceil\log(1000m)\rceil$ and $\varepsilon=1/(1000T)$. Suppose a reversible comparison circuit, controlled by two candidate indices, uses at most $c$ queries and satisfies (4). There is a quantum algorithm making $O(c\sqrt m\,T^2\log T)$ queries on every branch and returning a list of at most $T$ candidates such that, if $a_{i^\star j}\ge1-\varepsilon$ for all $j\ne i^\star$, the list contains $i^\star$ with probability at least $1-2m2^{-T}-T\varepsilon$.* The algorithm samples a sequence of indices, called *pivots*, and returns them as its list. We first describe an ideal sampling process in which the comparison probabilities are known, and then implement it without knowing them. For deterministic comparisons one can retain the candidates selected over every previous pivot and draw uniformly from this set ([Ambainis et al. 2026](#cite-AIK2026), sec. 6.1). With probabilistic comparisons we weight each candidate by the probability of being selected over every previous pivot in fresh, independent comparisons. After pivots $\rho_1,\ldots,\rho_n$, the individual and total weights are $$ w_i=\prod_{h=1}^n a_{i\rho_h},\qquad W=\sum_i w_i. $$ Initially all weights are one. After drawing $j$, replace each $w_i$ by $w_i a_{ij}$, so the new weight of $j$ is zero. Suppose the probability of drawing $j$ is $q_j$. The contribution of an unordered pair $i,j$ to the expected remaining weight is $w_i q_j a_{ij}+w_j q_i a_{ji}$. With uniform sampling the two coefficients can differ, and the adversarial biases between losers could keep the remaining weight high. To cancel the bias of every pair we impose $w_i q_j=w_j q_i$; by (4) the contribution is then $w_iq_j$, whatever $a_{ij}$ is. Drawing $j$ with probability $w_j/W$ satisfies this for every pair, and summing over pairs gives, for $W>0$, $$ \sum_j\frac{w_j}{W}\sum_i w_i a_{ij} =\frac{W^2-\sum_i w_i^2}{2W}. \tag{5} $$ For $W>0$, the nonnegative sum of squares in (5) gives the bound $\mathbb E[W_{\rm new}\mid w]\le W/2$. Equivalently, draw two independent indices from the weights: the ordered pairs $(i,j)$ and $(j,i)$ have equal probability, their selection probabilities sum to one when $i\ne j$, and the diagonal contributes nothing. In the ideal process we stop if $W=0$. After $T$ steps the expected total weight is at most $m2^{-T}$. If the winner is still unlisted, its weight is at least $(1-\varepsilon)^T\ge1-T\varepsilon>1/2$. This single inequality does two jobs. First, by Markov's inequality, the probability that the winner remains unlisted is at most $2m2^{-T}$. Second, while the winner is unlisted the total weight exceeds $1/2$, which keeps the sampling step below affordable. The weights are quantities of the analysis; the algorithm never estimates or stores them. The quantum algorithm has only the reversible comparison circuit and the list of pivots drawn so far. To draw its next pivot, it prepares a uniform superposition of indices $i$ and compares $i$ with every listed pivot in fresh workspaces, coherently controlled by $i$. If $|\phi(i,\rho_b)\rangle$ is the entire state of one comparison, the preparation produces $$ \frac1{\sqrt m}\sum_i |i\rangle\bigotimes_{b=1}^n |\phi(i,\rho_b)\rangle. $$ Set a flag if every comparison selects $i$. For a fixed $i$ the comparison states form a tensor product, so the joint success probability is the product $w_i$, and states with distinct labels are orthogonal. Consequently $$ \Pr[i\text{ and flag}]=\frac{w_i}{m},\qquad \Pr[\text{flag}]=\frac Wm,\qquad \Pr[i\mid\text{flag}]=\frac{w_i}{W}. \tag{6} $$ The flagged branch therefore samples the next pivot from the ideal law, without the algorithm knowing any $a_{ij}$. It remains to make the flag likely without disturbing this law. **Lemma 4** (bounded amplification ([OpenAI 2026](#cite-OpenAI2026), Lemma 3.1); see @BBHT1998 and @BHMT2002). *Let $A$ prepare a state with a success flag, with success probability $p$. For $0<\gamma\le1/2$ and $0<\eta<1/2$ there is a procedure making $O(\gamma^{-1/2}\log(1/\eta))$ calls to $A$ and $A^{-1}$ on every branch, for every $p$, that either reports failure or produces a successful outcome. Conditional on success, the measured label has the same distribution as in the successful part of $A$'s state. If $p\ge\gamma$ it fails with probability at most $\eta$, and if $p=0$ it always fails.* The label law is preserved because each Grover iteration rotates within the plane spanned by the successful and unsuccessful components of $A$'s state, and so leaves the direction of the successful component unchanged. The [full reconstruction](/library/quartic/reconstruction/#upper-amplification-statement) gives the schedule and its proof. We apply Lemma 4 with $\gamma=1/(2m)$ and $\eta=\varepsilon$. Before the winner is listed the flag probability $W/m$ exceeds $1/(2m)$, so each stage fails with probability at most $\varepsilon$ and otherwise appends a pivot drawn exactly from the ideal law. We stop on failure or after $T$ stages. Once the winner is listed, later stopping cannot remove it, so the behaviour of the sampler afterwards is irrelevant. Coupling the algorithm with the ideal process at each history before the winner is listed gives $$ \Pr[i^\star\text{ absent from the list}]\le 2m2^{-T}+T\varepsilon. \tag{7} $$ Each stage rebuilds at most $T$ comparisons per call to the preparation, so the $T$ stages cost $O(c\sqrt m\,T^2\log T)$ queries on every input. This proves Proposition 3. ### 4.3 Verifying the listed columns For each listed column, decode a fresh address with error at most $\varepsilon$ on promised inputs and measure it. At this fixed address $s$, a uniformly chosen test of the $K$ tests in (2) fails with probability zero if all tests pass and at least $1/K$ otherwise. Lemma 4 with $\gamma=1/K$ and $\eta=\varepsilon$ searches for a failed test with $O(\ell\sqrt K\log(1/\varepsilon))$ queries. Accept the column if no failed test is found. The search is one-sided: exact testing cannot report a failure when all tests pass, so a winner whose address was decoded correctly is always accepted. A column that does not win has a failed test at every address, and is accepted with probability at most $\varepsilon$. On a one-input the algorithm accepts unless the winner is missing from the list or its address is decoded wrongly, so it errs with probability at most (7) plus $\varepsilon$. On a zero-input the comparisons may list columns with false transcripts, since a comparison never reads a transcript; but each listed column is accepted with probability at most $\varepsilon$, so the error is at most $T\varepsilon$. Both errors are below $1/3$. With $T=O(\ell)$, $c=O_k(\ell\log\ell)$ and $K=O_k(m\ell^3)$, the tournament costs $O_k(\sqrt m\,\ell^3\log^2\ell)$ and checking the list $O(T(c+\ell\sqrt K\log T))=O_k(\sqrt m\,\ell^{7/2}\log\ell)$. Both are at most $C_k\sqrt m\,\ell^6$, the bound in (1) with a generous $b_k=6$.

rows.label: sec-5
rows.text: ### 5.1 The hard distribution By Yao's principle it suffices to give two input distributions, one supported on zero-inputs and one on one-inputs, that every deterministic decision tree of depth $G=\lfloor mL/100\rfloor$ distinguishes with advantage less than $1/3$. We will show that the advantage is at most $$ \underbrace{\frac{4G}{m^2}}_{\text{find the erased zero}} +\underbrace{\frac{G}{mL}}_{\text{invest heavily in the planted column}} +\underbrace{G\beta^r}_{\text{query its cell while light}}, $$ with $\beta=2/3$; the three terms are proved in Sections 5.2 and 5.3. For the **dummy input** $Y^{(0)}$, choose the row $J_i$ of the sole zero in $X_i$ independently and uniformly in each column. Draw the address inputs independently of one another and of the zero positions, using a common law $\mu$ on the promise of $P$ chosen below. Set every cell bit to zero. Every column loses. Choose $I$ uniformly and independently of the entire dummy input. For the **planted input** $Y^{(1)}$, set $X_I[J_I]=1$, and in $B_{I,s_I}$ write the gate bits of all $r$ correct circuit evaluations and the row numbers $J_j$ for $j\ne I$. Column $I$ wins. Because the dummy cells are blank, querying them reveals nothing about which cell is correctly addressed. And because the entire dummy input, hence the tree's entire run on it, is independent of $I$, the tree's investment in the planted column is an average over columns. This independence is what gains the factor $m$ in the lower bound. \Needspace{17\baselineskip} ![The coupled inputs with $I=3$. Each horizontal row depicts one column of the construction: its string $X_i$, its address inputs and its cells. All dummy cells are zero. Both inputs share the strings $A_{i,h}$; they differ only in $X_I[J_I]$ and in the gate and pointer bits of $B_{I,s_I}$.](figures/expert_planted.svg) Run a deterministic decision tree on both inputs. The sequences of queried indices and answers coincide until the first query to $X_I[J_I]$ or to a bit of $B_{I,s_I}$. So the acceptance gap is at most the sum of the probabilities that the tree queries these locations on the dummy input ([Aaronson et al. 2016](#cite-ABK2016), Lemma 6; [Ben-David 2015](#cite-BenDavid2015), sec. 5.1). ### 5.2 Searching for the erased zero Let $Z$ count the columns $i$ in which the tree queries the unique zero of $X_i$ on the dummy input. By independence of $I$, the probability that $I$ is among these columns is $\mathbb E Z/m$. Before the first query to a column's zero, its row is uniform among the unqueried rows of that column, even conditional on the transcript. While the tree has queried fewer than half the rows of a column, its next query there finds the zero with probability at most $2/m$, so zeros found this way number at most $2G/m$ in expectation. Every other found zero costs at least $m/2$ queries in its column, so there are at most $2G/m$ of those. With at most $G$ queries in the dummy run, the erased-zero probability is therefore $$ \Pr[\text{query }X_I[J_I]]\le\frac{4G}{m^2}. \tag{8} $$ ### 5.3 Predicting the cell address The index of any query to a bit of $B_{i,s}$ includes $s$, and the tree chooses that index before any answer is returned. If $s=s_i$, the query has already named all $r$ values $P(A_{i,1}),\ldots,P(A_{i,r})$. A tree can therefore reach the planted cell only by predicting $r$ independent hard values, and a direct-product theorem bounds such predictions. **Lemma 5** (OpenAI ([OpenAI 2026](#cite-OpenAI2026), Lemma 4.1); @Shaltiel2003; @Drucker2012). *Let $P$ be a partial function and $\mu$ a distribution on its domain such that every deterministic algorithm making at most $L$ queries computes $P$ under $\mu$ with probability at most $\beta$. If $U_1,\ldots,U_r$ are independent samples from $\mu$, every algorithm making at most $L$ queries to each $U_h$ outputs $(P(U_1),\ldots,P(U_r))$ with probability at most $\beta^r$. The algorithm may be randomized, interleave its queries adaptively among the $r$ inputs, and receive additional information independent of $(U_1,\ldots,U_r)$.* *Proof.* Fix the coins and the additional information, leaving a deterministic algorithm. A transcript of positive probability fixes the answers to the queried bits of each input, and every tuple consistent with these answers follows the same query schedule. So the event of obtaining a transcript is a product of constraints on the separate inputs, and the conditional law of $(U_1,\ldots,U_r)$ given it is again a product. For each $h$ let $V_h$ be the largest probability of computing $P(U_h)$ from its current conditional law with its remaining queries. A query to $U_h$ cannot increase $V_h$ in expectation, since making that query and continuing optimally was already available, and it leaves the other factors unchanged. So $\prod_h V_h$ is a supermartingale. At the end the probability of a correct answer vector is at most $\prod_h V_h$, and initially $\prod_h V_h\le\beta^r$. $\square$ Conditioning on the transcript is legitimate here because the transcript constrains each input separately. Conditioning on an event such as "the tree makes few queries to this column" is different, since the tree's later choices depend on earlier answers.1 Since $L ### 5.4 The randomized bound Combining (8) and (10), the gap between the acceptance probabilities on the two distributions is at most $$ \frac{4G}{m^2}+\frac G{mL}+G(2/3)^r <\frac13. \tag{11} $$ Here $G\le mL/100\le m^2/100$, so the first two terms are at most $1/25$ and $1/100$, and $r=20\ell$ gives $G(2/3)^r\le Gm^{-10}$. Averaging over coins gives (11) for randomized trees, while an algorithm with error at most $1/3$ on both supports would need a gap of at least $1/3$. Hence $R(F_{k,m})>\lfloor mL/100\rfloor$. The heavy-column term sets the scale $mL$; the $r$ address bits only make a lucky guess of a whole address unlikely enough to survive a union bound over the $G$ query times. The constants $20$, $100$ and $1000$ leave ample slack.

rows.label: sec-6
rows.text:
For sufficiently large $m$, the floor in (3) gives $L\ge m^{1-1/k}/(2\ell^2)$ and $\lfloor mL/100\rfloor\ge mL/200$, so $R(F_{k,m})\ge m^{2-1/k}/(400\ell^2)$, a deliberately loose constant. Now fix $0\le\alpha<4$, choose $k\ge2$ with $k>2/(4-\alpha)$, and hold $k$ fixed as $m$ grows through powers of four. By (1) with $b_k=6$ and $c_k=1/400$,
$$
 \frac{R(F_{k,m})}{(1+Q(F_{k,m}))^\alpha}
 \ \ge\ \frac{1}{400(1+C_k)^\alpha}\,
 \frac{m^{2-1/k-\alpha/2}}{(\log_2 m)^{2+6\alpha}}
 \ \longrightarrow\ \infty.
$$
Thus for each exponent below four some fixed $k$ gives a counterexample, proving optimality of the quartic upper bound. The inequality $k>2/(4-\alpha)$ is strict because the logarithmic factors must be absorbed; for example $k=3$ excludes every $\alpha<10/3$. The order of quantifiers matters: $k$ is chosen first and then $m\to\infty$, and substituting a $k$ that grows with $m$ into (1) would not be justified, since $C_k$ and the threshold depend on $k$.

The two mechanisms of the proof are worth separating from this construction. Complementary comparisons support efficient quantum search even when most comparisons have no stable orientation, provided one candidate wins its comparisons reliably. And a classical algorithm can be charged for a simultaneous prediction that it reveals in the index of its query, before it receives any answer.

rows.label: sec-7
rows.text:
The full reconstruction proves several results that go beyond OpenAI's paper. AI systems produced them, and no person has reviewed them. Each item says whether a Lean theorem states it or it is written mathematics only.

**A direct proof of the fixed-$k$ Forrelation bound.** The [full reconstruction, §8](/library/quartic/reconstruction/#forr_target) and the Lean development prove (3) for each fixed $k$, with error $1/3$ and an unspecified threshold in $m$; the full quantitative theorem of Bansal and Sinha is not reproved. As in their proof, fair signs are compared with a correlated law obtained by pairing Gaussian vectors with their Walsh transforms. The reconstruction interpolates in the bias of the first block only, and repeated Gaussian integration by parts with a bounded algebraic transform carries the resulting bias factor through the remaining blocks, one Walsh entry of size $m^{-1/2}$ at a time. The mean of $\Phi$ separates the two laws, while a martingale argument adapted from Girish, Tal and Wu ([Girish et al. 2021](#cite-GTW2021)) bounds the change in any shallow adaptive tree. Lean checks this proof.

**Uniform dependence on $k$ and a single growing family.** A Lean theorem states $R(P_{k,4^t})>\frac{2}{18225}\,m^{1-1/k}/(k^2\ln(4km))$ whenever $15k+2\le2t$, and this uniformity is what allows $k$ to grow with $m$. Compare $\log_2R$ with $4\log_2Q$: the classical exponent $2-1/k$ loses $\ell/k$ against $2\ell$, and the factor $2^{10k}$ in the decoder's repetition count adds $40k$ to $4\log_2Q$. Balancing these losses gives $k\approx\sqrt{\ell/40}$. With $k=\lfloor\sqrt{t/20}\rfloor$ for $m=4^t$, $t\ge80$, the [full reconstruction](/library/quartic/reconstruction/#ROOT-GROWING-K) obtains a single family with $R\ge Q^{4-\varepsilon(\ell)}$ and $\varepsilon(\ell)=O(1/\sqrt\ell)$; its explicit rate is vacuous for small $\ell$. Diagonalizing the fixed-$k$ theorem already gives some such family; the addition is the explicit schedule and rate. The inputs are stated in Lean, the combining calculation is written mathematics only.

**Two steps in the proof of Bansal and Sinha.** [Appendix D.3](/library/quartic/reconstruction/#forr_bs_mismatch) of the full reconstruction finds two discrepancies in §5.4 of arXiv:2008.07003v3 (printed p. 38): two successive displayed bounds differ by a logarithmic factor that is unbounded for fixed $k\ge3$, and (5.31) subtracts $\delta^2/(4N)$ where their Theorem 3.1 gives the exceptional probability $4/(N\delta^2)$. The appendix derives from their displayed bounds a corrected estimate with a weaker logarithmic factor, which still exceeds $L$ in (3) for every fixed $k$ and large $m$; so the separation is unaffected, and the proof of (3) above uses neither step. Written mathematics only.

**The Sherstov–Storozhenko–Wu bound for the Walsh promise.** For $0<\eta\le1$ and powers of two $m\ge2^{15k+2}$, [Appendix D.3](/library/quartic/reconstruction/#forr_ssw_comparison) derives $R_{(1-\eta)/2}(P_{k,m})\ge\frac{\eta^2}{162eC^2}\bigl(m/(1+\ln(km))\bigr)^{1-1/k}$, where $C$ is the unspecified absolute constant of their Fourier-growth theorem ([Sherstov et al. 2023](#cite-SSW2023)). The Fourier bound is theirs; its transfer to the Walsh promise is the reconstruction's. Written mathematics only.

**A prefactor in Špalek and Szegedy.** For two-bit parity, which has an exact one-query algorithm, the printed prefactor of Theorem 3.1 of Špalek and Szegedy ([Špalek and Szegedy 2006](#cite-SS2006)) applied to a four-cycle adversary matrix would give $Q_{1/100}\ge2-\sqrt{99}/25>1$. At error $1/3$ there is no contradiction. The corresponding theorem of Høyer, Lee and Špalek ([Høyer et al. 2007](#cite-HLS2007), Theorem 1) has an extra factor $1/2$, which agrees with the witness. No erratum has been confirmed by the authors, and the asymptotic content is unaffected ([Appendix D.4](/library/quartic/reconstruction/#R3-A-PARITY-PREFACTOR); written mathematics only).

The reconstruction also contains alternative arguments for known bounds: Lean proves the sharper erased-zero bound $2G/m^2$, proves Lemma 5 by an induction over sub-distributions, and states the universal quartic bound along three routes with different constants.

rows.label: sec-8
rows.text: The Lean development is in the [quartic-query-lean repository](https://github.com/wcook04/quartic-query-lean); every link in this paper names one release. The theorem `theorem_1_1_unconditional` states Theorem 1 with no hypotheses, with both bounds of (1) beyond a threshold and the randomized bound in the finite form $R>\lfloor mL/100\rfloor$. A separate theorem, `construction_family_named`, states (1) with $b_k=6$ and $c_k=1/400$ beyond a threshold. The fixed-$k$ bound (3) is `ForrelationLower.bansalSinhaLower` and the uniform bound of Section 7 is `forrelation_lower_uniform_sharp`. The headline theorem and (3) depend only on the standard axioms `propext`, `Classical.choice` and `Quot.sound`, and the headline statement is accepted by Comparator against an independently compiled specification. Lean checks these proofs; whether the Lean statements say what OpenAI's paper says has been compared by AI agents only. The [theorem index](https://github.com/wcook04/quartic-query-lean/blob/v1.0.2/docs/proof_index.md) links each formal statement to its source.

rows.label: front
rows.text: # OpenAI’s nearly quartic query separation: a complete proof reconstruction Written by AI systems under the direction of Will Cook · November 2026 **Abstract.** Let $R(f)$ and $Q(f)$ denote the randomized and quantum query complexities of a Boolean function, with error at most $1/3$. We reconstruct OpenAI’s proof that four is the least exponent $\alpha$ for which $R(f)=O((1+Q(f))^\alpha)$ holds for every total Boolean function. The input consists of $m$ columns. A column wins if its bit string consists of ones and its correctly addressed cell contains valid circuit transcripts and the row of a zero in each other column. A quantum algorithm compares columns and verifies only the candidates on a short list. On the classical side, the algorithm must specify the entire address of a cell before reading even one of its bits. We choose the address bits as answers to independent instances of a partial function. With $k\ge2$ blocks in each auxiliary input and $k$ fixed, the quantum algorithm uses at most $\sqrt m$ times a polylogarithmic factor in queries. Randomized algorithms require at least order $m^{2-1/k}/(\log m)^2$ queries. We give an alternative proof of the required $k$-fold Forrelation lower bound by Gaussian integration by parts. A separate quantitative argument, using estimates uniform in $k$, gives a single family with separation exponent tending to four. **About this reconstruction.** AI systems wrote this reconstruction, its two companion papers and the Lean development, under the direction of Will Cook. No human expert has reviewed them. In particular, no person has checked that the Lean statements say what OpenAI's paper says; AI agents made that comparison. The separation theorem, its construction and its proof are OpenAI's. Section 7.3, Section 8, Appendix C.2 and the comparisons in Appendices D.3 and D.4 go beyond OpenAI's paper, and each says so where it begins. The explicit constants and alternative arguments for known bounds are listed with them in §6 of the expert companion. **Reading this reconstruction.** This is the detailed proof reference for the [expert companion](/library/quartic/). It supplies the supporting derivations, alternative arguments and quantitative estimates that the companion cites. A specialist seeking the main mechanisms can start with that shorter account; the [worked exposition](/library/quartic/exposition/) develops the construction and its operations through examples. OpenAI’s preprint remains the source of the separation theorem and construction. For a continuous reading here, use the [three properties of one address bit](#forr_bundle) to build the total function in §4. The [quantum list](#upper-tournament-statement) and the [classical planting argument](#CL-first-difference) give the two bounds compared in §§7.1–7.2. With the universal upper bound of [Appendix A](#R3-A-RESULT), they determine the [optimal power](#ROOT-NO-SMALLER). That argument keeps $k$ fixed. The alternative Forrelation proof in [§8](#forr_target) can be read separately; its uniform estimate also supports the additional [growing-parameter consequence in §7.3](#ROOT-GROWING-K). The appendices retain the supporting proofs and conventions at the destinations cited in the main text. **From OpenAI’s statements to their proofs here.** The labels in the first column belong to the [5 October preprint][OpenAI2026]; those in the second belong to this reconstruction. | OpenAI’s preprint | Detailed destination here | |---|---| | Lemma 2.1: three Forrelation properties | [Lemma 3.1](#forr_bundle); alternative hardness proof in [§8](#forr_target), [decoder in Appendix G.2](#forr_quantum) and [exact circuit in G.3](#forr_circuit) | | Lemma 2.2: local certification | [§4.4](#AC-tests), with the reversible implementation in [Appendix E.4](#AC-coherent) | | Lemma 3.1: bounded amplification | [Lemma E.1 and its proof](#upper-amplification-statement), including the [retained-register argument](#upper-returned-register) | | Propositions 3.2–3.3: tournament and quantum bound | [§§5.1–5.4](#upper-tournament-statement) | | Lemma 4.1 and Proposition 4.2: classical lower bound | [Predictor and product lemma in §6.4](#CL-direct-product-statement); [product proof in §6.5](#CL-weighted-values); [bound in §6.6](#CL-concrete-lower) | | Theorem 1.1 and §5: optimal exponent | [§§7.1–7.2](#ROOT-RATIO); universal upper bound in [Appendix A](#R3-A-RESULT) | The [full correspondence](#record-numbering) also matches numbered equations and records the change from Walsh blocks $1,\ldots,k$ to $0,\ldots,k-1$. Section 6.5 proves the product lemma with unnormalized success masses; [Appendix B.1](#CL-product-law) recovers the source’s conditional-value proof. Section 8 and the growing-parameter calculation are additional derivations, with their antecedents identified in [Appendix D](#forr_credit). The [formal-proof note](#record-formal-proof-note) distinguishes checked statements from the additional assertions in their printed proofs.

rows.label: sec-1
rows.text: Let $f:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}$ be a total Boolean function. The input $x$ is unknown. A classical query chooses a coordinate $i$ and returns $x_i$; the quantum model permits a query on a superposition of indices, as defined in §2. Write $R(f)$ and $Q(f)$ for the smallest numbers of queries sufficient in the randomized and quantum models, respectively, to return $f(x)$ with probability at least $2/3$ for every $x$. We count the maximum over inputs and branches of the computation. How large a power of $Q(f)$ can be necessary to bound $R(f)$? Define \[ \alpha_{\mathrm{tot}} =\inf\left\{\alpha\geq0:\ \exists C_\alpha>0\ \forall n\geq1\ \forall f:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\},\quad R(f)\leq C_\alpha(1+Q(f))^\alpha \right\}. \tag{1.1} \] One constant must work for every input length and every total function. The additive $1$ includes constant functions without requiring a convention for $0^0$. **Theorem 1.1 (OpenAI).** The optimal power is $\alpha_{\mathrm{tot}}=4$. By the universal upper bound of [Aaronson et al., Theorem 2][ABKRT2020], there is an absolute constant $C>0$ such that every total Boolean function satisfies \[ R(f)\leq C(1+Q(f))^4. \] For each fixed integer $k\geq2$, there are positive constants $c_k,C_k,b_k$, a threshold $m_0(k)$, and total Boolean functions $F_{k,m}$, defined for all powers of four $m\geq m_0(k)$, for which \[ Q(F_{k,m})\leq C_k\sqrt m\,(\log_2 m)^{b_k}, \qquad R(F_{k,m})\geq c_k\frac{m^{2-1/k}}{(\log_2 m)^2}. \tag{1.2} \] Here $m$ is the number of columns, each with an $m$-bit string; the final Boolean input also contains address inputs and certificate cells. The integer $k$ counts the blocks of signs in each auxiliary input. A subscript $k$ on an asymptotic bound permits its constant to depend on $k$. The total number of input bits is counted in [§4.2](#AC-layout). The two inequalities concern the same function at each pair $(k,m)$. For the circuit family fixed in §4 we obtain $b_k=6$ in §5.4 and, after increasing the threshold, $c_k=1/400$ in §6.6. The powers in (1.2) have ratio $4-2/k$. Already $k=3$ excludes the proposed universal cubic bound; arbitrarily large fixed $k$ exclude every power below four. Earlier families had reached a separation with power $3-o(1)$. [OpenAI, §1.1][OpenAI2026]. To construct the functions in (1.2), we require a certificate for an all-one column to specify a zero in each of the other columns. One possible algorithm uses quantum search over the $m$ columns and verifies each queried candidate. With $\widetilde O(m)$ possible defects per candidate, the resulting bound is the product of two square-root factors: order $\sqrt m$ candidate checks, each requiring $\widetilde O(\sqrt m)$ queries. Here and below a tilde suppresses powers of $\log m$. For the smaller upper bound in (1.2), the algorithm may first return a short list containing false candidates, provided it includes the genuine one with high probability whenever a valid certificate exists. Consider the four columns in Figure 1. Each contains four bits and, below them, four cells indexed by two-bit words. For column 1 the two auxiliary inputs have answers $1,0$, so we examine cell $10$. Its three pointers specify row 1 of column 2, row 2 of column 3 and row 3 of column 4. Each of those bits is zero. In the reverse direction, the pointer from column 3 specifies row 3 of column 1, whose bit is one. In fact every bit of column 1 is one. ![A certificate in a four-column input. The auxiliary inputs $a^+,a^0,a^-$ have respective values one, zero and undefined. Cell $10$ of column 1 contains the row of a zero in each other column. The dashed arrow indicates row 3 of column 1, whose bit is one.](figures/fig2_board.svg) The diagram uses the same column bits and pointers as the worked exposition. The auxiliary inputs specified here in [§4.3](#AC-example-promise) have Forrelation values $+1/2,0,-1/2$; the exposition’s corresponding inputs have values $+1,0,-1$. The address values and winning column agree, but the quantum projection probabilities differ. The three pointers alone would also fit in a cell at the wrong address. To verify the address itself, the algorithm checks a stored list of all gate values of a Boolean circuit on each auxiliary input. Its two output bits specify whether the input is in the domain of the partial function and, if so, its value. A valid list must agree with the auxiliary input bits and with the rule at every gate. For a comparison the algorithm decodes an address in each of two columns and reads one pointer in each direction. If the first column has a valid certificate, all its auxiliary inputs belong to the domain, so a quantum procedure decodes its address with high probability. The pointer at that address specifies a zero in the second column. Whatever address the procedure returns for the second column, the indicated bit of the all-one column is one. This comparison needs no gate checks. Even with unrestricted comparison probabilities between two nonwinning columns, we will produce a list of $O(\log m)$ candidates. Constructing the list and then verifying it uses $\widetilde O(\sqrt m)+\widetilde O(\sqrt m)$ queries. For the classical lower bound, start with a zero in each column and blank cells throughout. Erase the zero in a uniformly chosen column and fill its correct cell with a valid certificate. A classical algorithm obtains a different answer only if it queries the erased zero or a changed bit in the cell. To query that cell it must specify its address before reading any bit there. Suppose $L$ queries are insufficient to predict one auxiliary answer with success greater than $2/3$ under a suitable input distribution. Choosing the column independently and using several independent auxiliary inputs will then give a lower bound of order $mL$. With $L=m^{1-o(1)}$, this gives the two scales $m^{2-o(1)}$ and $m^{1/2+o(1)}$. [OpenAI, §§1–4][OpenAI2026].

rows.label: sec-2
rows.text: A deterministic classical algorithm is a binary decision tree. Each internal node specifies the next coordinate of $x$ to query, its two children correspond to the possible answers, and each leaf specifies the output. A randomized algorithm draws such a tree independently of $x$. A quantum query acts on basis vectors by $|i,b,z\rangle\mapsto|i,b\oplus x_i,z\rangle$ and on their linear combinations by linearity. Here $i$ is the index, $b$ is an answer bit, $\oplus$ is addition modulo two, and $z$ labels the remaining work registers. The state $\psi$ is a unit vector in a finite-dimensional complex Hilbert space; a measurement outcome with orthogonal projector $\Pi$ has probability $\|\Pi\psi\|^2$ in this state. We count oracle calls. Input-independent operations and measurements cost no queries. For a partial function $P:D\to\{0,1\}$, with $D\subseteq\{0,1\}^n$, correctness is required only on $D$, the *promise*. The query cap applies on every input, including those outside $D$. Thus an algorithm for an address bit can always be run on the board, even for a column with an unpromised auxiliary input. Throughout, $m=4^t$, $t\ge1$, so the $m$ possible rows fit exactly in $\ell=\log_2m=2t$ bits. Unqualified logarithms are base two; $\ln$ denotes the natural logarithm. [Appendix F](#ROOT-PARTIAL) derives the finite models and their equivalence with the usual bit-query conventions. In each column there are $r$ auxiliary inputs to the same partial function $P$. If their values are defined, those $r$ bits specify one cell. The two query bounds require three properties of $P$. *Choosing a candidate.* Following a pointer and reading its target costs $\ell+1$ queries. The algorithm must also compute a candidate address with few queries. It uses a coherent decoder: a unitary computation whose output bit remains in a register and can control later operations before measurement. The error must be small on the promise, and the query cap must hold for every input to the decoder. *Checking its cell.* Correct decoding on the domain gives no test for membership in the domain. We use an exact circuit with separate domain and value outputs. If it has $S$ non-input gates of fan-in at most two, each cell stores $S$ proposed gate values for each address bit. Three queries check any one gate. With $m$ bits in the column and $m-1$ outward pointers, verifying a candidate will mean searching $O(m+rS)$ tests. Taking $r=O(\log m)$ and $S=\widetilde O(m)$ keeps this search within the quantum budget. *Classical prediction.* Choose a distribution of promised inputs on which no depth-$L$ decision tree predicts even one answer with probability greater than $2/3$. We draw the $r$ auxiliary inputs independently from this distribution. We will bound the chance that an algorithm predicts every bit while making at most $L$ queries in a column. Averaging over a uniformly chosen column gives a lower bound of order $mL$ for the board. The classical power $2-1/k$ in (1.2) thus requires $L$ of order $m^{1-1/k}$ up to logarithmic factors. The following promise provides all three properties. These are the only properties used to deduce the two query bounds on the board.

rows.label: sec-3
rows.text: ### 3.1. The normalized Walsh product and the promise A Forrelation input consists of $k$ sign vectors $z_0,\ldots,z_{k-1}$ of length $m=4^t$, with $k\ge2$. A raw bit $x_j(a)$ denotes $z_j(a)=(-1)^{x_j(a)}$. Index the entries by $a\in\mathbb F_2^{2t}$ and write $a\cdot b$ for the binary inner product. We use the normalized Walsh matrix $H$, the uniform unit vector $u$, and a sign diagonal $D_z$: $$ W_{ab}=(-1)^{a\cdot b},\qquad H=m^{-1/2}W, \qquad u=m^{-1/2}(1,\ldots,1)^{\mathsf T}, \qquad D_z=\operatorname{diag}(z). $$ We define the real Forrelation value and the threshold by $$ \Phi(z)=u^{\mathsf T}D_{z_0}H D_{z_1}H\cdots H D_{z_{k-1}}u, \qquad \delta=2^{-5k}. \tag{3.1} $$ There are $k$ sign diagonals and $k-1$ Walsh matrices. The partial function is $$ P_{k,m}(z)= \begin{cases} 1,&\Phi(z)\ge\delta,\\ 0,&|\Phi(z)|\le\delta/2,\\ \text{undefined},&\text{otherwise}. \end{cases} \tag{3.2} $$ The asymmetry matters for the board. Start in state $u$ and apply the matrices of (3.1) from right to left. Each diagonal sign matrix takes one phase query (a query multiplying the amplitude at $a$ by $z_j(a)$). The inner product of the final state with $u$ is $\Phi$, so projection onto $u$ succeeds with probability $\Phi^2$. This distinguishes the promised cases after repetition. A large negative overlap can give just the same projection probability as a yes input, however. The domain output of the exact circuit is what will distinguish these cases in a certificate. The one-input query allowance will be $$ L_{k,m}=\left\lfloor\frac{m^{1-1/k}}{(\log_2m)^2}\right\rfloor. \tag{3.3} $$ Here $\log_2m=2t$. ### 3.2. The complete Forrelation ingredient **Lemma 3.1 (the Forrelation ingredient).** Fix $k\ge2$. For $m=4^t$, the function (3.2) and the allowance (3.3) have the following properties. 1. For all sufficiently large $t$ (depending on $k$), $R(P_{k,4^t})>L_{k,4^t}$, by [§8.10](#forr_uniform_assembly). 2. For every $t\ge1$ and $0<\eta<1/2$, a single coherent quantum preparation, which retains its workspace, has a Boolean output on every input, error at most $\eta$ on every promised input, and bit-query cap $O_k(1+\log(1/\eta))$ on all inputs, by Appendix G.2. 3. For every $t\ge1$, one fan-in-at-most-two circuit $C_{k,t}$ of size $O_k(m(\log_2m)^2)$ has a domain bit $d$ and value bit $b$ with $d(x)=1$ exactly when $P_{k,m}(x)$ is defined, and $b(x)=P_{k,m}(x)$ on that domain, by [Appendix G.3](#forr_circuit). For the size in part 3, evaluating the $m^k$ terms of the expanded product separately would cost too much. The exact circuit instead applies integer Walsh transforms successively, using additions and subtractions on pairs of entries at each stage; since $\sqrt m=2^t$ and the thresholds are dyadic, its final comparisons use integer arithmetic. The verifier can inspect this short computation even though computing a promised answer classically requires many queries. Aaronson and Ambainis introduced the Walsh experiment. Bansal and Sinha proved hardness for the one-sided thresholds in (3.2). OpenAI invokes their result for part 1. Section 8 gives a direct proof, including the uniform dependence on $k$ used in §7.3. The remaining parts are constructed in Appendix G. [Aaronson and Ambainis, §1.1.3][AA18], [Bansal and Sinha, Theorem 1.3][BansalSinha2021], [source comparison](#forr_credit).

rows.label: sec-4
rows.text: Fix a column number and a cell address. To test the winning condition at this pair, the verifier must first check whether each stored transcript is the evaluation of the given circuit on the corresponding auxiliary input. If the transcript is incorrect, we will exhibit a single failed gate test. The other tests check the domain and value outputs and the bits at the indicated rows. [OpenAI, §2.2, Lemma 2.2][OpenAI2026]. ### 4.1. What a transcript certifies Let $P:D\to\{0,1\}$, where $D\subseteq\{0,1\}^{n}$, and let $C$ be a Boolean circuit of fan-in at most two. We number its $S$ non-input gates in topological order; these gates include its two designated outputs, $d$ and $b$. We assume that, on every raw input $a\in\{0,1\}^{n}$, $$ d_C(a)=1\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad a\in D, \qquad a\in D\quad\Longrightarrow\quad b_C(a)=P(a). \tag{4.1} $$ Thus the value output on an unpromised input is unrestricted, while the domain output must be correct there as well. In the application $P=P_{k,m}$ and $n=km$, and §3.2 supplies a circuit with $S=O_k(m(\log_2m)^2)$. The construction below uses (4.1); its logical properties use no lower bound for computing $P$. The $S$ entries of a transcript $\tau\in\{0,1\}^{S}$ are proposed output bits for the non-input gates, in topological order. At a gate, we read an input predecessor from the actual string $a$ and a gate predecessor from its earlier entry in $\tau$; a constant predecessor is known without a query. We call the transcript *gate-consistent* when every proposed gate value agrees with that gate's Boolean truth table on these predecessor values. Let $\operatorname{ev}_C(a)$ denote the transcript obtained by evaluating the circuit in topological order. For example, a gate with rule $v=\operatorname{AND}(a_j,\tau_u)$ must satisfy $\tau_v=a_j\land\tau_u$: one predecessor is an actual input bit and the other is an earlier claimed gate value. **Transcript lemma.** For every circuit $C$, every input $a$, and every proposed transcript $\tau$, $$ \operatorname{GateConsistent}(C,a,\tau) \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \tau=\operatorname{ev}_C(a). \tag{4.2} $$ **Proof.** The evaluated transcript satisfies each gate equation by definition. Conversely, assume all gate equations hold; we argue by induction along the topological order. At the first gate each predecessor is an input or a constant, so the claimed output equals the evaluated output. If equality holds at every earlier gate, then each predecessor of the next gate has its evaluated value, so its gate equation gives the evaluated output there as well. Hence equality holds at every gate. The argument applies equally to inputs outside $D$, since $C$ is a total circuit. In particular, every input has exactly one gate-consistent transcript. ∎ Combining (4.1) with (4.2), we see that gate consistency together with the two tests $\tau_d=1$ and $\tau_b=c$ certifies $a\in D$ and $P(a)=c$; conversely, the true transcript of a promised input of value $c$ passes these tests. Both the gate equations and the domain-output test are needed, since a correct transcript of an unpromised input has domain output zero. ### 4.2. Columns and their selected cells For the separation family, fix $k\geq2$ and $m=4^t$ with $t\geq1$. Put $$ \ell=\log_2m=2t, \qquad r=\lceil20\log_2m\rceil=40t=20\ell. \tag{4.3} $$ The four-column example uses $r=2$. For the theorem we must account for a guess at each possible query time. Suppose that with at most $L$ queries to one auxiliary input every algorithm predicts its answer with probability at most $2/3$ under the chosen distribution. For $r$ independent inputs and the same cap on each, we will bound the probability of correctly naming their whole address by $(2/3)^r$. Choose $r=20\log_2m$. This probability is then at most $m^{-10}$, small enough for a union bound over $m^2$ query times, while the number $2^r=m^{20}$ of cells per column is still polynomial in $m$. There are $m$ columns, indexed by $[m]=\{1,\ldots,m\}$. Column $i$ contains the following disjoint blocks of input bits. **$X_i$.** A string of $m$ bits. **$A_{i,1},\ldots,A_{i,r}$.** $r$ strings of $n=km$ bits. **$B_{i,s}$, for each $s\in\{0,1\}^{r}$.** One $\ell$-bit pointer $p_{i,s,j}$ into each column $j\ne i$, and one length-$S$ transcript $\tau_{i,s,h}$ for each $h\in[r]$. A fixed bijection from $\{0,1\}^{\ell}$ to $[m]$ decodes the pointers, so in an expression $X_j[p]$ the pointer word $p$ is decoded by this bijection before indexing. Because $m=2^{\ell}$, every pointer word names a row. A cell is a collection of bits, and consulting a chosen pointer costs its $\ell$ individual bit queries. The $A$-strings and the contents of every cell may be arbitrary bit strings. The input has $m\bigl[m+rkm+2^r\bigl((m-1)\ell+rS\bigr)\bigr]$ bits, since each column holds its string, its $r$ Forrelation inputs of $km$ bits and $2^r$ cells of $(m-1)\ell+rS$ bits each. With $r=20\ell$ we have $2^r=m^{20}$, and the circuit of Appendix G.3 has size $S=O_k(m\ell^2)$, so the input length is $O_k(m^{22}\ell^3)$, polynomial in $m$. Computing an index from known bits is input independent. Only the reads of input bits count as queries. Thus the addressed function is a total Boolean function of that many bits, and reading any pointer or transcript bit costs one query. If every $A_{i,h}$ lies in $D$, its partial-function values determine the *true address* $$ s_i=(P(A_{i,1}),\ldots,P(A_{i,r})). \tag{4.4} $$ If any of these instances is unpromised, the column has no true address. For an arbitrary candidate address $s$, we define $W(y;i,s)$, with $y$ the complete input, by the conjunction $$ \begin{aligned} &X_i[q]=1 &&\text{for every }q\in[m],\\ &A_{i,h}\in D\text{ and }P(A_{i,h})=s_h &&\text{for every }h\in[r],\\ &\tau_{i,s,h}=\operatorname{ev}_C(A_{i,h}) &&\text{for every }h\in[r],\\ &X_j[p_{i,s,j}]=0 &&\text{for every }j\ne i. \end{aligned} \tag{4.5} $$ We say that $i$ *wins at $s$* when these four lines hold. The second line forces $s$ to equal the true address. A column with an unpromised address input cannot win at any cell. Define $$ F(y)=1\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \exists i\in[m]\ \exists s\in\{0,1\}^{r},\ W(y;i,s), \tag{4.6} $$ and let $F(y)=0$ otherwise. This defines a total Boolean function, since (4.5) is a predicate on finitely many input bits and an unpromised instance prevents its column from satisfying it; the definition consults a partial-function value only where it is defined. With the specified $P_{k,m}$, $C_{k,m}$, and parameters (4.3), this function is $F_{k,m}$. **Uniqueness lemma.** For any $P,C$, pointer bijection, and complete input $y$, at most one pair $(i,s)$ satisfies (4.5). **Proof.** Suppose, for contradiction, that $W(y;i,s)$ and $W(y;j,a)$ hold with $j\ne i$. The pointer from $B_{i,s}$ into column $j$ then exhibits a zero in $X_j$, whereas the winning condition for $j$ makes every bit of $X_j$ one. Hence any two satisfying pairs share their column. For a fixed column, the second line of (4.5) determines each address bit as the value of the same promised input, so the addresses agree as well. ∎ Totality and uniqueness follow from (4.5). We use (4.1) to check the defining conditions with queries. ### 4.3. A four-column instance Take $P_{2,4}$ and use just two address bits, giving four cells per column. We use a circuit for its finite truth table; the asymptotic family has $r=40$ at this size and uses the arithmetic circuit of Appendix G.3. Figure 1 uses $a^+,a^0,a^-$ for the following three eight-bit inputs. The table gives their Forrelation values and the two exact circuit outputs.
