[Appendix G.4](#AC-example-tests) checks the arithmetic. | Eight-bit string | $\Phi$ | Partial-function value | Exact outputs $(d,b)$ | |---|---:|---|---| | $0000\,0000$ | $1/2$ | $1$ | $(1,1)$ | | $0001\,0010$ | $0$ | $0$ | $(1,0)$ | | $1111\,0000$ | $-1/2$ | undefined | $(0,0)$ | The projection decoder succeeds in a single projection with probability $\Phi^2$. Its success probability is $1/4$ on both the first and third rows, although the third input has no promised value. Their domain bits differ. This is precisely the distinction the transcript must certify. The [worked exposition](/library/quartic/exposition/#forrelation-primitive) uses different auxiliary strings with values $+1$ and $-1$, whose projection probabilities are both one; it illustrates the same promise distinction on different inputs. The same board can now be specified by its raw strings. A true address exists only when both partial values are defined. | Column $i$ | $X_i$ | $A_{i,1}$ | $A_{i,2}$ | True address | |---:|---|---|---|---| | $1$ | $1111$ | $00000000$ | $00010010$ | $10$ | | $2$ | $0111$ | $11110000$ | $00010010$ | none | | $3$ | $1011$ | $00000000$ | $00010010$ | $10$ | | $4$ | $1101$ | $00000000$ | $00010010$ | $10$ | We encode the rows $1,2,3,4$ by $00,01,10,11$, respectively, and store in $B_{1,10}$ the true transcripts for column 1 together with the pointer words $$ p_{1,10,2}=00\longmapsto1,\qquad p_{1,10,3}=01\longmapsto2,\qquad p_{1,10,4}=10\longmapsto3. \tag{4.7} $$ The pointers all reach zeros, and $X_1=1111$. Hence column 1 wins at $10$. Each other column has a zero of its own. In column 2 there is also an unpromised address input. In each cell store the two true transcripts for its column. Every pointer into columns 2–4 goes to the designated zero of its target. For every pointer back into column 1, set its row number equal to the address of the cell containing it. Thus, for every decoded label of column 2, the indicated bit in column 1 equals one. ### 4.4. The local tests Fix a candidate pair $(i,s)$. We replace the partial-function conditions in (4.5) by the following tests on the stored transcripts, writing $g_e(y;i,s)=1$ when the test with label $e$ passes. **Column tests.** For each of the $m$ bits of $X_i$ there is one test, which reads that bit with one query and passes exactly when it is one. **Pointer tests.** For each of the $m-1$ other columns, a test reads the selected outward pointer in $B_{i,s}$ and checks that it reaches a zero in its designated target column. It reads the $\ell$ pointer bits, decodes the row without a query, and then reads that target bit, so its worst-case depth is $\ell+1$ although its target coordinate depends on the earlier answers. **Gate tests.** For each of the $r$ stored transcripts and each of its $S$ non-input gates, the test checks that the claimed output equals the gate's truth table on its two predecessors. These $rS$ tests each read the claimed value and at most two predecessor values, so each uses at most three queries; an input predecessor is read from the actual address string, a gate predecessor from the transcript, and a constant costs no query. For example, a gate $v=\operatorname{AND}(x_a,\tau_u)$ is checked by reading the actual input bit $x_a$, the earlier transcript bit $\tau_u$ and the proposed output $\tau_v$, and testing $\tau_v=x_a\land\tau_u$. The test reads an input wire from the input itself. **Output tests.** For each $h\in[r]$, one test requires the transcript's domain output to be one, and another requires its value output to equal $s_h$. These $r$ domain tests and $r$ value tests each use one query. They check the meaning of the output bits once gate consistency holds, because a gate-consistent transcript can have domain output zero or a value output different from the proposed address bit. To make the index set the same for every candidate, we list the other columns in increasing order, skipping $i$, and label their pointer tests by $[m-1]$. The common test set is then $$ E=[m]\;\sqcup\;[m-1]\;\sqcup\; \bigl([r]\times([S]\sqcup\{d,b\})\bigr). \tag{4.8} $$ The labels $d,b$ in the last summand denote the two output *tests*, which come in addition to the consistency tests at the corresponding output gates. Consequently $$ K=|E|=m+(m-1)+r(S+2). \tag{4.9} $$ For $S\le A m\ell^2$, substituting $r=20\ell$ gives \[ K=2m-1+20\ell(S+2)\le(42+20A)m\ell^3. \tag{4.10} \] The square root of this count will be the cost of searching for a failed test, up to logarithms. **Lemma 4.1 (local verification).** Suppose $C$ satisfies (4.1). On every complete input $y$, and for every candidate $(i,s)$, $$ W(y;i,s)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad g_e(y;i,s)=1\text{ for every }e\in E. \tag{4.11} $$ Every test is computed by an exact deterministic adaptive decision tree of depth at most $$ q_*=\max\{3,\ell+1\}=\ell+1 \qquad(m\geq4). \tag{4.12} $$ **Proof.** Suppose all tests pass. The column-bit and pointer tests give the first and last lines of (4.5). For each $h$, the gate tests and (4.2) identify $\tau_{i,s,h}$ as the true evaluation of $C$ on $A_{i,h}$, and its two output tests then give $A_{i,h}\in D$ and $P(A_{i,h})=s_h$ by (4.1); these are the remaining lines of (4.5). Conversely, (4.5) supplies true transcripts of promised inputs with the required values, so every test passes. The procedures defining the tests use at most one, three or $\ell+1$ queries, according to their type, and they are exact on every input, including inputs at which the candidate is a nonwinner or its address instances are unpromised. Their largest depth is (4.12). ∎ It follows that a winning column passes all tests at its unique true address and fails at least one test at every other address. A nonwinner, including any column with an unpromised instance, fails some test at every address, since an address at which all tests passed would contradict (4.11). For an unpromised instance the true transcript has domain output zero, and changing that output to one makes at least one gate equation fail; hence gate consistency cannot repair the instance. On Figure 1’s board, all tests pass at $(1,10)$. Change the address to $00$: the stored computations still agree with the two inputs and the pointers still find zeros, but the first value-output test now fails. In column 2 the first computation reports domain bit zero, so every address fails even with a true transcript. [Appendix G.4](#AC-example-tests) counts the tests on this board. An oracle for the local tests must allow their indices in superposition. Retain each queried bit, compute the next address reversibly, copy the test result, and run the computation backwards. The forward depth is $\max\{3,\ell+1\}$ and the clean oracle costs $O(\ell+1)$ physical bit queries. [Appendix E.4](#AC-coherent) gives the construction, including the cost of a read active on only some branches. ### 4.5. Comparing a winning column with an arbitrary column For distinct columns $i,j$, the comparison routine in §5.3 decodes one address label for each column and, at those labels, follows the pointer from each column into the other, disqualifying a column if its $X$-bit at the row indicated by the other column is zero. If exactly one is disqualified, the other wins; a fixed rule resolves the remaining cases. On every raw input each decoded label is a bit string, possibly unrelated to any true address, and it is produced within a query cap fixed for all inputs. **Winner-comparison implication.** Fix $0<\varepsilon<1/2$, and suppose column $i^\star$ wins. For any other column $j\ne i^\star$, every decoded address $a$ in that column, and every pointer stored there, $$ X_{i^\star}[p_{j,a,i^\star}]=1. \tag{4.13} $$ This follows from the winner's all-one string alone, so the winner is never disqualified. Whenever the decoder for $i^\star$ returns the true address $s_{i^\star}$, the pointer stored at that address satisfies $$ X_j[p_{i^\star,s_{i^\star},j}]=0, \tag{4.14} $$ so only the second column is disqualified on this event. Therefore $$ \Pr[i^\star\text{ wins against }j] \ \geq\ \Pr[\widehat s_{i^\star}=s_{i^\star}] \ \geq\ 1-\varepsilon. \tag{4.15} $$ All $r$ auxiliary inputs in the winning column are promised. A union bound over their decoding errors, at most $\varepsilon/r$ each, proves the last inequality. For example, whichever label the decoder returns for column 2 in Figure 1, the pointer there specifies a one in column 1. Conversely, the pointer in $B_{1,10}$ specifies the zero in column 2. Only the decoding probability for column 1 enters the lower bound.

rows.label: sec-5
rows.text: The comparison requires only polylogarithmically many queries, whereas verifying one candidate costs $\widetilde O(\sqrt m)$. Comparison outcomes need not define a total order. In a pair of nonwinning columns either output can have probability arbitrarily close to $1/2$, so repetition cannot determine a fixed ordering with a uniformly bounded number of trials. Consider an abstract four-vertex example. A dominant vertex $s$ beats $a,b,c$ with certainty, while $a$ beats $b$, $b$ beats $c$, and $c$ beats $a$. Pick one of the four vertices uniformly as pivot and keep everyone who beats it. The four possible pivots $s,a,b,c$ leave, respectively, \[ \varnothing,\qquad \{s,c\},\qquad \{s,a\},\qquad \{s,b\}. \] The expected number of remaining vertices is $3/2$. For any pivot other than $s$, the remaining set contains $s$. For probabilistic comparisons, give each candidate a nonnegative weight. After choosing a pivot, multiply the candidate’s weight by its probability of winning that comparison. The identity below bounds the expected sum of the updated weights. OpenAI’s tournament uses this identity to produce a short list. A verifier then checks the listed columns for defects, accepting at the first candidate for which none is found. [OpenAI, §3][OpenAI2026]. ### 5.1. Complementary comparisons and the weight of a winner We fix an input oracle for the duration of the argument. There are $m\geq2$ vertices, and each unordered pair of distinct vertices has one designated coherent comparison circuit, with an ordering convention determining which output bit means that the first named vertex wins. Let $a_{ij}$ be the probability that $i$ wins its comparison against $j$, and define $a_{ii}=0$; this fixes the comparison table. Since both orders use the same circuit with its two outcomes interpreted oppositely, we obtain equation (5.1): $$ 0\leq a_{ij}\leq1, \qquad a_{ij}+a_{ji}=1\quad(i\ne j), \qquad a_{ii}=0. \tag{5.1} $$ The table may be intransitive: a cycle of certain wins is allowed, as is a pair with winning probability exactly one half, and comparisons made in separate fresh registers have their designated probabilities, which may lie far from zero and one. In the algorithmic theorem, all pair circuits are available coherently, including under control of their indices, with a uniform cap of $c\geq1$ bit queries for each comparison and for its inverse. When a controlled query is implemented from an ordinary bit query, the cap $c$ includes the constant overhead established below. The expected remaining weight after a round will be at most half the current weight. Starting from $m$, this takes about $\log_2m$ rounds to leave weight of order one. We also need the weight of the dominant index to stay above $1/2$ until selection. For $T$ rounds it suffices to take the error of each comparison at most a small constant times $1/T$. Choose $$ T=\left\lceil\log_2(1000m)\right\rceil,\qquad \varepsilon=\frac{1}{1000T}. $$ The base two ensures $2^T\ge1000m$. Dominance means $$ a_{sj}\ge1-\varepsilon\qquad(j\ne s). \tag{5.2} $$ With this choice of parameters there are three error contributions: winner-address error in §5.3 gives dominance, stage-sampler failure contributes at most $T\varepsilon$ before the winner is selected, and fresh verification contributes at most $\varepsilon$ for the winner or $T\varepsilon$ on a zero input. The ideal miss term $2m/2^T$ is separate. **Proposition 5.1 (OpenAI, probabilistic-comparison tournament).** With the parameters and comparisons above, one algorithm returns at most $T$ vertices and costs $O(c\sqrt m\,T^2\log T)$ queries on every input. For each dominant $s$ its list contains $s$ with probability at least $1-2m/2^T-T\varepsilon$. The algorithm is independent of $s$. *Proof of [Proposition 5.1](#upper-tournament-statement).* Fix the comparison table and parameters just stated. The weights below are analytical quantities of the proof, unavailable to the algorithm. We begin with weights $w_i=1$ and an empty ordered list $L$, and write $W=\sum_iw_i$. In one ideal step, if $W>0$, we choose a pivot $p$ with probability $w_p/W$, append it to $L$, and make the update in equation (5.3): $$ w_i\longleftarrow w_i a_{ip}\qquad(1\leq i\leq m). \tag{5.3} $$ If $W=0$, we leave the weights zero and append nothing. Running exactly $T$ steps, with this zero state absorbing, specifies the ideal process on every history. All weights remain nonnegative and at most one, because they are products of numbers in $[0,1]$; after a history $L=(p_1,\ldots,p_h)$, \[ w_i(L)=\prod_{b=1}^{h}a_{ip_b},\qquad w_i([])=1. \] A selected vertex receives the factor $a_{pp}=0$, so its weight is zero thereafter and it is never again selected on a positive-weight step. These observations also cover histories of probability zero, where they avoid any division by zero. We condition on any current weights with $W>0$. For pivot $p$ the new total weight is $\sum_iw_ia_{ip}$, and averaging over its probability $w_p/W$ gives the first expression in equation (5.4). We write its numerator as the sum over ordered pairs $(i,p)$. The diagonal terms vanish because $a_{ii}=0$, and pairing the term for $(i,p)$ with the term for $(p,i)$, for each unordered pair with $i\ne p$, gives $w_iw_p(a_{ip}+a_{pi})=w_iw_p$. Since the sum of the $w_iw_p$ over unordered pairs is half of $W^2-\sum_iw_i^2$, we obtain $$ \mathbb E[W_{\rm new}\mid w] =\frac1W\sum_{p,i}w_pw_i a_{ip} =\frac{W^2-\sum_iw_i^2}{2W}. \tag{5.4} $$ When $W>0$, equation (5.4) gives $\mathbb E[W_{\rm new}\mid w]\leq W/2$ because the sum of squares is nonnegative. At $W=0$ both the current and the next total weight are zero, so the same bound still holds, and taking expectations over histories gives $\mathbb E W_{h+1}\leq\tfrac12\mathbb E W_h$. Starting from $W_0=m$ and applying this inequality $T$ times, we obtain: $$ \mathbb E W_T\leq\frac{m}{2^T}. $$ Since the calculation uses only complementarity and nonnegativity, it applies equally to deterministic or cyclic tournaments and to comparisons whose probabilities are bounded away from both zero and one. Suppose that $s$ is dominant and has not appeared among the first $h\leq T$ pivots. Then every factor in its weight is at least $1-\varepsilon$, which gives: $$ w_s(h)\geq(1-\varepsilon)^h \geq1-h\varepsilon \geq1-T\varepsilon =\frac{999}{1000}>\frac12. $$ Bernoulli’s inequality gives the middle bound. Thus, until $s$ is selected, the total weight exceeds one half; in particular, the process stays out of the absorbing zero state before selecting $s$. If $s$ is missing from the ideal list at time $T$, the same argument gives $W_T>1/2$, so the indicator of this event is at most $2W_T$ pointwise. Taking expectations proves equation (5.5) for every weight distribution: $$ \Pr[s\notin L_T] \leq\Pr[W_T\geq1/2] \leq2\,\mathbb EW_T \leq\frac{2m}{2^T}. \tag{5.5} $$ The conclusion uses only complementarity and the lower bounds on the distinguished row, so comparisons between other candidates may be inconsistent with every ordering. ### 5.2. Drawing the next pivot Given the stored pivots $p_1,\ldots,p_h$, prepare the candidate register in a uniform superposition of indices $i$. Controlled by $i$, compare it to each pivot on **fresh registers**, retaining the full state $|\phi(i,p_b)\rangle$ of each comparison. The joint state is $$ \frac1{\sqrt m}\sum_{i=1}^m |i\rangle \bigotimes_{b=1}^{h}|\phi(i,p_b)\rangle. \tag{5.6} $$ Compute the all-wins flag reversibly, retaining the outcomes and work. At $h=0$ the empty conjunction succeeds for every index. For fixed $i$, the different comparisons act on separate initially fixed registers, so projection onto all successful outcome bits is a tensor product of their success projections. The squared norm of the projected state is therefore the product of their squared norms, namely the product of $a_{ip_b}$, which is $w_i$. Since distinct index values remain orthogonal, summing their squared norms and including the initial factor $1/\sqrt m$ proves: $$ \Pr[\text{success and index }i]=\frac{w_i}{m}, \qquad \Pr[\text{success}]=\frac Wm, \qquad \Pr[i\mid\text{success}]=\frac{w_i}{W}\quad(W>0). $$ Use [bounded amplification (Lemma E.1 in §E.2)](#upper-amplification-statement) with threshold $\gamma=1/(2m)$ and error $\varepsilon$. On success it preserves the normalized success component of the preparation. Measuring the index therefore draws exactly from $w_i/W$. The algorithm appends this pivot, stops on failure, and makes at most $T$ draws. Failure has probability at most $\varepsilon$ whenever $W/m\ge\gamma$, and probability one when $W=0$. The cap of $O(\sqrt m\ln(1/\varepsilon))$ preparations or inverses holds on **every** branch, however small $W$ is. While the real and ideal lists agree, the next successful draw has exactly the ideal law. Couple them by using the same pivot on success, as in the [transition calculation](#upper-quantum-tournament). Until the dominant vertex $s$ appears, its weight exceeds $1/2$. Hence $W/m\ge1/(2m)$ at every such history and the chance of a first disagreement there is at most $\varepsilon$ conditionally. Summing over the $T$ possible stages costs at most $T\varepsilon$. Once $s$ appears it stays on the list. By (5.5), $$ \Pr[\text{the real list misses }s]\le\frac{2m}{2^T}+T\varepsilon. $$ Only the pivot labels persist. Recomputing the $h$ comparisons at a new stage costs $O(c(h+1))$ queries per preparation or inverse, so summing the amplified costs for $0\le h $$ \text{queries} =O\!\left(c\sqrt m\,T^2\ln(1/\varepsilon)\right) =O\!\left(c\sqrt m\,T^2\log T\right). $$ Here $1/\varepsilon=1000T$. This proves Proposition 5.1 without ever estimating the $a_{ij}$. Appendix E.3 gives a [cyclic example](#upper-cyclic-example) and the [finite query budget](#upper-padded-tournament-budget). ### 5.3. Decoding, comparison, and verification Return to the $m=4^t$ columns. For the tournament we must now construct one complementary comparison for each pair and prove that a winner is dominant. For the resulting list we have a different operation, a search over the $K=m+(m-1)+r(S+2)$ exact tests at a fixed address. Both query the same board. Keep $T$ and $\varepsilon$ from Proposition 5.1. Here $r=20\ell$ and $S=O_k(m\ell^2)$. To decode an address, we run the quantum decoder of Lemma 3.1, part 2 on each of the $r$ Forrelation instances in the selected column, reducing the error on each promised instance to at most $\varepsilon/r$, and implement its trials and decision rule reversibly, retaining the outcome labels and all intermediate work. The output register always holds an $r$-bit string; when some promises fail, the column has no true address but every measured label is still an $r$-bit string. The number of queries is nevertheless capped on every input, and the output label is defined even off promise. For fixed $k$, each instance is decoded with $O_k(\ln(r/\varepsilon))$ queries, and running the $r$ copies gives: $$ \text{address-decoding queries} =O_k\!\left(r\ln(r/\varepsilon)\right), \qquad \Pr[\text{correct address}]\geq1-\varepsilon \quad\text{if all }r\text{ promises hold}. $$ A union bound over the $r$ promised bits gives the probability estimate. [Appendix E.5](#upper-oracle-access) counts the physical queries. To compare two columns, we fix a numerical ordering of the columns. A distinct pair is first arranged with its smaller index first, so that both ordered calls use the same underlying circuit, and both addresses are decoded with fresh work registers. At the decoded address of the first column we read the pointer directed toward the second column and then the addressed entry of the second column's $X$-block; if that entry is zero, the second column is disqualified. The reverse operation, using the second decoded address, tests whether the first column is disqualified. If exactly one column is disqualified, return the other index. If both or neither are disqualified, return the smaller index. A self-comparison always returns false and makes no pointer query. Apart from address decoding, this comparison reads only the selected pointer fields and targeted $X$ bits; it does not inspect gate transcripts. The verifier checks those later. Reading a pointer takes its $\ell$ address bits followed by the targeted $X$-bit, and reversible reading keeps the pointer and the target address available for uncomputation. Thus the two pointer tests use $O(\ell+1)$ bit queries, up to a constant factor if controlled reads are needed, and together with the two decodings a comparison and its inverse have query cost $c=O_k(r\ln(r/\varepsilon)+\ell)=O_k(\ell\log\ell)$. The circuit is defined on all input strings, and since the bit oracle is its own inverse, reversing its gate sequence gives the inverse with the same number of queries. The retained label pairs occupy orthogonal registers. The pointer reads and the final winner test act separately on each such subspace, so the output probability sums the squared norms of the label branches on which the deterministic rule selects $i$. Both orientations of a pair use the same circuit; reversing the names counts the complementary event. Thus $a_{ij}+a_{ji}=1$ for $i\ne j$, and $a_{ii}=0$, on the entire cube. The [event inclusion in §4.5](#AC-comparison) now applies to this mixture. For a winning column $i^\star$, the decoder returns its correct address with probability at least $1-\varepsilon$, hence $$ a_{i^\star j}\ge1-\varepsilon\qquad(j\ne i^\star). $$ This is exactly the dominance hypothesis of Proposition 5.1. Comparison retains both decoded labels coherently while using them to control pointers. Verification instead samples one fresh label before any test search: to verify a candidate, we decode its address afresh, measure it, and fix the resulting address $a$. Lemma 4.1 provides a finite list of exact local tests, whose number is $$ K=m+(m-1)+r(S+2)=O_k(m\ell^3). $$ For this fixed address prepare a uniform test label, compute its failure bit with the [reversible test circuit](#AC-coherent), and apply Lemma E.1 with $\gamma=1/K$ and error $\varepsilon$. Reject if the search finds a failure. Verify the list in order with fresh preparations, returning one as soon as a candidate passes and zero if none does. If $h$ of the $K$ tests fail, the preparation flags a defect with probability $h/K$. At $h=0$ the search finds none with certainty. At $h\ge1$ it finds one with probability at least $1-\varepsilon$. By Lemma 4.1, $h\ge1$ at every address of a nonwinner. At the true address of a winner every test passes exactly, so $h=0$ and rejection is impossible. The winner can therefore be rejected only if its address was decoded incorrectly, an event of probability at most $\varepsilon$. Thus $$ \Pr[\text{accept a nonwinner}]\leq\varepsilon, \qquad \Pr[\text{reject the winner}]\leq\varepsilon. $$ Each preparation or inverse costs $O(\ell+1)$ queries, so the search costs $O(\sqrt K\ln(1/\varepsilon)(\ell+1))$, in addition to one fresh decoding. We now bound the error for every input of the total function. On a zero input every column is a nonwinner. We condition on the complete tournament transcript and on its list, which has at most $T$ entries; each subsequent fresh verification then accepts its candidate with probability at most $\varepsilon$, whatever the transcript. By the union bound, for any fixed list the probability of at least one false acceptance is at most $T\varepsilon$, and averaging over the tournament transcript preserves this bound. Early stopping at the first acceptance leaves the event that at least one acceptance occurs unchanged. On a one input, uniqueness of the winner gives a column $i^\star$, which the comparison argument makes dominant, so the tournament misses it with probability at most $2m/2^T+T\varepsilon$. If it occurs in the list, its fresh verification accepts with probability at least $1-\varepsilon$, even conditionally on the previous transcript, and any earlier acceptance already gives the correct output one. Thus an erroneous zero output is contained in the union of the miss event and the rejection of $i^\star$ when it is verified, and we obtain $$ \begin{aligned} \Pr_x[\text{error}]&\leq T\varepsilon &&\text{for every }x\text{ with }F_{k,m}(x)=0,\\ \Pr_x[\text{error}]&\leq\frac{2m}{2^T}+T\varepsilon+\varepsilon<\frac13 &&\text{for every }x\text{ with }F_{k,m}(x)=1. \end{aligned} $$ Indeed $2^T\ge1000m$ and $T\varepsilon=1/1000$. ### 5.4. The cost of the list and its verification Each of the $T=O(\log m)$ pivot stages makes at most $O(\sqrt m\log T)$ preparations, and a preparation compares its candidate with at most $T$ previous pivots. A comparison costs $c=(\log m)^{O_k(1)}$ bit queries. The list therefore costs $O(c\sqrt m\,T^2\log T)$. For a listed candidate the search is instead over $K=O_k(m(\log m)^3)$ possible defects. Its $O(\sqrt K\log T)$ test calls and one fresh address decoding cost $\sqrt m(\log m)^{O_k(1)}$ queries altogether. There are at most $T$ such candidates. Adding the two costs proves the upper bound. **Proposition 5.2 (quantum evaluation).** $$ Q(F_{k,m})\leq\sqrt m\,(\log m)^{O_k(1)} \qquad(k\geq2,\ m=4^t,\ t\geq1). $$ For the circuit of §3 the logarithmic factor can be bounded by $C_k(\log_2m)^6$ on every input and every branch. The [finite budget](#upper-finite-budget) and [constant $C_k$](#upper-explicit-log6) are derived in Appendix E.5. The total is a sum: the algorithm constructs the candidate list once, then searches for a defect in each listed candidate.

rows.label: sec-6
rows.text: Run the same tree on a zero input and a one input. As long as its answers agree, its next queries agree as well. Figure 2 shows the two places where a first difference can occur. The dummy board $Y^{(0)}$ has one zero at row $J_i$ of each column $i$. Choose a column $I$ uniformly and independently. Erase its zero and fill its cell at address $s_I$, the string of its $r$ auxiliary answers. This gives the planted board $Y^{(1)}$. All auxiliary inputs are identical on the two boards. ![The two possible locations of a first differing answer. The dummy board has one zero in every column and blank cells. In the planted board, the zero in column $I=3$ is replaced by one and cell $B_{I,s_I}$ contains a valid certificate. Both panels use identical address inputs, drawn from the distribution $\mu$ of §6.1.](figures/expert_planted.svg) To read the erased zero, the tree must query a particular bit among $m^2$ bits. To read a changed bit of the cell, it must specify the entire string $s_I$ in the query. Assume that under the chosen distribution a depth-$L$ tree predicts one auxiliary answer with probability at most $2/3$. We will show that with budget $G=\lfloor mL/100\rfloor$ the probability of reading either change is below $1/3$. We bound three probabilities: $2G/m^2$ for reading the erased zero, $G/(mL)$ for making more than $L$ auxiliary queries in the chosen column, and $G(2/3)^r$ for querying its correct cell while making at most $L$ such queries. Their sum bounds the difference between the tree’s acceptance probabilities. ### 6.1. The hard distribution and the hidden address Use the board of §4 with $m=4^t$, $r=40t$, a partial function $P:D\to\{0,1\}$ and a circuit $C$ computing its domain and value outputs. For the lower bound we need valid transcripts, whatever their length. The factor $m$ comes from choosing the planted column uniformly: few columns can receive more than $L$ of the $G$ queries. The factor exponential in $r$ bounds the chance of guessing all address bits when the chosen column receives at most $L$ queries. Addressing a certificate by partial-function values follows [Aaronson, Ben-David and Kothari, §6][ABK2019]. Assume that \(L\) is a nonnegative integer and \(L \[ \exists\mu\text{ on }D\quad \forall T\text{ with }\operatorname{depth}(T)\le L,\qquad \Pr_{x\sim\mu}[T(x)=P(x)]\le\frac23. \] Indeed the finite game has depth-$L$ trees as rows, promised inputs as columns and correctness as payoff. No mixed row attains $2/3$ on every column. Finite minimax therefore gives a mixed column against which every row has success below $2/3$. [Appendix B.4](#record-minimax-proof) derives this from finite convex separation. We draw the address strings independently from this promised-input law. ### 6.2. Coupled zero and one inputs **Generic lower bound.** Let \(m=4^t\), \(t\ge1\), and \(r=40t\). Let \(P:D\to\{0,1\}\) be a partial Boolean function on a finite set of input coordinates, let \(C\) realize its promise and value, and let \(F_{P,C,m}\) be the addressed function just described. If \[ 1\le L\le m,\qquad L \[ R(F_{P,C,m})>\left\lfloor\frac{mL}{100}\right\rfloor. \] The implication holds whatever the size of the circuit. Only the one-input lower bound $L \[ G=\left\lfloor\frac{mL}{100}\right\rfloor \tag{6.1} \] and fix a deterministic tree \(T\) of depth at most \(G\), together with the hard distribution \(\mu\) of §6.1. We construct both input distributions on one probability space. For each column \(i\), we choose \(J_i\) independently and uniformly from its \(m\) rows, and in the dummy input \(Y^{(0)}\) we put \[ X_i[j]= \begin{cases} 0,&j=J_i,\\ 1,&j\ne J_i. \end{cases} \] Independently, we draw every \(A_{i,h}\) from \(\mu\) and fill every bit of every cell \(B_{i,s}\) with zero, so every query to a cell on the dummy input returns the same bit regardless of the zero locations and the values of \(P\). Next we choose \(I\) uniformly from the \(m\) columns, independently of the entire dummy input, and obtain the planted input \(Y^{(1)}\) by replacing \(X_I\) by \(1^m\) and filling only \(B_{I,s_I}\). This cell receives the evaluation transcript of \(C\) on \(A_{I,h}\) in its \(h\)-th transcript field, and its pointer into column \(j\ne I\) receives the value \(J_j\). Since every \(A_{i,h}\) is promised, all true addresses exist. Every dummy column has a zero, while column \(I\) of the planted input meets every winning condition. Thus \[ F_{P,C,m}(Y^{(0)})=0,\qquad F_{P,C,m}(Y^{(1)})=1. \] The two coupled inputs can differ only at \(X_I[J_I]\) and inside \(B_{I,s_I}\). Until \(T\) receives different answers on the two inputs, its histories coincide, and so do its next query and stopping decision. Hence, if the dummy execution never queries a differing bit, the two executions end at the same leaf. Since the outputs are Boolean, \[ \left|\mathbb E T(Y^{(1)})-\mathbb E T(Y^{(0)})\right| \le\mathbb E\left|T(Y^{(1)})-T(Y^{(0)})\right| =\Pr[T(Y^{(1)})\ne T(Y^{(0)})]. \] On the dummy board, a query to the erased zero or to the filled cell is therefore necessary for different outputs. A union bound gives \[ \begin{aligned} \left|\Pr[T(Y^{(1)})=1]-\Pr[T(Y^{(0)})=1]\right| &\le \Pr[T\text{ on }Y^{(0)}\text{ queries }X_I[J_I]]\\ &\quad+ \Pr[T\text{ on }Y^{(0)}\text{ queries a bit of }B_{I,s_I}]. \end{aligned} \tag{6.2} \] All probabilities on the right can be evaluated on the dummy run, whose law is independent of $I$. A visit to the planted cell suffices for the bound even if the queried bit happens to keep its blank value. The blank-array argument in Aaronson, Ben-David and Kothari has only the cell term. Erasing a zero here gives the tree an additional way to distinguish the boards. [Aaronson, Ben-David and Kothari, Lemma 6, proof, pp. 12–13][ABK2019]. ### 6.3. Discoveries and the erased zero Let \(Z\) count the columns whose unique zero is queried during the complete dummy run: \[ Z=\sum_{i=1}^{m} \mathbf1\{T\text{ on }Y^{(0)}\text{ queries }X_i[J_i]\}. \] Repeated queries to a discovered zero still contribute only one to \(Z\). Once all the dummy data are fixed, \(Z\) is fixed, and exactly \(Z\) of the \(m\) possible choices of \(I\) select a discovered zero. Averaging over \(I\) and then over the dummy data, we obtain the identity \[ \Pr[T\text{ on }Y^{(0)}\text{ queries }X_I[J_I]] =\frac{\mathbb EZ}{m}. \] The identity uses only the independence and uniformity of \(I\) (it holds at every depth and for every \(P\)), and a separate search estimate will bound its right-hand side. **Proof of the search bound.** Fix a column, its address data, and everything outside its bit string. Run \(T\) on the reference input in which this column is all ones. List the distinct $X$ positions on that reference path as \(p_1,\ldots,p_d\), in order of first appearance. Matching the reference path is needed only until the first differing answer. Repeated calls and calls after discovery can only increase the counted $X$-query cost. If the zero is at \(p_s\), the tree follows the reference path until it reads that zero and thus makes at least \(s\) column queries. For a zero outside the list the tree follows the entire reference path, makes at least \(d\) column queries, and reads no zero. Thus the tree reads the zero at exactly \(d\) of the \(m\) possible positions. Summed over its positions, the query count is at least \[ 1+\cdots+d+(m-d)d =\frac{d(2m-d+1)}2 \ge\frac{d(m+1)}2. \] Let $Q_i$ count all reads of column $i$’s bit string and $Q_X=\sum_i Q_i\le G$. Averaging over the $m$ possible zero positions and then the fixed data shows that the discovery probability in column $i$ is at most $2\mathbb E Q_i/(m+1)$. Sum over $i$ and use the selection identity to get \[ \mathbb EZ\le\frac{2}{m+1}\mathbb E Q_X, \qquad \Pr[T\text{ on }Y^{(0)}\text{ queries }X_I[J_I]] \le\frac{2G}{m(m+1)}. \] Scanning one column without repetition until its zero is found attains the first, expectation-cost inequality, since its expected cost is \((m+1)/2\). Its worst-case cost is \(m\), and the example does not establish an optimal success curve for each prescribed worst-case budget. In particular the erased-zero probability is at most $2G/m^2$. For any $m=2^\ell$, the original early/late argument gives the bound $4G/m^2$ on the erased-zero probability for a tree of depth at most $G$, under the same independent sampling of the address inputs, zero rows and erased column. [Appendix B.2](#CL-early-late) proves the bound and the charging argument for the factor two. ### 6.4. A capped simulator for the planted cell To read a bit in a certificate cell, the algorithm must first specify the cell address in its query coordinate. We will regard that address as a prediction of the $r$ hidden answers. Fixing a column and a query time will give one prediction. To bound its success we first need a product estimate that allows adaptive queries. **Lemma 6.1 (separate-cap direct product).** Let $D\subseteq\{0,1\}^{n}$, let $P:D\to\{0,1\}$, let $\mu$ be a probability distribution supported on $D$, and let $L,r\geq0$ be integers. Suppose that every deterministic Boolean-output decision tree of depth at most $L$ has success probability at most $\beta$ for computing $P$ under $\mu$. Draw $U_1,\ldots,U_r$ independently from $\mu$. A classical algorithm may choose queries adaptively among these inputs, use random coins, and receive side information, provided that the side information and coins together are independent of the entire tuple $(U_1,\ldots,U_r)$. If it makes at most $L$ queries to each input on every run, counting repeated queries, then \[ \Pr\!\left[\mathcal A(U_1,\ldots,U_r) =\bigl(P(U_1),\ldots,P(U_r)\bigr)\right]\leq\beta^r. \tag{6.3} \] This is OpenAI’s separate-cap form of the direct product. The choice of which input to query next can depend on every answer so far. Section 6.5 proves the bound by splitting the probability mass at each query. [OpenAI, Lemma 4.1][OpenAI2026]. Apply Lemma 6.1 to independent \(U_1,\ldots,U_r\sim\mu\): if an algorithm makes at most \(L\) queries to each \(U_h\) on every execution, then \[ \Pr[\widehat s=(P(U_1),\ldots,P(U_r))]\le(2/3)^r. \] This uses the one-input success bound even when $\mu$ biases the answer bit. It requires the predictor to obey the cap on every run. The board tree has only the global budget $G$. Let \(N_i\) be the number of queries made during the complete dummy run to the strings \(A_{i,1},\ldots,A_{i,r}\), counting repetitions, and call column \(i\) heavy when \(N_i>L\). Since \(\sum_iN_i\le G\), at most \(G/L\) columns are heavy, and \(I\) remains uniform conditional on the dummy run. Thus \[ \Pr[I\text{ is heavy}]\le\frac{G}{mL}. \tag{6.4} \] The threshold bounds the total number of queries to all \(r\) strings of a column, so in particular a nonheavy run uses at most \(L\) queries to each of those strings. **Fixed-column, fixed-time prediction.** Fix $i\in[m]$ and $q\in\{1,\ldots,G\}$ before drawing the board. We claim \[ \Pr[i\text{ is nonheavy and query }q\text{ lies in }B_{i,s_i}] \le(2/3)^r. \tag{6.5} \] A run that stops before its $q$-th query does not contribute. Why keep nonheaviness inside the event? Whether the algorithm queries column $i$ again can depend on the answers already returned. For example, it can stop when an answer determines the value of $P$ and continue otherwise. Conditioning on a light run can then increase the success probability. [Appendix B.3](#CL-conditioning-counterexample) gives a one-query instance with conditional success one. We need a predictor that operates on the original independent inputs. *Proof.* Give the predictor $r$ independent target strings $U_h\sim\mu$. Fill column $i$ with them. Supply the zero locations of all columns, the address strings of every other column, and the blank cells. Together these data are independent of the target tuple and specify the rest of the dummy board. Replay the queries *before time $q$*. Forward a query to a target string if fewer than $L$ target queries have been forwarded, and otherwise abort. Answer every other query from the supplied data. At time $q$ inspect just the proposed coordinate: if it lies in $B_{i,s}$, output $s$ without reading the bit. Output a fixed default vector on abort, early termination, or any other proposal. Thus $q$ counts all proposed board queries, while $L$ caps the forwarded target queries in total. On every run each target has been queried at most $L$ times, so (6.3) bounds the predictor’s success by $(2/3)^r$. On the joint event in (6.5), even the *complete* dummy run uses at most $L$ target queries. The replay therefore agrees up to time $q$ and outputs $s_i$. The joint event is therefore contained in predictor success, which can also include a correct default guess. This proves (6.5). For a fixed $i$, any nonheavy visit to the true cell has a witness among the $G$ query times. Union over these times, average over the independent uniform column $I$, and add the heavy-column bound (6.4). This gives \[ \Pr[T\text{ on }Y^{(0)}\text{ queries a bit of }B_{I,s_I}] \le\frac{G}{mL}+G(2/3)^r. \tag{6.6} \] To see the cancellation, let $E_{iq}$ be the joint event in (6.5). The contribution from nonheavy columns is bounded by \[ \frac1m\sum_{i=1}^m\sum_{q=1}^G\Pr(E_{iq}) \le\frac1m\sum_{i=1}^mG(2/3)^r=G(2/3)^r. \] Thus query times cost a factor $G$; the column index costs no factor because it is sampled uniformly. When $G=0$ there is no query time to consider. ### 6.5. Proof of the separate-cap direct product Fix the coins and the independent outside data, leaving a deterministic predictor on $r$ independent inputs. Its guesses for the $r$ answers can be correlated: the next input to inspect and the entire output word may depend on the same history. Fix a transcript up to some node. The recorded answers determine every query the tree made on the way there, including which input it chose next. A tuple reaches that node exactly when each input agrees with its own recorded answers. Thus the compatible tuples form a product set, and their unnormalized weight factors even on a branch of weight zero. The induction will bound the correct mass there by a product of one-input values, each with its own remaining allowance. We extend $\mu$ by zero outside $D$ and regard $P$ as a partial Boolean function on the full cube, so that off-promise inputs never count as correct. For any nonnegative weight $\nu$ on that cube, write $\nu_{a,b}(x)=\nu(x)\mathbf1_{\{x_a=b\}}$, and define \[ \begin{aligned} W_0(\nu)&=\max_{b\in\{0,1\}}\sum_{x\in D:P(x)=b}\nu(x),\\ W_{c+1}(\nu)&=\max\!\left\{W_c(\nu),\ \max_{a}\bigl(W_c(\nu_{a,0})+W_c(\nu_{a,1})\bigr)\right\}. \end{aligned} \tag{6.7} \] (If there are no coordinates, the inner maximum is omitted.) The first term in the second line keeps every strategy within the old allowance, and the remaining terms query $a$ and then use its two best continuations. Induction on depth shows that $W_c(\nu)$ is the maximum weighted success of a tree of depth at most $c$. At depth zero the two constants are the only choices. At the next depth, each displayed candidate is attained by an old optimal tree or by a query followed by two optimal smaller trees; conversely, every tree is a constant or starts with some query $a$, and splitting its success sum by that answer bounds it by the corresponding candidate. In particular, $W_c$ is nonnegative and nondecreasing in $c$, and the two branch values with one fewer query sum to at most the old value. Since a nonnegative weight of mass zero vanishes pointwise, all its success values are zero. Now give input $h$ its own nonnegative weight $\nu_h$ and allowance $c_h$. We claim that every vector-output tree $T$ respecting these allowances on every branch satisfies \[ \sum_{u_1,\ldots,u_r\in D} \left(\prod_{h=1}^{r}\nu_h(u_h)\right) \mathbf1_{\{T(u_1,\ldots,u_r)=(P(u_1),\ldots,P(u_r))\}} \leq\prod_{h=1}^{r}W_{c_h}(\nu_h). \tag{6.8} \] At a leaf with output $s$, the success mass is exactly \[ \prod_h \sum_{x\in D:P(x)=s_h}\nu_h(x)\le \prod_h W_{c_h}(\nu_h). \] For the induction step, suppose $T$ queries coordinate $a$ of input $h$, so $c_h>0$. On answer $b$, only the $h$-th factor changes: the new weight is $\nu_{h,a,b}(x)=\nu_h(x)\mathbf1_{\{x_a=b\}}$ and the allowance is $c_h-1$. Apply the induction hypothesis to both subtrees and add. Their combined success mass is at most \[ \left(\prod_{j\ne h}W_{c_j}(\nu_j)\right) \bigl(W_{c_h-1}(\nu_{h,a,0})+W_{c_h-1}(\nu_{h,a,1})\bigr) \le \prod_jW_{c_j}(\nu_j) \] by (6.7). The next query can involve different inputs in the two subtrees. At their parent, only the factor associated with input $h$ changes. This proves (6.8). At the root take every $\nu_h=\mu$ and $c_h=L$. Since $W_L(\mu)\le\beta$, the product is at most $\beta^r$. Finally average the bound over the coins and outside information. Their joint independence from the input tuple leaves its law equal to $\mu^{\otimes r}$ for each induced tree. This proves Lemma 6.1. The word *joint* matters: for independent fair bits $X,Y$, their parity is independent of either one, but knowing it lets a zero-query tree guess the pair with probability $1/2$. $\square$ OpenAI proves the separate-cap product bound by multiplying conditional continuation values, following [Drucker, Lemmas 3.1–3.2][Drucker2012]. [Appendix B.1](#CL-product-law) gives that proof and identifies its potential with the weighted mass in (6.8). Drucker’s global-budget theorem and Shaltiel’s separate-cap XOR bound have related hypotheses and different conclusions. [OpenAI, §4.1][OpenAI2026]; [Shaltiel, §5][Shaltiel2001]. ### 6.6. The discrepancy contradiction and the floors On the dummy board three events account for any distinguishing advantage: finding the selected zero, spending more than $L$ address queries in the selected column, or guessing the selected address at one of the $G$ query times. By the reference-path bound of §6.3, the count of heavy columns, and the capped prediction bound, \[ \left|\Pr[T(Y^{(1)})=1]-\Pr[T(Y^{(0)})=1]\right| \le\frac{2G}{m^2}+\frac{G}{mL}+G(2/3)^r. \tag{6.9} \] Using the original early/late estimate gives the slightly weaker form \[ \left|\Pr[T(Y^{(1)})=1]-\Pr[T(Y^{(0)})=1]\right| \le\frac{4G}{m^2}+\frac{G}{mL}+G(2/3)^r. \tag{6.10} \] Take $G=\lfloor mL/100\rfloor$. Since $L\le m$, the zero and heavy-column terms are at most $4/100$ and $1/100$, even with the weaker zero estimate. As $r=20\log_2m$ and $(2/3)^2<1/2$, the remaining term satisfies \[ G(2/3)^r\le\tfrac1{100}m^{2-20\log_2(3/2)} \le\tfrac1{100}m^{-8}. \] The entire bound is therefore at most $6/100<1/3$. Suppose, for contradiction, that a randomized algorithm with worst-case query cost at most \(G\) computed \(F_{P,C,m}\) with error at most \(1/3\) on every input. Since every dummy input is a zero-input and every supported planted input is a one-input, averaging the pointwise correctness requirements gives an output-one probability gap of at least \(2/3-1/3=1/3\). Once we fix the algorithm's random coins, the resulting deterministic tree has depth at most \(G\), so its gap is at most \(6/100\). Averaging over the coins preserves that upper bound, contradicting the preceding lower bound. The total function has finitely many input bits, so reading all of them computes it exactly and its randomized complexity is a finite minimum. Since no algorithm of budget \(G\) exists, \(R(F_{P,C,m})>G\), which proves the generic theorem. Returning to the Forrelation family, we fix \(k\ge2\), let \(P=P_{k,m}\) on \(km\) bits, and choose \[ L=\left\lfloor\frac{m^{1-1/k}}{(\log_2m)^2}\right\rfloor. \] The hardness theorem of [§8.10](#forr_uniform_assembly) gives $L For $t\ge8$ the unfloored allowance is at least one. Both floors, first in $L$ and then in $G$, cost at most a factor two apiece since $\lfloor x\rfloor\ge x/2$ for $x\ge1$. The [finite inequalities](#CL-floors) give the coefficient $1/400$ below. We choose \(t\) beyond both \(8\) and the fixed-\(k\) Forrelation threshold, and take the circuit $C_{k,t}$ (also denoted $C_{k,m}$ when $m=4^t$) that §4 used to define \(F_{k,m}\) and §5 used to prove its quantum upper bound. Since it realizes the same promise and value, the generic lower theorem applies to this circuit. **Proposition 6.2 (randomized lower bound).** For each fixed integer \(k\ge2\), for every sufficiently large power of four \(m\), the total function from the construction satisfies \[ R(F_{k,m})> \left\lfloor\frac m{100} \left\lfloor\frac{m^{1-1/k}}{(\log_2m)^2}\right\rfloor\right\rfloor. \] Together with the floor calculation, this yields \[ R(F_{k,m})\ge \frac1{400}\frac{m^{2-1/k}}{(\log_2m)^2} =\Omega_k\!\left(\frac{m^{2-1/k}}{(\log m)^2}\right). \] The arithmetic coefficient is uniform in $k$, and $t\ge13669k^2$ is an explicit sufficient combined threshold for the hardness and floor estimates. The fixed-$k$ formulation allows the threshold to depend on $k$. (With natural logarithms the coefficient becomes \((\ln 2)^2/400\).) The circuit $C_{k,t}$ needed only to realize the promise and its value. We may therefore use the very circuit that the quantum algorithm verifies. Both costs now apply to one function.

rows.label: sec-7
rows.text: On the quantum side the power of $m$ is $1/2$; on the classical side it is $2-1/k$. Their ratio is \[ \frac{2-1/k}{1/2}=4-\frac2k . \] Below this ratio the quotient of the bounds contains a positive power of $m$, which grows faster than each fixed power of $\log m$. To exclude a proposed universal power we may choose $k$ *after* the power is proposed, then keep it fixed while $m$ grows. This is the last step in [OpenAI’s proof, §5][OpenAI2026]. Fix \(k\geq2\), write \(m=4^t\), and let \(C_{k,t}\) be the exact circuit for the promise and value of \(P_{k,m}\) specified in §3.2 and constructed in Appendix G.3. In the notation of §4, set \(F_{k,m}=F_{k,m}[C_{k,t}]\). The quantum estimate of §5.4 and the randomized estimate of §6.6 give constants \(C_k>0\), \(b_k\in\mathbb N\), and \(t_0(k)\) such that \[ Q(F_{k,m})\leq C_k\sqrt m\,(\log_2m)^{b_k}, \qquad R(F_{k,m})\geq\frac1{400}\, \frac{m^{2-1/k}}{(\log_2m)^2} \qquad(t\geq t_0(k)). \tag{7.1} \] The quantum estimate allows \(b_k=6\) for every \(k\); its constant and the threshold may depend on \(k\) and are independent of \(t\), and the circuit has size \(O_k(m(\log_2m)^2)\). Both inequalities in (7.1) concern this one circuit, since a separation needs a single function witnessing both estimates. These are the conclusions of [OpenAI (2026), Propositions 3.3 and 4.2][OpenAI2026]; the explicit logarithmic power and floor constant come from the accompanying formal development. ### 7.1. A fixed parameter and a strict exponent gap Fix \(0\leq\alpha<4\). Choose an integer \(k\geq2\) with \[ k>\frac{2}{4-\alpha}. \tag{7.2} \] This choice ensures that \[ \varepsilon_\alpha=2-\frac1k-\frac\alpha2>0. \] We keep \(k\) fixed from now on. Since \(\sqrt m(\log_2m)^{b_k}\geq1\) for \(m\geq4\), the upper estimate in (7.1) gives \[ 1+Q(F_{k,m})\leq(1+C_k)\sqrt m\,(\log_2m)^{b_k}. \] All bases are positive and \(\alpha\geq0\), so exponentiation preserves this inequality, and combining it with the lower estimate yields the finite quotient bound \[ \frac{R(F_{k,m})}{(1+Q(F_{k,m}))^\alpha} \geq \frac{1}{400(1+C_k)^\alpha}\, \frac{m^{\varepsilon_\alpha}}{(\log_2m)^{2+\alpha b_k}} \qquad(t\geq\max\{t_0(k),1\}). \tag{7.3} \] The numerator is a positive power of $m$ and the denominator a fixed power of $\log_2m$, so the quotient tends to infinity. At the threshold $\alpha=4-2/k$ the power gap in (7.3) vanishes. The divergence follows for every proposed power $\alpha<4$ by choosing $k$ with $2-1/k-\alpha/2>0$. In particular $k=3$ rules out even the shifted cubic bound, and therefore the original conjecture: \[ \nexists C\in\mathbb R\quad\forall n\ge1\quad \forall f:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\},\qquad R(f)\le C Q(f)^3. \] Indeed any such $C$ would bound the quotient on the left of (7.3) by $\max\{C,1\}$ at $\alpha=3$. [Aaronson et al., Conjecture 2][ABKRT2020]. ### 7.2. Excluding all smaller universal powers Let \(K>0\) be any proposed universal constant. With \(k\) already chosen by (7.2), the quotient in (7.3) exceeds \(K\) for every sufficiently large \(t\), so the corresponding function violates \[ R(f)\leq K(1+Q(f))^\alpha. \tag{7.4} \] The construction uses a finite nonempty set of input coordinates, and a bijection with \([n]\), where \(n\geq1\) is its cardinality, preserves both query complexities: we rename each queried coordinate and leave every answer, probability and query count unchanged. Consequently the structured function is also a counterexample among the total functions \(\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}\) quantified in (7.4). Thus every $0\le\alpha<4$ fails on a total Boolean function. [Appendix A](#R3-A-RESULT) gives one absolute constant for the power four on all such functions. Four is therefore the minimum in (1.1), and $\alpha_{\mathrm{tot}}=4$. The proof chooses the parameters in the order \[ \alpha<4\ ;\quad k=k(\alpha)\ ;\quad K>0\ ;\quad t\text{ sufficiently large}. \] Letting \(k\) grow with \(t\) requires estimates uniform in \(k\); these go beyond what the theorem just proved requires, and §7.3 shows what they give. ### 7.3. Letting $k$ grow with $t$ *This section goes beyond OpenAI's paper. AI systems produced it, and no person has reviewed it.* This is a quantitative consequence of the estimates developed in this reconstruction, beyond the fixed-$k$ argument needed for OpenAI’s Theorem 1.1. It uses the uniform lower bound of Theorem 8.2 and the explicit quantum constant in Appendix E.5; substituting a growing $k$ into (7.1) alone would not justify it. The final choice of $k(t)$ and its rate are an ordinary deduction in [Appendix C.2](#record-schedule-proof), separate from the formally stated fixed-$k$ family. Write $m=4^t$, $\ell=2t$. To let $k$ grow, compare the bounds on $\log_2 R$ and $4\log_2 Q$. The classical exponent $2-1/k$ gives $2\ell-\ell/k$ in the lower bound. In the quantum upper bound the decoding factor $2^{10k}$ adds $40k$ after taking the fourth power and the logarithm. Balancing $\ell/k$ with $40k$ gives \[ k(t)=\left\lfloor\sqrt{t/20}\right\rfloor,\qquad F_t=F_{k(t),4^t}\quad(t\ge80). \] Both losses are of order $\sqrt\ell$, while the logarithm of the quantum budget is $\ell/2+O(\sqrt\ell+\log\ell)$. The [uniform Forrelation estimate](#forr_proof_spine) applies since $15k+2\le2t$. With the [finite rate in Appendix C.2](#record-schedule-proof) we obtain $R(F_t)\ge Q(F_t)^{4-O(1/\sqrt\ell+\log\ell/\ell)}$. The classical lower bound diverges along this family, so the universal quartic bound gives $Q(F_t)\to\infty$ as well.

rows.label: sec-8
rows.text: *This section goes beyond OpenAI's paper. AI systems produced it, and no person has reviewed it.* Lean checks the proof of the fixed-$k$ estimate (8.3); only AI agents have compared that statement with the one OpenAI's paper uses. Up to this point Lemma 3.1 let us treat the classical hardness of one address bit as given. For a fixed $k$ the published Forrelation bound suffices. To see how the power $1-1/k$ arises, and to control the cost when $k$ grows, we now prove that bound directly for the promise used on the board. ### 8.1. The Walsh correlation and the classical lower bound Fix $k\ge2$ and $m=4^t$. The bits in block $j$ specify signs $z_j(a)$ indexed by $a\in\mathbb F_2^{2t}$. Let $W_{ab}=(-1)^{a\cdot b}$, $H=W/\sqrt m$, $u=m^{-1/2}(1,\ldots,1)^{\mathsf T}$, and $D_z=\operatorname{diag}(z)$. The normalization makes $H$ orthogonal. Indeed, the inner product of rows $a,c$ of $W$ is $\sum_{b\in\mathcal X}(-1)^{(a+c)\cdot b}$. If $a=c$, the sum is $m$. Otherwise we choose a coordinate in which $a+c$ is one and pair every $b$ with the vector obtained by flipping that coordinate, so the terms cancel in pairs. Together with the symmetry of $a\cdot b$ and the identity $z(a)^2=1$, this gives $$ WW^{\mathsf T}=mI,\qquad H^{\mathsf T}=H,\qquad H^2=I, \qquad \|u\|_2=1,\qquad D_z^{\mathsf T}D_z=I. $$ Thus $|u^{\mathsf T}D_{z_0}H\cdots HD_{z_{k-1}}u|\le1$ by Cauchy–Schwarz. In fact a quantum algorithm can apply this product to $u$, from right to left, using one phase query per sign diagonal. The overlap with $u$ is the statistic in [§3.1](#forr_definition): \[ \Phi(z)=u^{\mathsf T}D_{z_0}H\cdots H D_{z_{k-1}}u,\qquad \delta=32^{-k}. \tag{8.1} \] The two promised sets are \[ P^{-1}(1)=\{\Phi\ge\delta\},\qquad P^{-1}(0)=\{|\Phi|\le\delta/2\}. \tag{8.2} \] **Theorem 8.1 (fixed-parameter Forrelation hardness).** For every fixed integer $k\ge2$, there is an integer $t_0(k)$ such that, for every $t\ge t_0(k)$, \[ R(P_{k,4^t})> L_{k,4^t},\qquad L_{k,m}=\left\lfloor\frac{m^{1-1/k}}{(\log_2m)^2}\right\rfloor. \tag{8.3} \] This is the lower-bound assertion of OpenAI's Lemma 2.1(i), with the same normalization and promise [OpenAI (2026), §2.1, pp. 3–4]. The proof gives the sufficient choice $t_0(k)=13669k^2$. All analytic logarithms below are natural (the logarithm in $L_{k,m}$ is base two). **Theorem 8.2 (uniform Forrelation hardness).** For integers $k\ge2$ and $t\ge1$, let $m=4^t$. If $15k+2\le2t$, then \[ R(P_{k,m})>\frac2{18225}\frac{m^{1-1/k}}{k^2\ln(4km)}. \] This estimate implies (8.3) for fixed $k$ and supplies the lower bound for the growing family of §7.3. Its proof concludes in [§8.10](#forr_uniform_assembly). The [formal uniform estimate](proof_index.md#the-partial-function-and-its-certificates) has this same numerical constant and dimension condition. This correspondence concerns the stated bound; it does not certify every source comparison in Appendix D or independently review the printed derivation. We compare two distributions on the same signs. In the first the signs are independent and fair. In the second we sample independent Gaussian vectors, pair each with its Walsh transform, and then sample signs with biases depending on the resulting pairs. We will prove that the mean of $\Phi$ differs appreciably between the two distributions, while the mean output of every sufficiently shallow decision tree differs very little. For both comparisons we interpolate between the distributions and expand the derivative as a sum over paths, with one coordinate per block and a Walsh entry for each consecutive pair of coordinates. The Gaussian pairing and transformed integration by parts follow Bansal and Sinha. We use a bounded algebraic transform and interpolate only the first block. To bound the difference between the expected outputs of an adaptive tree we adapt the martingale argument of Girish, Tal and Wu to the product biases arising along that interpolation. [Bansal and Sinha, §3 and Lemma 4.3][BansalSinha2021], [Girish, Tal and Wu, §1.3][GirishTalWu2021]. ### 8.2. Multilinear expectation and derivatives Let $I$ be a finite coordinate set and $g:\{-1,1\}^I\to\mathbb R$. Its multilinear extension is \[ F_g(\mu)=\mathcal E_\mu g =\sum_{z\in\{-1,1\}^I}g(z) \prod_{i\in I}\frac{1+\mu_i z_i}{2}. \tag{8.4} \] For $|\mu_i|\le1$ the weights are nonnegative and sum to one, so these factors define independent signs of means $\mu_i$. Thus $F_g$ is an expectation on that cube, and $|F_g(\mu)|\le\max_z|g(z)|$. For arbitrary real $\mu$, the same finite sum defines a polynomial that is affine in each coordinate. For one coordinate $i$, the discrete difference \[ \partial_i g(z)=\frac{g(z_{i\leftarrow1})-g(z_{i\leftarrow-1})}{2} \] is independent of $z_i$, and separating the terms of (8.4) with signs $+1$ and $-1$ gives \[ \partial_i F_g(\mu)=F_{\partial_i g}(\mu),\qquad \partial_i^2F_g=0,\qquad \partial_i\partial_jF_g=\partial_j\partial_iF_g. \tag{8.5} \] The derivative on the left is an ordinary polynomial derivative, and the subscript on the right is the discrete difference just defined. Every iterated discrete derivative is bounded in absolute value by $\max|g|$. For example, $g(z)=z_i z_j$ (with $i\ne j$) has $F_g(\mu)=\mu_i\mu_j$, $\partial_iF_g=\mu_j$, $\partial_i\partial_jF_g=1$ and $\partial_i^2F_g=0$. When $|\mu_i|<1$, we define the centered derivative character \[ \xi_i(z_i)=\frac{z_i-\mu_i}{1-\mu_i^2}. \] The one-coordinate identity \[ \frac{1+\mu_i z_i}{2}\,\xi_i(z_i)=\frac{z_i}{2} \] and finite multiplication over distinct coordinates imply \[ \partial_JF_g(\mu) =\mathcal E_\mu\!\left[g(z)\prod_{i\in J}\xi_i(z_i)\right], \qquad \mathcal E_\mu\xi_i=0, \qquad |\mu_i|\le\tfrac12\ \Longrightarrow\ |\xi_i|\le2. \tag{8.6} \] Here $J$ is a set of distinct coordinates, and $\partial_J$ means one derivative in each coordinate of $J$. These raw derivatives let us work under the biased product measure itself, in place of an orthonormal biased Fourier basis. ### 8.3. A bounded Gaussian integration identity We choose the rounding function so that Gaussian integration by parts differentiates the remaining factor. With $Z$ standard Gaussian we want $\mathbb E[\varphi(Z)g(Z)]=\mathbb E[\Psi(Z)g'(Z)]$. Integration by parts against the Gaussian density suggests starting with a positive weight $\Psi$ and setting $\varphi=x\Psi-\Psi'$. The bias must stay inside $[-1/2,1/2]$ for the tree bound, and $\varphi'>0$ will make the Gaussian factors in the expectation of $\Phi$ positive. Try $\Psi=c(a+x^2)^{-1/2}$, with $a,c>0$. Then $x\Psi-\Psi'$ tends to $\pm c$ at the two ends of the line. Its derivative is \[ c\,\frac{a(a+1)+(a-2)x^2}{(a+x^2)^{5/2}} . \] Choosing $a=2$ cancels the quadratic term and gives a positive derivative everywhere. With $c=1/2$ the limiting biases are the required endpoints. Thus put \[ q(x)=\sqrt{2+x^2},\qquad \Psi(x)=\frac1{2q(x)},\qquad \varphi(x)=\frac{x(3+x^2)}{2q(x)^3}. \tag{8.7} \] Differentiation gives \[ \varphi'(x)=\frac3{q(x)^5},\qquad \Psi'(x)=-\frac{x}{2q(x)^3},\qquad \varphi=x\Psi-\Psi'. \tag{8.8} \] The function $\varphi$ is odd and $|\varphi|\le1/2$; for the latter bound, we square the nonnegative sides of $|x|(3+x^2)\le q(x)^3$ and use \[ (2+x^2)^3-x^2(3+x^2)^2=8+3x^2\ge0. \] Since both denominators in the next product are minimized at zero, \[ 0<\Psi(x)\varphi'(y) =\frac{3}{2\sqrt{2+x^2}(2+y^2)^{5/2}} \le\frac3{16}. \tag{8.9} \] Equality holds at $x=y=0$. We use this sharp product estimate only after establishing the integration identity. The functions $\Psi$ and $\varphi$ are bounded, and so are their derivatives used below. Let $\gamma(x)=(2\pi)^{-1/2}e^{-x^2/2}$, so that (8.8) gives $(\Psi\gamma)'=-\varphi\gamma$. If $G$ is continuously differentiable and both $G$ and $G'$ are bounded, we integrate $(\Psi G\gamma)'$ over $[-A,A]$ and let $A\to\infty$ to obtain \[ \mathbb E[\varphi(Z)G(Z)] =\mathbb E[\Psi(Z)G'(Z)],\qquad Z\sim N(0,1). \tag{8.10} \] Indeed, the boundary term tends to zero, and the two remaining integrands are bounded multiples of the Gaussian density. Holding the other independent Gaussian coordinates fixed gives the coordinatewise version, and the uniform bounds used below ensure absolute integrability when we then average over those coordinates. We also use two elementary facts about a standard Gaussian vector $U\in\mathbb R^m$. First, if $e$ is a unit vector, then $R_eU=U-2\langle e,U\rangle e$ has the same law as $U$, since the reflection is orthogonal: it preserves $\|U\|_2^2$ and its Jacobian has absolute determinant one. Second, \[ \mathbb E\langle e,U\rangle^2=\sum_i e_i^2=1, \tag{8.11} \] because independent centered standard coordinates have covariance $I$. Both facts concern the underlying product Gaussian measure; the pair $(U,HU)$ is correlated, and we never assign it an independent product law. Gaussian integration by parts and bounded truncation have antecedents in the work of Bansal and Sinha [Bansal and Sinha, §4, especially Lemma 4.3], whose truncation is the Gaussian distribution function minus $1/2$. Formula (8.7) makes a different choice, so we prove its distribution and moment bounds here. ### 8.4. The rounded Gaussian chain and its zero endpoint Write $h=k-1$ for the number of Gaussian links. We draw independent standard Gaussian vectors $U_0,\ldots,U_{h-1}\in\mathbb R^m$ and set \[ V_j=HU_j,\qquad X_j(a)=\varphi(U_j(a)),\qquad Y_j(a)=\varphi(V_j(a)). \] For $0\le s\le1$, we give each coordinate of the $k$-block sign cube the bias \[ w_s(r,a)= \begin{cases} sX_0(a),&r=0,\\ Y_{r-1}(a)X_r(a),&1\le r \[ h_g(0)=F_g(0)=\mathbb E_{\mathcal U}g, \tag{8.14} \] where $\mathcal U$ is the uniform distribution on the sign cube. Since the argument applies to every $g$, it identifies the whole distribution. ### 8.5. The iterated chain rule across the Gaussian blocks The endpoints of $h_g$ are now identified: $h_g(0)$ is the uniform expectation of $g$, and $h_g(1)$ is its expectation under the correlated sign law. We must bound their difference for a shallow tree. Differentiating the interpolation introduces one bias factor in the first block. We apply (8.10) and the chain rule successively. After each application the mixed partial involves one further block and its coefficient contains one more Walsh entry of magnitude $m^{-1/2}$. For fixed Gaussian vectors, $F_g(w_s(U))$ is a polynomial in $s$ of degree at most $m$, whose finitely many coefficients are bounded functions of $U$ because all factors $X_j,Y_j$ are bounded. Taking expectations coefficient by coefficient shows that $h_g$ is itself a polynomial. In particular, differentiation commutes with the Gaussian average by finite linearity, and the ordinary chain rule gives \[ h_g'(s)=\sum_a\mathbb E_U \left[X_0(a)\,\partial_{(0,a)}F_g(w_s(U))\right]. \tag{8.15} \] We apply (8.10) in $U_0(a)$. The chain rule has one term from bias $(0,a)$ and a sum over the coordinates in block 1. The first term contains a second derivative of $F_g$ in $(0,a)$ and is zero by multilinearity. If $k\ge3$, the term indexed by $b$ in the sum contains a Walsh entry and the factor $\varphi'(V_0(b))X_1(b)$, and the next Stein identity removes $X_1(b)$. If $k=2$, the next block is already the last, so there is no $X_1$ factor. For the two-block calculation, write $U=U_0$, $V=HU$ and $F=F_g$, so the biases are $w_s=(s\varphi(U),\varphi(V))$. Write $F_{0a}$ for the derivative in coordinate $(0,a)$, appending subscripts for further derivatives. For a coordinate $a$ of block zero, \[ \frac{\partial}{\partial U_a}F_{0a}(w_s) =s\varphi'(U_a)\underbrace{F_{0a,0a}(w_s)}_{0} +\sum_b H_{b,a}\varphi'(V_b)F_{0a,1b}(w_s). \] The first term vanishes because a multilinear polynomial has zero second derivative in any one coordinate. Applying (8.10) to the remaining factor $\varphi(U_a)$ in (8.15) gives \[ h_g'(s)=\sum_{a,b}H_{b,a}\mathbb E\!\left[ \Psi(U_a)\varphi'(V_b)F_{0a,1b}(w_s)\right]. \] There is one derivative in each block and one Walsh factor. For three blocks, the same step leaves another Gaussian bias factor, so integration by parts must be applied again. The next calculation shows why that iteration creates no extra term. For $k=3$, write $U=U_0$ and $U'=U_1$ for the two independent Gaussian layers, $V=V_0=HU$, $V'=V_1=HU'$ and $F=F_g$. The first integration by parts differentiates $F_{0a}(w_s)$ with respect to $U_a$ and gives a sum over $b$ in block 1. In the summand indexed by $b$, the second differentiates $F_{0a,1b}(w_s)$ with respect to $U'_b$ and gives a sum over $c$ in block 2. The three biases are \[ w_s=(s\varphi(U),\ \varphi(V)\varphi(U'),\ \varphi(V')). \] With $F_{0a,1b}$ denoting the indicated mixed derivative, the first full coordinate derivative is \[ \frac{\partial}{\partial U_a}F_{0a}(w_s) =s\varphi'(U_a)\underbrace{F_{0a,0a}(w_s)}_{0} +\sum_bH_{b,a}\varphi'(V_b)\varphi(U'_b)F_{0a,1b}(w_s). \tag{8.16} \] Hence (8.15) becomes \[ h_g'(s)=\sum_{a,b}H_{b,a}\mathbb E \left[\Psi(U_a)\varphi'(V_b)\varphi(U'_b)F_{0a,1b}(w_s)\right]. \tag{8.17} \] Since the accumulated factor $\Psi(U_a)\varphi'(V_b)$ is independent of the entire layer $U'$, we may apply (8.10) once more, and the remaining derivative is \[ \frac{\partial}{\partial U'_b}F_{0a,1b}(w_s) =\varphi(V_b)\varphi'(U'_b) \underbrace{F_{0a,1b,1b}(w_s)}_{0} +\sum_cH_{c,b}\varphi'(V'_c)F_{0a,1b,2c}(w_s). \tag{8.18} \] ![The three-block chain rule for coordinates $a,b,c$. The two differentiations give the factors $H_{b,a}$ and $H_{c,b}$. The term containing a second derivative in the middle coordinate $(1,b)$ is zero by multilinearity.](figures/forrelation_chain.svg) The weights accumulated at the first crossing depend only on the first Gaussian layer. Differentiation in the second layer therefore leaves them fixed. Thus \[ h_g'(s)=\sum_{a,b,c}H_{b,a}H_{c,b}\mathbb E \left[\Psi(U_a)\varphi'(V_b)\Psi(U'_b)\varphi'(V'_c) F_{0a,1b,2c}(w_s)\right]. \tag{8.19} \] The index of the $U'$ coordinate in (8.18) is the same $b$ as the middle coordinate of $F_{0a,1b}$ in (8.17). We apply the Stein identity to the factor $\varphi(U'_b)$ multiplying that derivative. Hence we differentiate $F_{0a,1b}(w_s)$, and its same-coordinate term is precisely $F_{0a,1b,1b}=0$. **Path identity.** For general $k$, each summand contains one differentiation in each successive block. Induct on $j$, for $0\le j\le k-2$. At $j=0$, (8.15) contains $\partial_{(0,p_0)}F_g$ and $X_0(p_0)$ with weight one. After the first $j$ applications of (8.10), the derivative of $F_g$ includes $(j,p_j)$, the remaining $X$ factor is $X_j(p_j)$, and the weight accumulated so far depends only on $U_0,\ldots,U_{j-1}$. We apply (8.10) in $U_j(p_j)$, holding that weight fixed. Differentiation through the bias in block $j$ gives zero by multilinearity. The term indexed by $p_{j+1}$ from block $j+1$ adds one partial derivative and multiplies the weight by \[ H_{p_{j+1},p_j}\Psi(U_j(p_j))\varphi'(V_j(p_{j+1})). \] In the last block there is no further $X$ factor. For $k=2$ only one application of (8.10) is needed. Defining the coordinate set of a path by $S_p=\{(r,p_r):0\le r \[ h_g'(s)=\sum_{p\in[m]^k} \left(\prod_{j ### 8.6. The mean of Forrelation under the two sign distributions Apply the identity first to $g=\Phi$. In its Walsh expansion, the coefficient of each monomial is $1/m$ times the Walsh product for that same path: \[ \Phi(z)=\frac1m\sum_{p\in[m]^k} \left(\prod_{j \[ \mathbb E_{\mathcal U}\Phi=0,\qquad \mathbb E_{\mathcal U}\Phi^2=\frac1m. \tag{8.23} \] We apply (8.20)–(8.21) with $g=\Phi$. Each monomial of $\Phi$ has one variable in every block. Differentiating at the selected coordinate in every block kills any monomial that uses a different coordinate in even one block, leaving precisely the path coefficient. Thus its path derivative is the constant \[ \partial_{S_p}F_\Phi =\frac1m\prod_{j \[ q(x)\le\sqrt3\,e^{(x^2-1)/6},\qquad \Psi(x)\varphi'(y)\ge \frac1{18}\exp\!\left[-\frac{x^2-1}{6}-\frac{5(y^2-1)}6\right]. \tag{8.24} \] Multiplying these bounds along a path will produce an exponential $e^{-T_p}$. Its expectation is bounded below using only $\mathbb E T_p=0$, without independence between the selected $U$ and $V$ coordinates. For a fixed path $p$, let \[ T_p=\sum_{j \[ \mathbb E_{\nu_1}\Phi\ge a_k:=18^{-(k-1)} \ge32^{-(k-1)}=32\delta. \tag{8.26} \] For example, the inequality $\Phi\le\delta+\mathbf1_{\{\Phi\ge\delta\}}$ gives $\nu_1(\Phi\ge\delta)\ge a_k-\delta\ge31\delta$, and Markov's inequality applied to (8.23) gives $\mathcal U(|\Phi|>\delta/2)\le4/(m\delta^2)$. ### 8.7. Distinguishing the two distributions with a shallow tree Now let $g$ be the output of a depth-$d$ tree on the $km$ signs, with leaf values in $[-1,1]$. For $\Phi$, multiplying the two Walsh products gave the same positive factor for each path. For $g$ the corresponding factor in (8.20) is a mixed derivative $\partial_{S_p}F_g$ at the random bias $w_{s_*}(U)$. The product of the absolute Walsh entries is $m^{-(k-1)/2}$ and the product of the remaining edge weights is at most $(3/16)^{k-1}$. We therefore need a bound for \[ \sum_{p\in[m]^k}|\partial_{S_p}F_g(\mu)| \] at every bias reached by the chain. A bound only at $\mu=0$ would leave a gap in this step. Indeed expansion of (8.4) in uniform Fourier characters gives \[ \partial_JF_g(\mu) =\sum_{T\supseteq J}\widehat g(T) \prod_{i\in T\setminus J}\mu_i, \qquad \widehat g(T)=2^{-|I|}\sum_zg(z)\prod_{i\in T}z_i. \tag{8.27} \] For example, the monomial $g(z)=\prod_{i\in T}z_i$ with $|T|=k+1$ has $\partial_JF_g(\mu)=\mu_q$ when $T=J\cup\{q\}$ and $|J|=k$. Thus a degree-$(k+1)$ term can have a nonzero order-$k$ derivative at a biased point. The following estimate covers all biases of magnitude at most $1/2$, including every $w_{s_*}(U)$. **Lemma 8.4 (derivative growth at a product bias).** Let $I$ have $n\ge1$ coordinates. Suppose that a deterministic decision tree with integer depth cap $d\ge1$ computes a real function $g$ with leaf values in $[-1,1]$. For every bias $|\mu_i|\le1/2$, every integer $r\ge1$, and every family $\mathcal J$ of distinct $r$-element subsets of $I$, \[ \sum_{J\in\mathcal J}|\partial_JF_g(\mu)| \le \bigl(16rd\ln(4n)\bigr)^{r/2}+2^{-r}. \tag{8.28} \] We use the bound at once. The [proof in §8.8](#forr_tree_growth_proof) controls the centered contributions from the signs actually revealed along a path. A path $p$ in (8.20) is a sequence of $k$ coordinates, one in each labeled block. Its set $S_p$ determines the sequence, since each block occurs exactly once. We can therefore apply (8.28) to the sets $S_p$ without a multiplicity factor $k!$. Substitute the lemma at the common bias inside the expectation in (8.20). With $r=k$ and $n=km$ the resulting bound is \[ \left|\mathbb E_{\nu_1}g-\mathbb E_{\mathcal U}g\right| \le \left(\frac{3}{16\sqrt m}\right)^{k-1} \left[\bigl(16kd\ln(4km)\bigr)^{k/2}+2^{-k}\right]. \tag{8.29} \] The bound (8.29) holds for every real-valued tree of depth at most $d\ge1$ with leaf values in $[-1,1]$ and, by linearity of expectation and the triangle inequality, for every convex mixture of such trees. In particular it holds for a randomized acceptance probability, since on a finite coordinate set with a fixed depth cap there are only finitely many deterministic bit-query trees, and arbitrary random coins can be collected into their probabilities. For fixed $k$, the main term scales as $m^{-(k-1)/2}d^{k/2}$ up to logarithms. Thus for each fixed $k$ the bound stays below the positive Forrelation mean in (8.26) until depth of order $m^{1-1/k}$ up to logarithms. We prove the derivative estimate next; [§8.9](#forr_promise_gap) then converts the comparison of means into a promise lower bound. ### 8.8. Proof of the biased derivative estimate Start with degree one. When the tree queries a fresh coordinate, the sum changes by that centered sign times a coefficient determined by the preceding queries. Even when the next index is chosen adaptively, this sum fluctuates on a $\sqrt d$ scale, up to a tail factor. At degree two, the coefficient of the newly revealed sign is itself a degree-one sum over previous reveals. Stop before any such coefficient exceeds its bound. Each of the next $d$ centered increments is then at most of order $\sqrt d$, and their sum has scale $d$. Each increase in degree multiplies the bound by a factor of order $\sqrt d$ up to a logarithmic tail factor. Counting queried $r$-tuples would give the much larger scale $d^r$. To relate these fluctuations to a derivative of the tree’s output, use the centered characters of (8.6) under the actual biased law. A monomial containing an unqueried coordinate has conditional mean zero at a leaf. Thus only the revealed polynomial needs to be controlled. *The revealed polynomial.* Fix $\mu$. Ultimately we will choose each coefficient to be the sign of the corresponding derivative $\partial_JF_g(\mu)$, and zero outside $\mathcal J$. These are deterministic choices, made before any input is drawn. We prove the bound for every coefficient array of magnitude at most one, since the induction also needs the arrays obtained by fixing one coordinate. Take independent signs with means $\mu_i$, so that their characters $\xi_i$ from (8.6) are independent, centered and bounded by $2$. Let $Q_j$ be the set of coordinates revealed after $j$ queries. A repeated query leaves this set unchanged, and once the tree reaches a leaf we hold the set fixed, so the process has the deterministic horizon $d$. For each degree $r$ and coefficient array $|c(J)|\le1$, we put \[ Y_r^c(Q,z)= \sum_{\substack{J\subseteq Q\\|J|=r}}c(J)\prod_{i\in J}\xi_i(z_i). \tag{8.30} \] \Needspace{8\baselineskip} For a fresh coordinate $q\notin Q$, splitting the subsets according to whether they contain $q$ gives \[ Y_r^c(Q\cup\{q\},z)-Y_r^c(Q,z) =\xi_q(z_q)Y_{r-1}^{c^q}(Q,z), \tag{8.31} \] where $c^q(J)=c(J\cup\{q\})$ when $q\notin J$, and $c^q(J)=0$ when $q\in J$; the contracted array is again bounded by one. For degree two, suppose the revealed set is $Q=\{a,b\}$ and the next fresh query is $q$. Before that query the process is $c(\{a,b\})\xi_a\xi_b$; the new terms are exactly \[ \xi_q\bigl(c(\{a,q\})\xi_a+c(\{b,q\})\xi_b\bigr). \] The factor in parentheses is already determined by the history and is $Y_1^{c^q}(Q,z)$. The fresh centered factor $\xi_q$ has conditional mean zero. In general the newly appearing $r$-subsets are exactly $J\cup\{q\}$ with $J\subseteq Q$ and $|J|=r-1$; removing $q$ is the inverse bijection. This proves the contraction for every degree, with the displayed calculation as its degree-two instance. A fresh coordinate keeps its original conditional distribution under adaptive querying. Indeed, a reachable root-to-node path fixes the values of its distinct queried coordinates, and conversely, by induction through the tree, every input with those values follows that path. The path event is therefore a cylinder under the original product measure, and all unqueried coordinates retain their independent laws on it. In particular, (8.31) is a centered increment conditional on the query history. The same observation gives the identity we use at leaves. A monomial involving an unqueried centered coordinate has conditional expectation zero, and a monomial supported on the leaf's queried set is already determined. Since $g$ is constant at a leaf, \[ \mathcal E_\mu[g(z)Y_r^c(I,z)] =\mathbb E_\mu[g(z)Y_r^c(Q_d,z)]. \tag{8.32} \] By (8.6), the left side is $\sum_{|J|=r}c(J)\partial_JF_g(\mu)$. Thus a bound on the terminal polynomial controls a signed sum of derivatives, even though the tree has seen at most $d$ of the $n$ coordinates. The right side is the sum, over reachable leaves, of each leaf's cylinder probability times its output and the terminal value of $Y_r^c$. Each leaf probability is the product of the answer probabilities at its distinct queried coordinates, with one factor per distinct coordinate however often it is queried. A zero-probability leaf contributes zero, so this finite-sum proof conditions only on events of positive probability. For $R,B>0$, a martingale $Z_j$ starting at zero and making $d\ge1$ increments of magnitude at most $B$ satisfies \[ \Pr\!\left(\max_{j\le d}|Z_j|>R\right) \le2\exp\!\left(-\frac{R^2}{2B^2d}\right). \tag{8.33} \] The [finite exponential-martingale proof](#record-maximal-inequality) appears in Appendix C.3. *Stopping by degree.* For degree one, (8.31) is a sum of at most $d$ centered increments bounded by $2$. For higher degree, each increment also contains a lower-degree polynomial. We control these factors inductively, paying one factor of order $\sqrt{d\Lambda}$ per degree. Fix $\Lambda>0$ and put $K=\sqrt{8d\Lambda}>0$. We claim that, for every bounded coefficient array and every $r\ge0$, \[ \Pr\!\left(\max_{j\le d}|Y_r^c(Q_j,z)|>K^r\right) \le(4n)^r e^{-\Lambda}. \tag{8.34} \] For $r=0$, the expression is the constant $c(\varnothing)$, of magnitude at most one, so the event is empty. Suppose the claim holds at degree $r-1$ for every bounded coefficient array, with the same fixed $\Lambda$ (and hence the same $K$). We stop the degree-$r$ process before any step at which one of the $n$ contracted degree-$(r-1)$ expressions has absolute value greater than $K^{r-1}$; by induction and a union bound, the probability of such a failure is at most \[ n(4n)^{r-1}e^{-\Lambda}. \] Each contracted expression is determined by the history before the next query. The stopping decision is therefore made before its fresh answer is read. Before the stop, the increment (8.31) is centered with magnitude at most $B=2K^{r-1}$, and after it the increment is zero. We apply (8.33) with $R=K^r$, whose exponent is \[ \frac{R^2}{2B^2d}=\frac{K^2}{8d}=\Lambda. \] Since the original and stopped processes agree until a coefficient failure, the probability of a crossing for the original process is at most \[ \bigl(2+n(4n)^{r-1}\bigr)e^{-\Lambda} \le(4n)^r e^{-\Lambda}, \] which proves (8.34). The stopping is essential here, because conditioning on the future event that every coefficient bound holds would not preserve the martingale property; Girish, Tal and Wu make this stopping-versus-conditioning distinction in the standard-decision-tree technical overview [Girish, Tal and Wu, arXiv v2, §1.3, footnote 2]. At any leaf we have the crude bound $|Y_r^c|\le(2n)^r$, from at most $n^r$ subsets with products bounded by $2^r$, and outside the crossing event in (8.34) the better bound $K^r$. Hence (8.32) and $|g|\le1$ give \[ \left|\mathcal E_\mu[gY_r^c(I,\cdot)]\right| \le K^r+(2n)^r(4n)^r e^{-\Lambda}. \tag{8.35} \] Choose the derivative-sign array described at the start of the proof. By (8.6), the left side of (8.35) is then exactly the sum of absolute derivatives in (8.28). Finally, take \[ \Lambda=2r\ln(4n),\qquad K^2=16rd\ln(4n). \] The residual term becomes \[ \frac{(2n)^r(4n)^r}{(4n)^{2r}}=2^{-r}, \] proving (8.28). Since $2^{-r}\le1$, the proof also recovers the original bound $\sum_{J\in\mathcal J}|\partial_JF_g(\mu)|\le(16rd\ln(4n))^{r/2}+1$. All constants are uniform in the bias, the tree and the selected subset family. ### 8.9. Error reduction and inputs outside the promise Under the correlated law the mean of $\Phi$ is at least $a_k$ by (8.26).
