rows.text: ### E.1. Acceptance probability of sequential verification Propositions 5.1 and 5.2 were proved in §§5.1–5.4. The Lean proof of Theorem 1.1 packages the same tournament and sequential verification as a Boolean continuation: its external result is one acceptance bit, rather than the intermediate list. The distinction is in the output and proof interface, not in whether candidates are verified sequentially. The induction below proves the acceptance guarantee directly from the measured-label law. Fix the input. Let $v(i)\in[0,1]$ be the full fresh verifier acceptance probability for candidate $i$, averaging both its newly decoded address and its local-test search, and let $V(L)$ be the probability that at least one fresh verification of a member of $L$ accepts. Sequential verification gives $V([])=0$ and $V(i::L)=v(i)+(1-v(i))V(L)$. Here $i::L$ puts the newest entry first, whereas §5.2 writes pivots in chronological order. Fresh independent verifier outcomes give \[ V(L)=1-\prod_{i\in L}(1-v(i)), \] where entries are counted with their multiplicities. Thus both this probability and the weight product are invariant under permutation, so the two storage conventions give the same quantities. From this recursion, $0\leq V(L)\leq1$; if $s\in L$, then $V(L)\geq v(s)$; and if all $v(i)\leq\varepsilon$, then $V(L)\leq|L|\varepsilon$. Each assertion follows by induction on the list, or equivalently by the union bound for the verifier outcomes. Let $R_n(L)$ be the acceptance probability with $n$ tournament stages still available after history $L$. The recursion is \[ \begin{aligned} R_0(L)&=V(L),\\ R_n(L)&=f(L)V(L)+(1-f(L))\sum_i\frac{w_i}{W}R_{n-1}(i::L) && (n>0,\ W>0),\\ R_n(L)&=V(L) &&(n>0,\ W=0). \end{aligned} \] The two terms for positive $W$ are immediate sampler failure followed by verification, and a successful pivot followed by continuation. At $W=0$ the guaranteed $f(L)=1$ forces the third line. For positive $W$, the weights in the sum are nonnegative and sum to one. It follows inductively that $R_n(L)\in[0,1]$. If all $v(i)\leq\varepsilon$, the same recursion gives $R_n(L)\leq(|L|+n)\varepsilon$, because an immediate stop has bound $|L|\varepsilon$, each successful successor has bound $(|L|+1+n-1)\varepsilon$, and a convex combination preserves the larger bound. For the lower bound, let $I_n(L)$ be the probability that $s$ is absent after $n$ further ideal stages. Suppose that $0\leq\varepsilon\leq1$, that $s$ is dominant, that $v(s)\geq1-\varepsilon$, and that a total horizon $T_0$ satisfies $T_0\varepsilon<1/2$. Suppose also that $f(L)\leq\varepsilon$ for every history of length at most $T_0$ missing $s$, and $f(L)=1$ whenever $W=0$. The inductive assertion is $$ R_n(L)\geq(1-\varepsilon)\bigl(1-I_n(L)-n\varepsilon\bigr) \qquad(|L|+n\leq T_0). $$ At $n=0$, if $s$ is in $L$, the right side is $1-\varepsilon$, which is at most $V(L)$; otherwise $I_0(L)=1$ and the right side is zero. For a positive number of stages, a history that already contains $s$ keeps it after every pivot and at every stopping point, so induction in the recursion gives $R_n(L)\geq v(s)\geq1-\varepsilon$, which suffices because the right side is at most $1-\varepsilon$. For a history missing $s$, its dominant weight is at least $1-|L|\varepsilon>1/2$, so $W>0$. Since the ideal miss probability is the weighted mean of the successor miss probabilities, averaging the inductive lower bounds at successors gives a lower bound $B=(1-\varepsilon)(1-I_n(L)-(n-1)\varepsilon)$ for the successful continuation, and since the immediate-stop term is nonnegative, $R_n(L)\geq(1-f(L))B$. We always have $B\leq1-\varepsilon$, even when $B$ is negative. The sign cases give \[ f(L)B\le \begin{cases} \varepsilon B\le\varepsilon(1-\varepsilon),&B\ge0,\\ 0\le\varepsilon(1-\varepsilon),&B<0. \end{cases} \] Subtracting the common upper bound from $B$ yields exactly the desired lower bound with $n\varepsilon$. The induction thus holds whether or not the failure probabilities at different histories are equal or independent. At the empty history with $n=T_0=T$, the ideal estimate gives $I_T([])\leq2m/2^T$, and expanding the product in the lower bound and discarding its nonnegative cross term gives $R_T([])\geq1-2m/2^T-T\varepsilon-\varepsilon$. This is the [acceptance guarantee of the formal tournament][src-tournament-runs], and it accounts for that theorem's additional verifier error. For a list-membership event, we use the perfect indicator $v(i)=\mathbf1_{\{i=s\}}$, in this analysis only; the same induction then starts from $1-I_0(L)$ without the factor $1-\varepsilon$ and yields $1-I_n(L)-n\varepsilon$, which is the list guarantee with no extra verifier error. This indicator is an analytical choice and is never supplied to the sampler as an oracle. ### E.2. Proof of bounded amplification and the retained-state assertion We prove Lemma E.1, including the measured-output contract used in §§5.2–5.4 and Appendix E.1. The first part proves the trial law and all-branch cap; the final part identifies a designated retained subsystem. The headline formal quantum bound uses the measured-label law. A separate formal theorem also supplies a retained original-register factor for a success condition defined on basis labels; the general-projector and physical correspondence qualifications are stated in the [formal-proof note](#record-formal-proof-note). Equality of measured probabilities alone does not give that factorization. **Lemma E.1 (bounded amplification with a retained state).** Fix real numbers $0<\gamma\leq1/2$ and $0<\eta<1/2$, a finite register interface, and a success subspace whose projector, reflection and measurement are available without input queries. These choices are independent of the unknown input. There is one procedure, depending only on these choices and using $A,A^{-1}$ as black boxes, with the following guarantees for every unitary preparation $A$ and every fixed input oracle. Let $p$ be the probability that measuring $A|0\rangle$ in the success subspace succeeds. Only uncontrolled calls to $A$ and $A^{-1}$ are required; the [coherent implementation](#upper-returned-register) puts control on fixed reflections. - The procedure returns failure or a state. On every successful return, one designated subsystem, with the same full register interface as $A$, contains the normalized success component of $A|0\rangle$, up to global phase. This subsystem includes the preparation's original workspace; trial records occupy separate auxiliary registers. - If $p\geq\gamma$, the failure probability is at most $\eta$. If $p=0$, the procedure fails with certainty. - On every branch, for every $p\in[0,1]$, the call cap is $O(\gamma^{-1/2}\ln(1/\eta))$ uses of $A$ or $A^{-1}$. The procedure and stopping rule are fixed without knowledge of $p$. In particular, if success with classical label $b$ has unamplified probability $p_b$, measuring the retained label returns $b$ with probability $(1-f)p_b/p$ for $p>0$, where $f$ is the amplifier’s failure probability. Its zero-iteration trial has positive probability, so $p>0$ implies $f<1$. This yields the [exact pivot law](#upper-quantum-tournament) used in §5.2. This is the successful-state assertion of OpenAI's Lemma 3.1. In both applications below, the success subspace is specified by a stored Boolean flag; any input-dependent work needed to compute that flag is already charged to $A$. We need a fixed bound on every branch, which is stronger than a bound on the expected cost. Boyer, Brassard, Høyer, and Tapp analyze a random number of Grover iterations when the number of solutions is unknown [Boyer, Brassard, Høyer and Tapp (1996), arXiv v1, §4, Lemma 2 and Theorem 3, pp. 3–4](https://arxiv.org/abs/quant-ph/9605034v1), and Brassard, Høyer, Mosca, and Tapp extend the underlying two dimensional analysis to arbitrary preparation algorithms [Brassard, Høyer, Mosca and Tapp (2000), arXiv v1, §2, Lemma 1 and equation (8), pp. 5–7](https://arxiv.org/abs/quant-ph/0005055v1). BBHT also discusses a timeout for the no-solution case. The contract needed here combines an all-branch cap with the exact conditional successful state of an arbitrary preparation, so §E.2 gives OpenAI's bounded construction in full. \Needspace{18\baselineskip} Let $\Pi$ be the orthogonal projection onto the success subspace, let $\psi=A|0\rangle$, and let $p=\|\Pi\psi\|^2$. First suppose $0 $$ G^j\psi =\sin((2j+1)\theta)g+\cos((2j+1)\theta)b, \qquad \Pr[\text{success after }j]=\sin^2((2j+1)\theta). $$ Projection onto success removes the $b$ term, so whenever success has nonzero probability the normalized result is $g$ or $-g$. This conclusion concerns the whole workspace, including any registers in which $A$ has recorded intermediate data, and so it is stronger than a statement about the probability of a success flag alone. At $p=0$ the state lies in the failure subspace, where the success reflection fixes it; since the reflection about $\psi$ also fixes $\psi$, every iterate has zero success probability. At $p=1$ the success reflection sends $\psi$ to $-\psi$, so every iterate remains a scalar multiple of $\psi$ in the success subspace. Both endpoint cases are thus settled without normalizing a zero component. This is the trial-count construction used in [Appendix A.3 of the exposition](/library/quartic/exposition/#amplification-schedule). The averaged failure bound follows below. The procedure has two integer parameters: the iteration-range size $M$ within one trial, and the maximum number $N$ of fresh trials. Use natural logarithms in the second expression: $$ M=\left\lceil\frac{10}{\sqrt\gamma}\right\rceil, \qquad N=\left\lceil\frac{\ln(1/\eta)}{\ln(40/31)}\right\rceil. $$ In one trial we set $j=0$ with probability $1/2$ and otherwise, with the remaining probability $1/2$, choose $j$ uniformly from $0,\ldots,M-1$; we then prepare $\psi$, apply $G^j$, and measure success. We run at most $N$ such trials on freshly initialized registers, stop at the first success, and return failure if none succeeds. Equivalently, each iteration count $j We control the randomized iteration count by the exact averaging identity of Boyer, Brassard, Høyer and Tapp [Boyer, Brassard, Høyer and Tapp (1996), §4, Lemma 2, p. 3], which strengthens the inequality in OpenAI's equation (9): $$ \frac1M\sum_{j=0}^{M-1}\sin^2((2j+1)\theta) =\frac12-\frac{\sin(4M\theta)}{4M\sin(2\theta)} \quad(M\geq1,\ \sin(2\theta)\ne0). $$ To prove it, we write $\sin^2 u=(1-\cos(2u))/2$. The difference between $\sin(4(j+1)\theta)$ and $\sin(4j\theta)$ is $2\sin(2\theta)\cos((4j+2)\theta)$, so summing this equality over $j=0,\ldots,M-1$ cancels every interior sine term and leaves $\sin(4M\theta)$. Dividing by the nonzero $2\sin(2\theta)$ gives the sum of the cosine terms, and substituting it into the sum of the squared sines and dividing by $M$ proves the identity. Multiplying through by $\sin(2\theta)$ gives a division-free identity that holds also at the endpoints; we use the displayed quotient only when its denominator is nonzero. Suppose now that $\gamma\leq p\leq1/2$. The sine addition formula and the definitions of $\theta,g,b$ give: $$ \sin(2\theta)=2\sqrt{p(1-p)}\geq\sqrt\gamma. $$ Indeed, $1-p\geq1/2$, so the square of the left side is $4p(1-p)\geq2p\geq\gamma$, and both sides are nonnegative. Since $M\geq10/\sqrt\gamma$, we obtain $M\sin(2\theta)\geq10$. Because every sine has absolute value at most one, the exact average above implies the slightly weaker equation (9) of the paper, which suffices: $$ \frac1M\sum_{j=0}^{M-1}\sin^2((2j+1)\theta) \geq\frac12-\frac{1}{2M|\sin(2\theta)|} \geq\frac9{20}. $$ Thus the half of the trial that chooses a uniform iteration count contributes at least $9/40$ to its success probability. If instead $p\geq1/2$, the half that chooses zero iterations contributes at least $p/2\geq1/4\geq9/40$. Since these two cases cover every $p\geq\gamma$, including $p=1$, a trial fails with probability at most $31/40$ whenever the promise $p\geq\gamma$ holds. For a fixed oracle input, each fresh trial has the same failure probability $f$, and the fresh choices and registers make the failures independent. Hence the probability of $N$ failures is $f^N\leq(31/40)^N\leq\eta$, where the last inequality follows by taking logarithms, since $N\ln(40/31)\geq\ln(1/\eta)$. If $p=0$, the endpoint argument above gives $f=1$, hence certain failure. On a successful branch, the state of the successful trial is $g$ up to global phase, whatever its iteration count. Earlier failed trials occupy separate registers, which we may discard once their outcomes are recorded or keep, since in either case the designated output register is in the pure state $g$ up to phase. Mixing over iteration counts and over the index of the first successful trial leaves the density operator $|g\rangle\langle g|$ unchanged, so conditioning on success introduces no bias into any measurement of that output state. This proves every correctness clause of Lemma E.1. **An explicit cap constant.** The following calculation gives a constant for the cap in Lemma E.1. The [returned-register proof](#upper-returned-register) then establishes the stronger subsystem assertion. The padded product charged by the implementation satisfies the following bound: $$ \operatorname{calls}(\gamma,\eta) \leq N(2M+1) \leq138\,\gamma^{-1/2}\ln(1/\eta). $$ For $x\geq1$, the derivative of $\ln x-2(x-1)/(x+1)$ is $(x-1)^2/(x(x+1)^2)\geq0$, and the expression vanishes at one; at $x=40/31$ this gives $\ln(40/31)\geq18/71\geq1/4$. Also $\ln2=\int_1^2u^{-1}\,du\geq1/2$, and consequently $N\leq4\ln(1/\eta)+1\leq6\ln(1/\eta)$. Since $M\leq10/\sqrt\gamma+1$ and $\sqrt\gamma\leq1$, we have $2M+1\leq23/\sqrt\gamma$, and multiplying the two bounds gives 138. The estimates are uniform, so the bound holds on every run, including runs whose success probability is small. A positive original success probability also makes the conditioning legitimate, because the zero-iteration half of each trial succeeds with probability at least $p/2>0$ and $N\geq1$; thus the total success probability is positive whenever $p>0$. At $p=0$ we assert certain failure and make no conditional-state assertion about a null event. **Strengthening from labels to a retained state.** We now interpret the retained registers. On a successful measured history, we route the entire original register of the first successful trial to a fixed output register, whose state is $g$ up to phase. The earlier unsuccessful registers, the iteration-count records and the chosen trial index are additional registers, and keeping all of them leaves the pure reduced state $|g\rangle\langle g|$ of the output register unchanged. If the history is retained coherently, the phase of each history can be absorbed into its auxiliary amplitude: after the fixed routing, the unnormalized successful component factors as $g\otimes\xi$, with $\|\xi\|^2$ equal to the success probability. This is a statement about a designated subsystem; it does not identify the whole enlarged workspace with the smaller vector $g$. A coherent implementation may run all $N$ trial registers and then route the first success, keeping the same padded cap, and it calls the preparation unitary only without control. To control a Grover iterate, we apply $A$ and $A^{-1}$ unconditionally, control only the fixed reflections $S_0,S_\chi$, and apply the minus sign as a phase on the true control. Writing $C(U)=|0\rangle\langle0|\otimes I+|1\rangle\langle1|\otimes U$ and $Z_c=|0\rangle\langle0|-|1\rangle\langle1|$, the controlled product is \[ (Z_c\otimes I)(I\otimes A)C(S_0)(I\otimes A^{-1})C(S_\chi) =|0\rangle\langle0|\otimes I+|1\rangle\langle1|\otimes G. \] On a false control the reflections are identities and $AA^{-1}=I$; on a true control the product is $G$. The iteration-count record therefore controls only input-independent gates. Every trial has a fixed schedule of preparation calls, and its success projection can be recorded coherently in an auxiliary flag. After routing, the common factor $g$ on every successful history gives the stated factorization, and the first trial alone gives total success probability at least $p/2$ when $p>0$. The successful-state assertion needs more than equality of label distributions. Write $|\pm\rangle=(|0\rangle\pm|1\rangle)/\sqrt2$. The vectors $$ |+\rangle\otimes|0\rangle \quad\hbox{and}\quad \frac{|0\rangle|0\rangle+|1\rangle|1\rangle}{\sqrt2} $$ give the same uniform computational-basis distribution on the first register. In the first vector that register is in the pure state $|+\rangle$, and in the second it has density matrix $I/2$, so measuring it in the $\{|+\rangle,|-\rangle\}$ basis distinguishes the two laws: the probability of $+$ is respectively $1$ and $1/2$. The example shows why the formal successful-label theorem certifies less than the full successful-state assertion, which the ordinary proof of Lemma E.1 just given establishes. ### E.3. Finite examples, query budgets and earlier search **The transition law at an active history.** For a pivot list $L$ with $|L| $$ \Pr[\mathrm{stop}\mid L]=f(L),\qquad \Pr[\mathrm{next}=i\mid L]=(1-f(L))\frac{w_i(L)}{W(L)}\quad(W(L)>0). $$ If $W(L)=0$, then $f(L)=1$. At $|L|=T$ the list is returned deterministically without another sample. Here $\gamma=1/(2m)$ and $\eta=\varepsilon$. The bound $f(L)\le\varepsilon$ is guaranteed where $W(L)/m\ge1/(2m)$; this holds before a dominant vertex is selected. We couple the real process with the ideal one on a common probability space. While their lists agree, let $f(L)$ be the failure probability of the amplified sampler for the common list. If $W>0$, we independently choose a possible ideal next pivot with distribution $w_i/W$ and a Bernoulli variable that reports failure with probability $f(L)$. On nonfailure both processes receive the chosen pivot; on failure the real process stops and the ideal one continues with its ordinary transitions. Each process then has the correct marginal distribution, because the real sampler succeeds with pivot $i$ with probability exactly $(1-f(L))w_i/W$. Only the auxiliary Bernoulli draw in this coupling is taken independent of the ideal pivot. The prescribed transition law suffices to give the real list its correct marginal. If $W=0$, the ideal process appends nothing and the real process stops with certainty, because $f(L)=1$; this defines the coupling at every agreed list. **An exact four-candidate example.** Let the candidates be $s,a,b,c$, so that $T=\lceil\log_2(4000)\rceil=12$ and $\varepsilon=1/12000$. In the following table, the entry in row $i$, column $j$ is the probability that comparison with $j$ returns $i$. | $a_{ij}$ | $s$ | $a$ | $b$ | $c$ | |---|---:|---:|---:|---:| | $s$ | $0$ | $1-\varepsilon$ | $1-\varepsilon$ | $1-\varepsilon$ | | $a$ | $\varepsilon$ | $0$ | $1$ | $0$ | | $b$ | $\varepsilon$ | $0$ | $0$ | $1$ | | $c$ | $\varepsilon$ | $1$ | $0$ | $0$ | The candidate $s$ is dominant, while the comparisons among the other three indices form a cycle: on $\{a,b\}$, $\{b,c\}$ and $\{c,a\}$ they return $a$, $b$ and $c$, respectively, so these three certain comparisons are inconsistent with every total ordering. If the first pivot is $a$, the weights become $$ (w_s,w_a,w_b,w_c)=(11999/12000,0,0,1), \qquad W=23999/12000. $$ The unamplified preparation succeeds with probability $W/4=23999/48000$. Conditioned on success, the next pivot is $s$ with probability $11999/23999$ and $c$ with probability $12000/23999$. Bounded amplification changes the probability of obtaining a sample and preserves these two conditional probabilities exactly. If the next pivot is $c$, the only remaining positive weight is $w_s=(11999/12000)^2$, so the following successful sample is $s$. The first-step total weight is $3\varepsilon$ if the pivot is $s$, and $2-\varepsilon$ for each of the other three pivots. Since the first pivot is uniform, its expected value is $$ \frac{3\varepsilon+3(2-\varepsilon)}4=\frac32 =\frac{4^2-4}{2\cdot4}. $$ This is the exact drift identity in a cyclic example, and the ideal process selects $s$ within three pivots with probability one: a first pivot $s$ succeeds immediately, and first pivots $b$ or $c$ follow from the displayed $a$ case by cyclic relabeling. The example illustrates the weight calculation and conditional law; it is neither a construction of the full addressed-certificate input nor a proof of the general tournament bound. To obtain fractional weights for losing candidates on the same four vertices, change only $a_{ab}=a_{ba}=1/2$. This is an abstract comparison-table variation, not a new claim about the board in §4.3. After pivot $a$ its weights and success probability are $$ (w_s,w_a,w_b,w_c)=(11999/12000,0,1/2,1),\qquad W=29999/12000,\qquad p=29999/48000. $$ The next successful pivot has law $$ (\Pr[s],\Pr[a],\Pr[b],\Pr[c]) =(11999,0,6000,12000)/29999. $$ Amplification preserves this entire conditional law, including the fractional losing weights. If the real sampler fails after the first pivot $a$, its returned list $[a]$ misses $s$; this failure is charged in the coupling in §5.2. If a successful continuation first yields $s$ and a later sampler fails, the returned list already contains $s$ and that later failure is not charged. The ideal process's certain selection in the preceding deterministic-cycle example is therefore not a certainty claim for the real stopped algorithm. The following refinements supplement the tournament of §§5.1–5.2. They retain its all-input cap and specify the finite law used in the formal correspondence. Here a preparation call means one use of a unitary or its inverse; a logical read is one abstract oracle operation in that unitary; a physical query is a call to the bit oracle. The compiler of Appendix E.5 charges at most two physical queries per logical read. For the exact accounting of the compiled circuit, let $c_{\mathrm{rd}}$ be the number of logical reads in a comparison, let $M_0=\lceil10\sqrt{2m}\rceil$, and keep $N=\lceil\ln(1/\varepsilon)/\ln(40/31)\rceil$. Since the compiler uses two physical bit queries per logical read, padding every stage to $T$ comparisons gives $$ B_{\mathrm{list}} =2T^2c_{\mathrm{rd}}N(2M_0+1) \leq6072\,c_{\mathrm{rd}}\sqrt m\,T^2\ln T. $$ Indeed, the call-cap estimate in [§E.2](#upper-amplification-proof) gives the intermediate bound $$ 276\,c_{\mathrm{rd}}\sqrt{2m}\,T^2\ln(1000T). $$ Since $T\geq2$, we have $\ln(1000T)\leq11\ln T$ (using $1000\leq2^{10}$), and $\sqrt{2m}\leq2\sqrt m$; multiplying the constants gives $276\cdot2\cdot11=6072$. The estimate bounds the actual padded product directly and does not infer a bound on that product from a smaller procedure's call count. When a comparison is given with $c$ ordinary bit queries, each such query is one logical read in this representation, so the same bound with $c_{\mathrm{rd}}=c$ proves the order asserted in Proposition 5.1. For the concrete construction, Appendix E.5 counts logical reads and physical queries separately. **Finite-law correspondence.** We can also express the list guarantee as a probability law on the finite set $$ \mathcal L_T=\{L:\ L\text{ is a list of candidates and }|L|\leq T\}. $$ There is one input-independent bounded sampler, with output law $\lambda_x$ on $\mathcal L_T$, such that for every input $x$, $\lambda_x(L)\geq0$, $\sum_L\lambda_x(L)=1$, and, for every dominant $s$, $$ \sum_{L:\,s\in L}\lambda_x(L) \geq1-\frac{2m}{2^T}-T\varepsilon. $$ The sampler is chosen before both $x$ and $s$, so it operates without knowing which vertex is dominant, and the indicator of membership of a particular $s$ appears only in the analysis. This is the bounded-list form of Proposition 5.1. Decoding and verification are given in §5.3, and [§E.1](#upper-continuation-induction) analyzes the variant used by the Lean proof, which verifies the listed candidates in sequence. Høyer, Mosca and de Wolf [Høyer, Mosca and de Wolf (2003), arXiv v2, §1, pp. 1–3, and §3, pp. 4–7] study search with imperfect subroutines, where each underlying Boolean predicate is computed correctly with probability at least $9/10$. Here the comparison of two nonwinning columns need not satisfy such a correctness guarantee for either orientation, since its probability may be $1/2$, or arbitrarily close to $1/2$, so their result does not directly turn these comparisons into a fixed tournament oracle. We therefore work with the comparison probabilities themselves; the final search, once an address has been fixed, uses exact Boolean tests. **Comparison with earlier search procedures.** The same organization into candidate generation, comparison and certificate checking appears in Ben-David and Kothari [Ben-David and Kothari (2026), §3, Lemma 5, pp. 3–5] and in Ambainis, Iraids and Kokainis [Ambainis, Iraids and Kokainis (2026), arXiv v2]; the preprint cites these two certificate-complexity separations as recent work whose comparison-based viewpoint is particularly relevant [OpenAI (2026), §1.1, p. 2]. Their comparison concerns certificate complexity $C$, the number of bits in a certificate, rather than randomized query complexity $R$, the cost of a bounded-error algorithm, and they search for a distinguished column by a procedure different from the fractional-weight theorem proved here. Dürr and Høyer's minimum-finding algorithm uses ordered table values and a decreasing rank [Dürr and Høyer (1999), Theorem 1 and Lemmas 1–2, pp. 1–2], and Mande, Paraashar and Saurabh give a quantum algorithm for finding a king with exact edge-direction queries [Mande, Paraashar and Saurabh (2023), Theorem 19, §4, pp. 30:11–30:13]. These are antecedents and comparisons; the fractional-weight argument we follow is the one in OpenAI's Proposition 3.2. In particular, the available comparisons need not be bounded-error evaluations of any fixed orientation. ### E.4. Reversible local tests **Adaptive lookup.** The pointer bound measures adaptive depth; it does not give a fixed set of only $\ell+1$ input coordinates on which the test depends. For one pointer test, the complete relevant coordinate set consists of the $\ell$ pointer bits and all $m$ bits of the target column, and each of them is essential when $\ell\geq1$. For a target bit, we set the pointer to that row, hold every other coordinate fixed and flip the selected bit; the test changes. For a pointer bit, we choose two pointer words differing only in that bit, which the pointer bijection sends to distinct rows, assign different Boolean values to those two target bits and hold all other physical coordinates fixed; changing the chosen pointer bit then changes the test. Thus the support is exactly $m+\ell$, although every evaluation path reads only $\ell+1$ bits. In the four-column example a pointer test has six essential coordinates and depth three. The preprint gives an adaptive depth bound [OpenAI (2026), Lemma 2.2, p. 6], so its bound is consistent with the larger support calculated here. **Coherent evaluation.** The final verifier searches over local tests in superposition. It needs one reversible evaluator controlled by the test index, including its inverse; a separate classical evaluation for each index would not specify that operation. Fix $(i,s)$ and hold the test label $e$ in a register. A single coherent implementation evaluates all tests on any superposition of labels, and in its retained-workspace form it acts as $$ \sum_{e\in E}\alpha_e\,|e\rangle|0_e\rangle \longmapsto \sum_{e\in E}\alpha_e\,|e\rangle|\psi_{e,y}\rangle, \tag{E.1} $$ where the coefficients $\alpha_e$ are arbitrary, each $\psi_{e,y}$ has norm one, and its output label equals $g_e(y;i,s)$ with certainty. Normalization of the whole state requires $\sum_e|\alpha_e|^2=1$, while the linear identity holds for all coefficients. The test workspaces may have index-dependent finite dimensions, embedded into one finite workspace, and their dimensions and initial states are fixed before the input is given. The index register stays unmeasured, so the controlled unitary has exactly the linear action (E.1). The index can become entangled with the final workspace state, which may depend on $y$ and remains available for inversion. **Proof and query count.** For each test we run its decision tree from (4.12). At every level we retain the earlier answers and compute the next queried location from them by an input-independent reversible operation (this is how the pointer lookup works), then query into a fresh answer register, keeping enough history to make each update reversible. A leaf determines the test output exactly, and we pad shorter branches to the common depth $q_*$ with inactive reads. A controlled bit read costs two ordinary oracle calls: we load the bit into a temporary register, use it conditionally, and query again to clear that register, retaining the queried coordinate until this second call. The two calls still occur when the control is false and cancel on that branch. The basis calculation extends linearly to superposed coordinates and controls. Hence all branches have a common physical query cap $2q_*$. The entire construction is controlled by $e$, so its action is the direct sum of the individual test unitaries and linearity gives (E.1) for arbitrary complex coefficients. Distinct index blocks remain orthogonal, and the output in each block is the correct test value. This proves the arbitrary-index coherent part of OpenAI’s Lemma 2.2, with retained workspace and at most $2(\ell+1)$ ordinary bit queries for $m\geq4$. The verifier of §5.3 may use the retained-workspace evaluator (E.1). An optional stronger interface resets the work registers by a compute–copy–uncompute step. Controlled query-free gates prepare the fixed index-dependent starting states from a common all-zero ancilla and restore that convention at the end. We apply the implementation in (E.1), XOR its exact output label into a separate target bit, and apply the full inverse implementation. Since the computed output is certain in each index block, copying it leaves that block's workspace unchanged, so the inverse restores the starting state and gives $$ |e\rangle|b\rangle|0_{\rm work}\rangle \longmapsto |e\rangle|b\mathbin\oplus g_e(y;i,s)\rangle|0_{\rm work}\rangle \tag{E.2} $$ with at most $4q_*$ physical queries. By linearity, (E.2) holds on arbitrary superpositions of the label and target. The certainty of each test value is essential here. The noisy decoder of [Appendix G.2](#forr_coherent) instead retains its workspace, as its output may be a superposition of correct and incorrect labels. The formal construction theorem states the retained-workspace form (E.1), and we derive the reset-workspace interface (E.2) from it here as a corollary. Uniform-index evaluation is a special case of (E.1): we prepare the input-independent state $K^{-1/2}\sum_e|e\rangle$ and run the controlled evaluator. If $h$ tests fail, a failed test is observed with probability $h/K$, because the index blocks are orthogonal and each test is exact. Thus the failure-detection probability is zero when all tests pass and at least $1/K$ for a nonwinner at any proposed address. The search in §5.3 uses the evaluator and its inverse with the retained work registers. A theorem only about this uniform distribution would not imply the arbitrary-index action (E.1). ### E.5. Physical queries and the explicit logarithmic bound For the address decoder take $q=\lceil16\delta^{-2}\ln(r/\varepsilon)\rceil$ independent trials per bit. Each uses $k$ abstract reads, giving $rqk$ reads before controlled-oracle overhead. The circuit retains the count and the thresholded label. [Repetition bound][src-repetitions]. Since the algorithm uses addresses and candidate indices in superposition, we spell out their coherent implementation. The input oracle acts on a coordinate register, an answer bit, and workspace by sending $|u,b,z\rangle$ to $|u,b\mathbin\oplus x_u,z\rangle$, and a superposed address is an allowed coordinate state for this same oracle. Computing the coordinate from already stored labels is an input-independent reversible operation, so it costs no query. A pointer is stored in $\ell$ separate input bits, and reading them, reversibly forming the indicated coordinate, and querying that coordinate costs $\ell+1$ ordinary queries before any uncomputation. The [two-query construction in Appendix E.4](#AC-coherent) implements a controlled read: load the selected bit, use it under the desired control, and unload it while preserving the coordinate. It works on superposed coordinates, and even disabled branches execute the cancelling pair. We now apply that common physical cap to the whole algorithm. An exact adaptive local test is made coherent by retaining its previous query answers, using them to compute the next coordinate, and padding its computation to the fixed maximum depth; at a branch that has halted early, the remaining controlled reads are disabled. Every gate thus remains a fixed function of the retained labels, and the query count is at most a constant times the decision-tree depth. Reversing the full circuit gives the inverse at the same cost. These operations implement, within the ordinary bit-oracle model, the coherent comparisons and their inverses, the uniform local-test preparation, and the reflections used by amplification. The load–use–unload construction above implements one logical read with at most two ordinary queries. Composing these read implementations adds their caps, and reversing their logical circuit uses the same number of reads, so a circuit of $q$ logical reads is implemented with at most $2q$ ordinary bit queries, also when its indices are superposed. For classical-label continuations, one may measure the complete computational-basis state and then apply a basis permutation taking the known outcome back to the fixed initial basis state, a reset with no query cost. This reset reproduces the classical output law exactly, but because it measures the state it differs from returning the unmeasured original quantum state. The final bound thus concerns the same total input function on every bit string, with a syntactic maximum over branches. It bounds the worst-case number of queries, with no averaging, and it gives no bound on the number of elementary gates or the amount of workspace, which are free in the stated query model. Before simplifying asymptotically, we state an exact finite budget that records the padding and the repetitions together with the compilation constants. An amplification call is one preparation or its inverse; convert calls to ordinary bit queries by multiplying by the implemented preparation cap. The quantities $c_{\mathrm{rd}}$ in Appendix E.3 and $c_c$ below count logical reads in one comparison, each costing at most two bit queries. The same two-query compiler applies to the decoder and local-test counts $a$ and $c_0$. The final budget $B_{k,t}$ counts physical input-bit queries and already includes these factors. The finite budget uses the following parameters; the first four count logical operations, before the two-query compilation factor. \Needspace{17\baselineskip} | Symbol | Definition | Role | | --- | --- | --- | | $q$ | $\lceil16\delta^{-2}\ln(r/\varepsilon)\rceil$ | Forrelation repetitions for error $\varepsilon/r$ | | $a$ | $rqk$ | Reads for one address | | $c_c$ | $2a+2(2t+1)$ | Reads for one comparison | | $c_0$ | $\max\{3,2t+1\}$ | Reads for one exact local test | | $N$ | $\lceil\ln(1/\varepsilon)/\ln(40/31)\rceil$ | Amplification trials | | $M_0$ | $\lceil10\sqrt{2m}\rceil$ | Tournament iteration-range size | | $M_1$ | $\lceil10\sqrt K\rceil$ | Verifier iteration-range size | The physical query budget is $$ B_{k,t} =T\bigl[2N(2M_0+1)T c_c\bigr] +T\bigl[2a+2N(2M_1+1)c_0\bigr]. $$ The first bracket is one tournament stage: at most $N$ trials, at most $2M_0+1$ preparation or inverse calls per trial, at most $T c_c$ abstract reads per such call, and two bit queries per read. Every stage is padded to the maximum history length $T$, and there are at most $T$ stages. The second bracket is one verifier, which uses $2a$ bit queries on its fresh address decoder and then runs the amplified local-test search with its corresponding trial and iteration bounds; at most $T$ candidates are verified. Every random branch and every off-promise input obeys this same integer budget. By the preceding construction and error analysis, this integer budget bounds $Q(F_{k,m})$ for every realizing circuit with the stated local tests, so correctness is established before we substitute the size of the particular circuit chosen in §4. The conversion factors in this budget are convenient upper bounds, and the earlier expression with $h$ comparisons at history length $h$ gives the same asymptotic result with less padding. For the circuit fixed in §4, the same budget gives logarithmic exponent six: there is a positive integer $C_k$, depending only on $k$, such that the particular Forrelation circuit used in the construction satisfies $$ Q(F_{k,4^t})\leq C_k\,2^t(2t)^6 \qquad(t\geq1). $$ We deliberately enlarge logarithms and square roots to obtain one convenient fixed power, six; this is not an optimization claim. The size arithmetic below shows that $C_k$ is independent of $t$, starting from the finite budget already proved. Put $\tau=\ell=2t$ and $u=2^t$, so $m=u^2$, $r=20\tau$, and $\tau\geq2$. For the chosen circuit we set $C_F(k)=200(k+1)^2$, the circuit-size constant of the source, so that $S\leq C_F(k)m\tau^2$. We define $R_k=1+1920000\cdot2^{10k}$, $C_c(k)=40R_kk+4$ and $C_K(k)=42+20C_F(k)$, each independent of $t$. First, $1000<2^{10}$ implies $T\leq\tau+10\leq6\tau$, hence $1/\varepsilon=1000T\leq6000\tau$. Using $\ln(1/\varepsilon)\leq1/\varepsilon$ and $\ln(40/31)\geq1/4$, the ceiling defining $N$ gives $N\leq4/\varepsilon+1\leq24001\tau$, and likewise $r/\varepsilon\leq120000\tau^2$. The decoder's repetition count is at most $16\cdot2^{10k}\ln(r/\varepsilon)+1$, hence at most $R_k\tau^2$, and so $a=rqk\leq20R_kk\tau^3$. Since the remaining comparison cost $2(\tau+1)$ is at most $4\tau^3$, we get $c_c\leq C_c(k)\tau^3$. Second, the formula for $K$ gives $K=2m-1+20\tau(S+2)\leq C_K(k)m\tau^3$, since the circuit term is at most $20C_F(k)m\tau^3$, the $2m$ term is at most $2m\tau^3$, and $40\tau\leq40m\tau^3$. Because $C_K(k)\geq1$ and $\tau\geq1$, this implies $\sqrt K\leq C_K(k)u\tau^2$, and together with $\sqrt{2m}\leq2u$ the ceilings give $2M_0+1\leq43u$ and $2M_1+1\leq23C_K(k)u\tau^2$. Finally, $c_0\leq3\tau$. We insert these bounds into the two brackets of $B_{k,t}$. One tournament stage is at most $48002\cdot258\,C_c(k)u\tau^5$, with factors twice $24001\tau$, then $43u$, then $6\tau\,C_c(k)\tau^3$, and its at most $6\tau$ stages contribute at most $6(48002\cdot258\,C_c(k))u\tau^6$. One verifier is at most $(40R_kk+48002\cdot69\,C_K(k))u\tau^4$, where the decoder cost $2a$ has been enlarged using $u,\tau\geq1$ and the search term has factors twice $24001\tau$, then $23C_K(k)u\tau^2$, then $3\tau$; multiplying by $T\leq6\tau$ and enlarging $\tau^5$ to $\tau^6$ gives the remaining contribution. Thus we may take $C_k=6(48002\cdot258\,C_c(k))+6(40R_kk+48002\cdot69\,C_K(k))$, which is the deliberately loose [constant of the formal budget][src-budget-constant]. This completes the quantum half of the family bounds, with the same chosen circuit that appears in the total function. The bound holds for each fixed $k$, and its proof uses only the fixed-$k$ estimates above, with no randomized lower bound.

rows.text: ### F.1. Inputs and partial functions Let $I$ be a finite set of coordinates and put $\mathcal X_I=\{0,1\}^I$. A partial Boolean function is a domain $\mathcal D\subseteq\mathcal X_I$ together with a map $f:\mathcal D\to\{0,1\}$. Equivalently, it is a map from $\mathcal X_I$ to $\{\mathrm{none},\mathrm{some}(0),\mathrm{some}(1)\}$: the value $\mathrm{none}$ means that no correctness requirement is imposed at that input. Taking the defined inputs as the domain and their unique Boolean labels as the values reverses the translation. An algorithm for a partial function is one algorithm that works on every promised input. Its behavior outside $\mathcal D$ can be arbitrary, but its query cap still applies there. In particular, the program, its random probabilities and its quantum starting state cannot be chosen after learning the input. This separates the quantifiers “there is an algorithm, for every input” from the incorrect “for every input, there is an algorithm.” A total function is the special case $\mathcal D=\mathcal X_I$. An algorithm for $f$ may output either bit outside $\mathcal D$; the function is defined only on $\mathcal D$. The [theorem index](https://github.com/wcook04/quartic-query-lean/blob/v1.0.2/docs/proof_index.md#def-partial) links the corresponding formal definitions. ### F.2. Deterministic trees and finite random mixtures A deterministic query tree has a Boolean label at every leaf and a coordinate $i\in I$ at every internal node. At that node, the next subtree is selected by the input bit $x_i$. Write $T(x)$ for the resulting output. We charge the syntactic depth \[ \operatorname{depth}(\operatorname{leaf}(b))=0, \qquad \operatorname{depth}(\operatorname{query}(i,T_0,T_1)) =1+\max\{\operatorname{depth}(T_0),\operatorname{depth}(T_1)\}. \] Repeated queries are charged again. A repeated query can create a branch inconsistent with answers already obtained; syntactic depth still counts it. Such branches can be removed by carrying the previously known answers down the tree and replacing a repeated query by its consistent child. Evaluation is unchanged and depth cannot increase. In the resulting tree every path has a consistent input assignment, so its depth is attained on an input. Thus this convention preserves the minimum worst-case query cost. The predicate $D_{\leq}(f,q)$, the [deterministic budget test][def-DLe] of the formal statement, means that there is one tree $T$ of depth at most $q$ with $T(x)=f(x)$ for every $x\in\mathcal D$. Define \[ D(f)=\min\{q\in\mathbb N:D_{\leq}(f,q)\}. \] A randomized program is a finite list of trees $T_1,\ldots,T_s$ with real weights $p_j>0$ and $\sum_jp_j=1$. It selects $j$ independently of the input and runs $T_j$. Its depth is $\max_j\operatorname{depth}(T_j)$, and its success probability on a promised input is $\sum_{j:T_j(x)=f(x)}p_j$. We have omitted trees assigned probability zero. Since the weights sum to one, $s\ge1$. Write $R_{\leq}(f,q)$ for the existence of such a mixture with depth at most $q$ and success at least $2/3$ on every promised input; this is the [randomized budget test][def-RLe] of the formal statement. The randomized complexity is \[ R(f)=\min\left\{q\in\mathbb N:\ \exists(p_j,T_j)_{j=1}^s\quad \begin{array}{l} p_j>0,\quad \sum_jp_j=1,\quad \operatorname{depth}(T_j)\leq q\ \text{for every }j,\\[2pt] \displaystyle \sum_{j:T_j(x)=f(x)}p_j\geq\frac23\ \text{for every }x\in\mathcal D \end{array}\right\}. \] This is the distribution-over-trees convention in [Buhrman and de Wolf, §§3.1–3.2, printed pp. 5–6][BDW02]. For fixed $I$ and $q$, there are finitely many trees of depth at most $q$: at depth zero there are two leaves, and a larger tree chooses a coordinate and two smaller trees. Fixing all random choices of a capped randomized algorithm selects one such tree; grouping outcomes that select the same tree gives a finite mixture. Conversely, a finite distribution can be selected with finitely many biased coin choices before reading the input. These observations preserve the cap and pointwise success probabilities. They use the allowed arbitrary real biases; a separate restriction to a bounded number of fair coin flips requires care at an exact error threshold. The minima exist. Query all coordinates once, then output the prescribed value on the promise and any bit elsewhere. This tree has depth at most $|I|$, including when $I$ is empty. A tree is also a one-element randomized mixture. The admissible budgets are therefore nonempty upward-closed subsets of $\mathbb N$, giving \[ R(f)\leq q\iff R_{\leq}(f,q),\qquad D(f)\leq q\iff D_{\leq}(f,q),\qquad R(f)\leq D(f)\leq |I|. \] **Formal representation.** In the source these minima are natural-number infima. A tree that reads every coordinate gives an admissible query count, so each set is nonempty and its infimum is its minimum. The constructor-by-constructor translation to the decision trees of complexitylib preserves both evaluation and depth, and for total functions it gives the [exact equality of the two deterministic complexities][src-complexitylib]. ### F.3. The oracle and finite workspaces For nonempty $I$, use a finite-dimensional complex Hilbert space with basis $|i,b,z\rangle$, where $i\in I$, $b\in\{0,1\}$, and $z$ is a workspace label. The workspace label set is finite and nonempty. All gates are input-independent linear isometries of this space. In finite equal dimensions an isometry is surjective and hence unitary. No bound on gate count, gate synthesis or workspace size is part of query complexity. The bit oracle acts by \[ O_x|i,b,z\rangle=|i,b\oplus x_i,z\rangle. \] It permutes an orthonormal basis and is its own inverse, so it is unitary. With the answer bit in $|-\rangle=(|0\rangle-|1\rangle)/\sqrt2$, one call multiplies the amplitude at $i$ by $(-1)^{x_i}$. With the answer bit in $|+\rangle=(|0\rangle+|1\rangle)/\sqrt2$, the same call acts as the identity; this is an idle bit query. For a converse that preserves one query, retain the control bit: define \[ P_x|i,b,z\rangle=(-1)^{b x_i}|i,b,z\rangle. \] If $H_b$ denotes a Hadamard on that bit, $H_bP_xH_b=O_x$, because $HZH=X$ on the answer bit when $x_i=1$ and $HIH=I$ when $x_i=0$. Thus the bit oracle and this **controlled phase oracle** are interchangeable at one call. A bare oracle $|i\rangle\mapsto(-1)^{x_i}|i\rangle$, without a control or idle facility, does not justify the converse: complementing every input bit changes that oracle only by a global sign. The distinction appears in [de Wolf, v6, §2.4, printed pp. 17–18, footnote 7 and Exercise 10][DW26]. The finite coordinate projector onto a basis subset $S$ is $\Pi_S$. A two-outcome measurement uses the branches $\Pi_S\psi$ and $(I-\Pi_S)\psi$. These span orthogonal subspaces and have squared norms summing to $\|\psi\|^2$. General binary orthogonal projectors can be put into this form by an input-independent change of orthonormal basis. An arbitrary normalized pure starting state can likewise be prepared from a chosen basis vector by a free unitary. These are the pure-state, finite-projective-measurement conventions described in [Buhrman and de Wolf, §3.3][BDW02] and [de Wolf, §§1.2.2 and 2.1.2][DW26]. Mixed initial states and finite generalized measurements can be represented with a finite ancillary space by purification and measurement dilation, but that ordinary model comparison is not a new formal theorem claimed here. The source represents the nonempty workspace by $\operatorname{Fin}(w+1)$ for $w\in\mathbb N$. ### F.4. Measurements, probability mass and the quantum minimum A source program is a finite expression made from four operations: return a Boolean answer; apply a unitary and continue; apply the oracle and continue; or measure a basis subset and follow one of two continuations. Its query cap is zero at a return, unchanged at a unitary, increased by one at a query, and the maximum of the two continuation caps at a measurement. Even a branch of probability zero for a particular input is charged by this syntactic cap. This makes the cap independent of the input, including off-promise inputs. Keep branch vectors unnormalized. For example, if a normalized state splits into two orthogonal branches of squared norms $1/4$ and $3/4$, their conditional states have norm one, but their contributions to an output probability still carry weights $1/4$ and $3/4$. The recursion below retains those weights in the branch vectors themselves. For program $A$, input $x$, vector $\psi$, and output bit $b$, let $M_A(x,\psi,b)$ denote its output mass. A return of $a$ contributes $\|\psi\|^2$ if $a=b$ and zero otherwise. A gate or query substitutes the transformed vector into the continuation. A measurement with continuations $A_1,A_0$ gives \[ M_A(x,\psi,b) =M_{A_1}(x,\Pi_S\psi,b) +M_{A_0}(x,(I-\Pi_S)\psi,b). \] For every starting vector, including the zero vector, \[ M_A(x,\psi,b)\geq0, \qquad M_A(x,\psi,1)+M_A(x,\psi,0)=\|\psi\|^2. \] Both claims follow by structural induction. At a return they are immediate. A unitary or oracle preserves the norm, so the induction hypothesis applies after that transformation. At a measurement, nonnegativity is preserved by addition; summing over the two output bits and applying the induction hypotheses gives $\|\Pi_S\psi\|^2+\|(I-\Pi_S)\psi\|^2=\|\psi\|^2$. Thus a normalized starting vector gives an ordinary probability distribution. Renormalizing each branch and then adding its mass without restoring the branch probability would fail this identity. On a nonempty coordinate set, a budget $q$ is admissible when one normalized starting state and one program of cap at most $q$ achieve the required success on every promised input. To include the empty coordinate set, where a constant answer needs no query register, we also allow the constant case explicitly. The resulting condition, the [quantum budget condition](https://github.com/wcook04/quartic-query-lean/blob/v1.0.2/docs/proof_index.md#def-QLe), is \[ \begin{split} &\bigl[\exists b\in\{0,1\}\ \forall x\in\mathcal D,\ f(x)=b\bigr]\\ &\quad\lor\ \bigl[\exists w,\psi_0,A:\ \|\psi_0\|=1,\ \operatorname{cap}(A)\leq q,\ \forall x\in\mathcal D,\ M_A(x,\psi_0,f(x))\geq2/3\bigr]. \end{split} \] Every existential choice in the second clause precedes the input quantifier. The first clause permits a constant answer with no query register. It is redundant when a nonempty query register is available, but necessary for this representation when $I=\varnothing$: there is then one possible input and no unit vector in the zero-dimensional indexed query space. Every partial Boolean function on that singleton input set is constant on its promise, including an empty promise. The clause therefore supplies exactly the expected zero-query behavior. Define $Q(f)=\min\{q\in\mathbb N:q\text{ is admissible for }f\}$. To see that this minimum exists, simulate a deterministic tree. On a nonempty coordinate set, prepare the basis state for its next query with answer bit zero, query once, measure the answer bit, and follow the corresponding child. Each child has its own input-independent basis permutation preparing its next coordinate. The classical history is already encoded by the program branch. Induction on the tree gives the same output and no larger cap. Constant trees, including those on empty coordinates, use the first clause. Hence \[ Q(f)\leq D(f)\leq |I|, \qquad Q(f)\leq q\iff q\text{ is admissible for }f. \] As in the classical case, nonemptiness and monotonicity of admissible budgets justify the source's natural-number infimum. ### F.5. Renaming coordinates and deferring measurements Two bridges connect the models of Appendix F.3–F.4 with conventional formulations. Renaming coordinates leaves every complexity unchanged. Deferring measurements turns a program with cap $T$ into a fixed sequence of $T$ controlled phase queries between input-independent gates, with the same acceptance mass for every input and every starting vector; the final states need not agree. A bijection $e:I\to J$ changes only the names of the queried bits. If $f^e(y)=f(y\circ e)$, relabel every classical query node by $e$. Evaluation and depth are unchanged. For quantum programs the corresponding basis permutation relabels the query register, conjugates each gate and projector, and transports the initial vector. It intertwines the two bit oracles; induction on the program preserves both output masses and the cap. Applying the inverse permutation gives \[ R(f^e)=R(f),\qquad D(f^e)=D(f),\qquad Q(f^e)=Q(f). \] This is why structured coordinates in the construction can be replaced by $\operatorname{Fin}(n)$ in (1.1). The deferred-measurement bridge has a more specific guarantee than a statement that measurements may be postponed. For $A$ on $\operatorname{Fin}(n)$ with cap at most $T$, the source constructs a larger finite workspace, an input-independent entry isometry $E$, a fixed sequence of $T$ controlled phase queries separated by input-independent gates, and a final accepting projector $\Pi$. If $\mathcal H$ is the original state space and $\mathcal K$ the enlarged one, the induction also retains an isometry $J:\mathcal H\to\mathcal K$ satisfying $P_x'J=JP_x$. This oracle-compatible embedding, together with $E:\mathcal H\to\mathcal K$, is the strengthened invariant needed to prepend a query. The mass identity is \[ \left\|\Pi\,U_TP'_xU_{T-1}\cdots P'_xU_0E\psi\right\|^2 =M_A(x,\psi,1) \quad\text{for every }x\text{ and every }\psi. \] Here $P'_x$ is the controlled phase oracle on the enlarged workspace. The compatible embedding lets a prepended query act on the original state before the continuation begins; acceptance mass alone would not specify that action. An output branch accepts either its whole space or the empty set; padding queries preserve its norm, although they may change its state. For an input-independent gate, compose it with the entry map. At a measurement, if $E_1,E_0$ are the continuation entry maps, enter their direct sum through \[ \psi\longmapsto E_1\Pi_S\psi\oplus E_0(I-\Pi_S)\psi. \] This is an isometry, the gates and oracle act block by block, and acceptance masses add. For a query followed by a continuation, write $L:\mathcal H\to\mathcal K$ for its entry map (the map denoted $E$ above), and let $J:\mathcal H\to\mathcal K$ be its compatible embedding. Extend the isometry $J\phi\mapsto LH_b\phi$ from $\operatorname{range}(J)$ to an input-independent unitary $Z$ of the larger finite space. The extension exists because the two isometric ranges have equal dimension, as do their orthogonal complements. Starting through $JH_b$, one controlled phase query followed by $Z$ gives \[ ZP'_xJH_b\psi=LH_bP_xH_b\psi=LO_x\psi. \] The remaining $T-1$ queries run the continuation. The output case allows both measurement continuations to be padded to the same $T$, so structural induction gives the displayed mass identity with exactly $T$ queries. This padding preserves acceptance mass; the source does not require a completed branch's state to remain unchanged. This is the [fixed-sequence normal form][src-fixed-sequence] of the formalization. The two programs have the same accepting mass for all inputs and starting vectors. To reuse the final workspace one also needs a result about the final state (§E.2). Conversely, a finite bit-query sequence followed by a binary basis measurement is already a finite adaptive program: write its gates and queries as successive constructors. This general bridge connects the formal model to the fixed-sequence model used by the Lean dependency proving the universal upper bound. The independent printed derivation is in [Appendix A](#R3-A-RESULT). The finite examples of Appendix F.6 only illustrate the model conventions. ### F.6. Exact small examples The following exact calculations distinguish the query-cap, promise and error conventions. **Zero queries.** For a finite coordinate set, \[ R(f)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad D(f)=0 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad Q(f)=0 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad f\text{ is constant on its promise}. \] A constant answer proves one direction. For the converse, a zero-depth tree is a leaf, and a zero-depth random mixture has an input-independent output distribution. A zero-query quantum program also has input-independent masses: induct on its syntax, observing that a query constructor is impossible at cap zero and that gates, projections and branch rules are input-independent. If both Boolean labels occurred on the promise, correctness would require the same distribution to put mass at least $2/3$ on each label. Their masses sum to one, a contradiction. **One-bit identity.** For $f(x)=x_0$, both labels occur, so zero queries are impossible. One classical query returns the bit, and one quantum bit query on $|0,0,z\rangle$ followed by measuring the answer does the same. Thus \[ D(\mathrm{id}_1)=R(\mathrm{id}_1)=Q(\mathrm{id}_1)=1. \] \Needspace{12\baselineskip} **Two-bit OR and the endpoint $2/3$.** With equal probabilities choose one of three trees: output $1$, query and output $x_0$, or query and output $x_1$. The maximum depth is one, and the exact successes are | Input | OR | Constant $1$ | Output $x_0$ | Output $x_1$ | Success probability | | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | | $00$ | 0 | 1 | 0 | 0 | $2/3$ | | $01$ | 1 | 1 | 0 | 1 | $2/3$ | | $10$ | 1 | 1 | 1 | 0 | $2/3$ | | $11$ | 1 | 1 | 1 | 1 | $1$ | Zero queries are impossible. A deterministic one-query tree reads at most one coordinate, and cannot distinguish $00$ from the input whose other bit alone is $1$. Therefore \[ R(\mathrm{OR}_2)=1,\qquad D(\mathrm{OR}_2)=2. \] The inclusive threshold is material. Under the uniform distribution on $00,01,10$, every deterministic tree of depth at most one is correct on at most two of those three inputs. A mixture therefore has average success at most $2/3$, and cannot succeed with probability strictly greater than $2/3$ at every input. Requiring strict success above $2/3$ raises the classical cap to two. This argument also shows that finite sampling with arbitrary biases cannot simply be replaced by a fixed finite number of fair flips. The six one-query response functions are $0,1,x_0,1-x_0,x_1,1-x_1$; only $1,x_0,x_1$ are correct on two of $00,01,10$. Attaining average success $2/3$ therefore permits only these three. If their weights are $a,b,c$, the pointwise requirements are $b+c\ge2/3$, $a+c\ge2/3$ and $a+b\ge2/3$. Together with $a+b+c=1$, they force $a=b=c=1/3$. Those probabilities are not dyadic. The selector can also be sampled quantumly before any input query: prepare three orthogonal selector states with amplitudes $1/\sqrt3$, measure the selector using binary coordinate projections, and follow the corresponding constant or one-query program. A larger finite workspace holds the selector. The branch cap is one and the success table is unchanged, so $Q(\mathrm{OR}_2)=1$ as well. The upper bound on one-query **classical** success above is not a quantum optimal-success statement. **A one-sided promise on one bit.** On one bit, let $f(1)=1$ and leave $f(0)$ undefined. The constant-one algorithm has success one on the entire promise and zero query cost. Consequently $D(f)=R(f)=Q(f)=0$. Replacing its undefined value by false creates one-bit identity, whose three complexities are one. Extending the domain thus changes the query complexities in this example. Empty promises and partial functions on empty coordinate sets also have all three complexities zero. For every one of these examples, a chosen program's cap remains a bound on its off-promise executions. **Two-bit parity checks the cost convention.** For $x_0\oplus x_1$, take the uniform law on all four inputs. Any deterministic one-query tree is then correct with probability exactly $1/2$. The same is true on average for every mixture, ruling out pointwise success $2/3$; reading both bits is exact. A quantum algorithm instead prepares \[ \frac{|0\rangle+|1\rangle}{\sqrt2}\otimes|-\rangle. \] After one bit query and a Hadamard on the index register, its index amplitudes are \[ \frac{(-1)^{x_0}+(-1)^{x_1}}2\quad\text{and}\quad \frac{(-1)^{x_0}-(-1)^{x_1}}2. \] Measuring the index returns the parity exactly. The zero-query argument excludes cost zero, so \[ D(\mathrm{XOR}_2)=R(\mathrm{XOR}_2)=2, \qquad Q(\mathrm{XOR}_2)=1. \] The supplied 1998 version of Beals et al., §3.2 and the paragraph following Proposition 6.4, measures classical randomized cost by **expected** queries. Its exact classical parity figure must not be imported into the present cap model. The later author-hosted journal version changes §3.2 to worst-case query cost and states the corresponding classical parity bound after Proposition 6.4. We cite these separately as [Beals et al. (1998)][BBCMW98] and [Beals et al. (2001)][BBCMW01]. The calculation above directly establishes the two-bit values needed here.
